1.0Overview

The Managalas Plateau in Oro Province is home to 10,000 villagers,
consisting of over 100 sub-clan groups (buy law the sub- clans own all land
and forest resources) who live in smail village communities surrounded by
subsistence gardens. The Managalas Plateau is an striking example of Papua
New Guinea's rich biodiversity and one of the areas highlighted in the 1992
Conservation Needs Assessment Report addressing critical issues
concerning conservation and sustainable development in Papua New Guinea.
The area encompasses of 300,000 hectares from alphine heaths at 12,000
feet to multi-altitude forest along with both primary and secondary lowland
rainforests. 10,000 villagers live in small communities surrounded by
subsistence gardens along a snake-like chains winding through a 2500-foot
plateau in the centre of the region. The Managalas Plateau is bounded by
vast forested ranges on all sides, the Owen Stanley's to the South and West,
the Sibium Ranges to the South East and Mount Lamington and the
Hydrographers to the North and East.

Papua New Guinea is fortunate that community-based tenurial systems on
rights to forests, land, water and fisheries are recognised by the national
government and protected under law. In addition the PNG Conservation
Areas Act provides a ready legal mechanisms for local groups to develop and
register locally defined resource management guidelines with the national
government.

The main aim of the project is to provide legai and technica! support to the
communities on the Managalas piateau in the preparation and development of
a proposal to the national government to designate the area as a conservation
area. The idea came from the cian groups on the piateau during the pianning
process for the Managalas Conservation Area Project because they want to
protect the area from industrial logging and other large-scale environmentally
destructive operations. The people on the plateau in their group discussion
first agreed the mapping project should be created in the organisation so
should had to do the boundary mapping to have the plateau secured or
protected from being destroyed by any giant companies such as mining or
logging. The group discussion went on from various clan groups in the plateau
for some times and there were disagreements from other clan groups, which
they don't agree for the project to be created. This sort of disagreement has
also gone on for a while however the group who have been working in the
programme were the one’s who were doing most of the awareness and
educating the people of the plateau the purpose of the boundary mapping that
it will not affect their livelihood. For this reasons the mapping project truly a
local initiative, which the project partners have supported because it is model
that can be replicated in other communities in Papua New Guinea.

The transferring of mapping technology to the Managalas people have enable
them to communicate their perception of land rights and ownership and

=== page 4 ===
resource management system with the government and outside companies. It
has also contributed to the process on resolving land disputes in the area and
in a way It has empowered them to make discussions on how best they can
manage their resources for their use now and for the benefit of the future

generations.
The main objectives of the project are as follows;

1. To asses the spatial interactions between communities and resources in
the proposed Managalas conservation area.

2. To document customary rights of local communities with regard to land
and natural resources and to gather and guard traditional knowledge.

3. To identify key decision-makers (clan elders) in relation to land and
resource use and management.

4. To identify and resolve boundary disputes between different landowners.

5. To facilitate community participation in the management of the proposed
conservation area.

6. To increase local capacity deals with external threats.

2.1. Planning and Recruitment of Project Team

CELCOR with regard to the implementation of the project was to liase with the
community based organizations in the project area to appoint the field
mapping team to carry out the project activities. The project is implemented
along participatory lines so it was important to have people on each side of
the plateau represented on the mapping team. It was agreed that Kingsford
Nichoi (East) and Malchus Kajia (West) would continue to be the field
coordinators. There are now two working teams set up in the plateau One on
the Eastern side and the other on the Western side of the plateau. The
Eastern side is made up of a Field mapping coordinator and two assistants
and the Western side is made up of a Field mapping coordinator and four
assistants due to a bigger area. The team of eight members working as
boundary mappers are trying to map an area of 300,000 hectares.

The idea about a Project coordinator based in Moresby and providing support
to the field mapping team was discussed and agreed by both partners. The
position was advertised and Dickson Darebo who is also from the plateau was
appointed to be the Mapping Coordinator. He is now based in the office of
Partners with Melanesians where he coordinates the project. See attached as
Appendix “1” the duty statement of the Mapping Project Coordinator.

Clan Elders Workshop

of the plateau.

and upon completion of the Managalas Boundary Mapping Project a combine

workshops will sign the MOU and that will support the proposal to the National
Government to designate the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area
Project.

2.2 Arrangement for Management of the project during the extension

The mapping project is one component of the larger Managalas Conservation
Area Project, which is implemented by Partners with Melanesians (PwM) a
national development and Conservation NGO. The initial work on the

Foundation through Education Development Centre; an USA based NGO
working with Partners With Melanesians. When the funding finished there was
a need for the continuation of the project so CELCOR secured additional
funding from the Rainforest Foundation and the UNDP/GEF Small Grant

As part of the arrangement PwM will now manage the funds and continue to
implementation of the project. All the equipment purchased and continues to

After the agreement by the clan elders the western flank mapping team

2.5 Recording of Clan Groups and Clan Elders.

There is no register of customary land and landowners in Papua New Guinea
including the Managalas plateau. This does not mean that things are chaotic
and unmanageable. Papua New Guinea has thousands of years of settled
agriculture and traditional land management systems. The people basically
know who owns what land and who belongs to which tribe or clan. This does
not mean that there are no disputes over land ownership. Among the
Managalas, as well as elsewhere in PNG, land was acquired and boundaries
established in different ways including the use of force. The land is owned
and controlled by small social units better known as clans, A landowning
group or clan is that group of peopie empowered by custom to make
fundamentai decisions about their land with reference to any other group.
The mapping project, which is a component of the Managalas Conservation
Area Project, seeks to strengthen plateau wide support for sustainable
developed by the cians and to secure partnership agreement between the
PNG government anc the pecple of the Managaias plateau. For this reason
part of the mapping teams effort was to record each clan group names and
clan elders by consulting the clan groups in each village on the plateau.
Attached as Appendix “VI” are the names of clan groups and the clan elders.

(2) Field Coordinators and the Project Coordinator are now in complete

shows that local people can do such projects if properly trained and exposed
to

similar activities elsewhere. itis also important to note that this project has

getting government recognition of the proposed Managalas Conservation

The awareness programme carried out by the mapping team is very critical for

on their future as far as sustainable management of their resource based is

successful implementation of the project. The training offered by WWF is
quite important and the Project Coordinator has attended all these courses.
The Field Coordinators have gone on to exchange programmes to indonesia
and Malaysia to be expertise in developing community maps to have their
rights recognised by the government and also for court cases.

With the actual mapping progress has been made by the mapping team and
half of the while plateau has been made. The progress was imposed by the
clan elder’s workshops, Para-legal training and external boundary awareness
and the Sarawak trip but now that it is over the team should be able to map
the remaining area. It is also a difficult task given the rugged mountain terrain
and so it may take some time to complete mapping of the remaining whole
boundary. The important factor is that actual mapping has started and so the
field mapping team needs to be supported with logistics etc... to have the
mapping completed by the end of the year. More specifically, significant
progress was made towards the participatory delineation of the perimeter of
the area legally owned by the clans if the Managalas plateau and for
preparation of a map that identifies the area. As a result,

1) the people of Managalas plateau are now familiar with and can use global
position systems (GPs) mapping equipment,

2) a designated project coordinator and two (2) local counterparts from the
plateau have being trained in the use of GPs, GIS and supporting
equipment,

3) a participatory approach involving both the population at large and close

collaboration with knowledgeable traditional elders have been developed
for mapping and marking the outer perimeter of the plateau zone by zone,

difficult and controversial zones have been corrupted. The remaining
zones will be easier as population pressures are not an issue and maintain
ridges define most of the boundaries,

counterparts in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, further
strengthening the capacity created under the project. In addition,
collaborative partnerships between PwM, CELCOR and for other sites in

the successful resistance the people of Managalas plateau has so far
being to maintain against recent government attempts to designate much

The main difficulties in terms of implementation and monitoring of the project
activities are communication difficulties and transportation problems. The
only contact on the plateau is by HF radio, which is sometimes not very clear,
and the Field Coordinators have to walk some distance to get to the nearest
station with a HF radio system. !n order to get over this a mobile radio was
bought with project funds and has been in use for a while but due to technical
problem it was sent back to PwM office for service. Partners with Melanesians
already have a HF radio installed in its office, which the Project Coordinator
has access to contact the field mapping team.

There are no regular flights to the plateau and the one-day a week flight by
one of the third level airlines are very unreliable as it does not sometimes land
on the airstrips in the project area. The road to the nearest Provincial town is
not accessible by vehicles because it has not been monitored since 1992 so it
is difficult to use the road transport system. The Field Coordinators
sometimes have to walk for two (2) days to Popondetta to get their flights to
Port Moresby or collect funds for project activities. This also makes it difficult
for monitoring by the Project Coordinator or the PwM and CELCOR
management. These two (2) problems are the major difficulties faced by the
project team in the implementation of the project.

A) Bearing and Back Bearing Exercise.

The team spent the early morning identifying peaks on Normandy Island, Ferguson Island and Good
Enough Island while there was no clouds to obscure their view. The bearings were then transferred to
the map using a protractor to identify the peaks observed and their Grid Location (Northing + Easting)
then noted.

Issues to arise from Exercise:

1) Difficulty with negative Drift

It can be difficult identify observation points on a map if the mapper does not take into account
magnetic drift. In PNG 7.1 degrees has to be added to all bearings observed with a magnetic compass
in order for it to be relevant to work done with official maps available for the country,

In relation to this exercise bearings taken by the team had to be increased by 7 degrees, then the
protractor applied with the modified bearing to calculate a back bearing, which would then be used as
one of the 2 points necessary to triangulate a correct position, or identify the peak on the map.

In order to be successful in this exercise.

* A good reading must be attained using an accurate / good quality compass.
7 degrees must be added to this and other bearings that may be taken.
The protractor be placed in the correct manner and on your exact location on the map. This means
0 degrees or 360 degrees must point to the map’s North (Grid North)
90 degrees must point East
180 degrees must point South
20 degrees must point West and.....
The centre of the protractor must point at your correct location.

© The modified bearing must then be used to plot the direction in which the mapper was observing.
¢ Feather on the map in that direction must then be interpreted well enough to what object was being
observed according to the map.

The last point basically outlines the most important factor. That is the mappers must do a lot of practise
in their own time shape this skill. This requires discipline and motivation to practise like a sports
person would practise skills for their chosen sport.

For this exercise the trainer transferred approximate waypoints of where the traii might lie from his
GPS to the other two GPS which would be used by Malchus and Kingsford. The two would then be
accompanied by guides (not including the trainer) in an attempt to locate this trail and mark way points
along it’s path to the top of the peninsular from Wagohuhu.

Sun 7 April:
This day the trainer took Malchus and Kingsford along the trail they had plotted in an exercise on using
routes with GPS. They returned in the evening and rested.

In both exercises the two mappers showed adequate skills with the GPS that could be iiproved with
further practise on the plateau.

Mon 8" April:
All the work that was done on the 6" and 7” of April around the alternate Wagohuhu to Lelehudi trail

was then complied by Malchus and Kingsford into a topographic sketch of the trail. They completed
this successfully and the rest of the time was spent talking about how all this training related to work in
Managalas.

One critical observation made by Kingsford involved the use of “Averaged” Waypoints on GPS. He
related this to the use of the “Observation points” in identifying Managalas Boundary Points. His
concern was that he had not been averaging the waypoints before saving them as Observation Points.
He worried that this may have created inaccuracies in bearings and positions he took of boundary
points, from the original Observation Points.

While this was an important critical factor for him to neglect in his work on the plateau it should not
have affected his identification of boundary points. in any case, it was planned that ali these points
would be double-checked when we next meet in May at Moresby.

To demonstrate the effect of “Averaging” a small exercise was set with the GPS and tape measure
around the trainer's home. Two GPS were used to provide 2 sets of data for 2 sketches. The GPS
recorded waypoints at a lower level of accuracy. This resulted in an accurate sketch, while the other
had greater differences to actual positions and distances. This lesson was very clear and now the use of
“Averaged” weypoints will be the role for work on the plateau.

DGPS, the Real time DGPS service providers. This means that what time the satellite was

The main aim of the training was to teach potential vanilla farmers to cultivate and
produce better and quality vanilla products in the Managalas plateau.

The training objectives were:

1. to provide knowledge and information on vanilla farming through:

¢ Vanilla project and calendar

This report covers a one-week incorporated Landuse Management and Vanilla workshops
that was conducted at Natanga village from the 6" -i0” October 2003. The incorporation
of these two workshops was schedule on the same week tc allow for easy funding support
for both training workshops by the funding organization Partners with Melanesians.
Landuse Management workshop was conducted on the first dav (6"’10/03) and the
vanilla workshop took the rest of the week. Since different facilitators conducted the two
workshops, each facilitator wil] compile two separate reports. Therefore this report will

3.0 Background:

Vanilla is a succulent climbing plant of the orchid's family. It grows up to more than
10meters before flowering. Vanilla was introduced into the Pacific in the 19" century and
remains as a curiosity and insignificant crop.

Vanilla has been one of the recent cultivated valuable cash crop exported to many
countries such as Australian and other European and Asian countries. In PNG, it is
referred to as the green gold as it's market value is going for K700 per kilogram, a market
value that is almost on the same level as gold. The high earnings have motivated a lot of
interest from individual farmers across the country however its’ cultivation is currently
restricted to lowland areas in a few provinces including, East and West Sepik, Madang,
Manus, East and West New Britain. The ripple wave of interest is now being experience
nation wide thus our current effort in training the people from the Managalas plateau is a
classical reflection of the growing interest.

§.2 Results and discussion

Pre-test and post-test activity and percentage

A Pre-test was also given to the participants to evaluate, asses and identify individual
understanding and knowledge of what a vanilla crop is. Four general question (copy
attached) were used which enable me as the facilitator to know how many participants in
the workshop have some fair ideas of vanilla crops and vise versa. Another test (post-test)
was conducted at the end of the training and the results are as follow:

a) Pre-test - 70% not clear , 30% understand
b) Post-test - 17% not clear, 83% understand

From these percentage it clearly indicates that almost all participants who came for the
training did not have any idea of how to cultivate and farm vanilla. Though the interest
was very high as obvious from the participation list, most participants (70%) came with
the intention to acquire some basic information and knowledge indicating fheir lack of
understanding on vanilla. Towards the end of the training, many came to understand how
to farm vanilla as indicated in the above 83%. As a result the training was very successful
and useful as most people were able to grasp a lot of knowledge in-order to set up their
own vanilla farms in their individual communities.

5.3 Methods /Activities conducted

¢ Method of Propagation (How to grow vanilla)
To start a vanilla farm, farmers must first clear a land area and establish shades and
support. The spacing of the shades must be a triangular spacing of 2.5m.
Planting should be done six months after the shade establishment. To piant vanilla,
cuttings should range from a measurement of 30cm-100cm. With two leaves removed
from the nodes, a hole is dug 10cm deep and 30cm long. Place the two nodes in the
hole and cover with soil. Leave the other portion to stick out to allow the wound to
heal up.

* Crop Husbandry
i) Weeding:
Weeding is not necessary however controlling of climbing plants must be carried out
to control overgrown of weeds. Spades are recommended to use to clean around the
vanilla garden and the weeds can be used as mulching

ii) Mulching:
Mulching is found to be a very important part in vanilla cultivation. There are two
types of mulching; temporary mulching and supplementary mulching.

1. Temporary mulching,
Placing of organic matters around the base of the vanilla plant, such as peelings
from vegetables, weeds from weeding. etc..

Natanga Vanilla Training Report -4-

=== page 6 ===
2. Supplementary mulching,
These are mulches that last longer such as coconut husks and betel nut skins that
can be used as sponges to hold the content of water to control the amount of water
that is needed by the vanilla crop to grow.

Researches have proved that mulching gives higher yield in terms of production
quantity.

iii) Pest and Diseases:

a) Pest:

There are three- (3) pest that attacks vaniila crop;

1. Hypochlorosis danis milo,

2. Pseudonotis danisoides nicer, and

3. Adoxophues species. .

They are small caterpillars that attacks the young shoots from sprouting, vanilla
flowers and the green vanilla beans. These caterpillars can be biologically controlled
by ants and hand picking by the farmers themselves. Chemicals are not
recommended since they wil! disturb the quality of the vanilla beans.

b) Diseases:

There are only two types of vanilla diseases.

1. Cola rot.

This is caused by fungus from the mulches. It only occurs to young shoots growing
towards the base of the vanilla. Looping a few centimeters above che mulch controls
it,

2. Root rot

It is caused by fungus. It aitacks the roots of the shade and the suppovt trees and
causes them to jail.

It doesn't have any control, therefore when this happens, new shade trees have to be
planted to support the vanilla plant prior to dipping the base of the support tree into
the fungicide. The vanilla growing point is directed to the new support tree.

* Blowering of vanilia

Flowering is one of the very important paris in vanilla sroduction In-order for the
vanilla io give plenty flowers. shades must be pruned before the HoOwering session,
Research has proved that sunlight gives of prolific flowering It takes vanilla planifclia
29manths from planting to first flower and vanilia Ghitensis 1 8months,

® inducing of vanilla flower:
Befcre the flowering session, 10cm of the vine apex must be pluck to induce
flowering. This must be done (S} months before flowering.

e Pollination of vanilla flower:

Pollination of vanilla is the transfer of the pollen to the stigma. Fertilization occurs
when pollination is successful. In vanilla this done on the same flower by using a splinter
to carry the pollen grain and care fully deposited to the female part or stigma.

e Method of pollination.

The vanilla flower is held in between the thumb and the pointer of one hand. Using a
small stick, carefully push back the cover covering the male and the female part of the
flower. Now use the same stick to carefully pick out the pollen grain and place it into the
cavity containing the female part or stigma

e Green bean harvesting

Vanilla beans are ready for harvesting 7-9months after pollination. When the vanilla
beans changes color from darkgreen to lightgreen, it is Sma for harvesting. The beans
are harvested by hand picking.

e Curing of vanilla beans

After harvesting the beans are placed or spread over a wooden tray and left indoors
for them to wilt and change color from green to brown. This is done for a period of 7-10
days. The beans are then spread on a dark blanket and left in the sunlight for hours
(10:00am- 1:00pm) for up to three weeks. When the beans get oily then reduce the time
to Lhour per day for 1 week. After this, the beans are sorted out into sound, split and
damage. The beans are then bundled in 200grams and sealed in an airtight container for
conditioning. It takes 5-6months for conditioning. After conditioning the vanilla beans
are now ready for sales.

6.0 Conclusion

As indicated in the pre & post-test results, the workshop was a success with a lot of
knowledge and skills passed on to a lot of vanilla farmers. With the current growing
interest to farm vanilla cash crops, the workshop was an answer to most farmers. It was a
timely exercise/activity now that about more than 50% of the Managaias plateau
population are setting up vanilla farms across the plateau.

7.0 Recommendation

Upon completion of the training a number of recommendation were raised. These are as
follows:

e Anevaluation monitoring programme should be carried out to ensure that the
knowledge have been grasp and effectively implemented in each respective
communities of the participants. This would help identify needs and problems
encountered while farming vanilla cash crops in their individual communities.
From this problems or needs, further plans to do follow-up training activities can be
identified.

e Efficient materials should be provided to enable the participants to really get the idea
of what is being given, and for them to understand what steps or process the
facilitator is explaining. Visual aid materials are one of the very important materials
to such training, because it has a lot of processes to explain that farmers should
understand. Furthermore, we are dealing with local communities thus the need to use
visual aids is very important to enable effective communication with the community

* There shouid be a proper planning set out prior to putting up such training to avoid
rushing and inconvenience faced by the facilitators and the participants.

e Plans for follow-up training’s should be developed to ensure that participants are
properly equip with the necessary and appropriate knowledge and skills in-order to
establish a vanilla production and enterprise. This is very important because in-order
for a learning process to take place, there must be consistence education and training
to allow for a particular person to fully capture what is taught during the workshop
sessions.

plateau.

have advised the Management team to identify the activities they need to

charter with MBA was arranged by Partners with Melanesians for the two (2)
CBOs. The two (2) CBO representatives said that the nuts are all sold out;
monies were sent to the Plateau for the payment for the farmers and paid their

the attempts were all in vain.

amount of kilograms MBA would have carried to Port Moresby.

The Okari season is at its peak and the CBO and the communities are waiting and
anticipating about the next charter.

Crispin and I (PM could not make it due to work commitment) attended the
workshop conducted by Dr. Mike, Mrs. Konia and Mr. Savaiko.

It was a

and West side of the plateau attended the workshop. In addition, observers also
attended and the community of Nakunane village also participated for the trial
exercise for the radio program.

* Women tendering the garden.
* Villagers picking coffee cherries,

Sustainable Development programs through the Newsletter.

CARBON ACCOUNTING METHODS FOR USE IN CDM PROJECTS

Simon Saulei
Centre for Research & Postgraduate Studies
University of Papua New Guinea

introduction

The mechanism by which the quantum of carbon sequestrated in the biomass of trees
is calculated is referred to as “carbon accounting”. For such an accounting to be used
in any CDM project, it is essential that tt should have a correct and defensible system
te undertake in accounting for the amount of carbon that is captured in biomass. It is
also necessary that correct accounting treatment 1s applied to situations in which that
carbon is no longer sequestered in biomass, such as through fire, disease or
destruction of the biomass. Such a carbon accounting mechanism must be sufficiently
rebust that the carbon trading market has confidence that the amount of carbon
sequestered can be considered to be equivalent in its impact on global warming
potential to the carbon released to the atmosphere from activities producing
greenhouse gases. The mechanism must be credible in building confidence in use of
carbon sequestration in a carbon trading market, thereby underpinning growth and
investment in new planted forests to create new carbon credits from sequestration.

A carbon accounting system needs to assess the changes in the amount of carbon
stored in each of the carbon pool over the life of the forest. In the case of a planted
forest, this would cycle from predominantly soil carbon and grasses prior to tree
planting, through any soil carbon losses as trees are planted, to progressively more
carbon stored in the above and below ground parts of trees as they grow, to substantial
carbon emissions at the time of harvest.

There are two key points to note with regard to carbon accounting under the Kyoto
Protocol. The first is that the amount of carbon sequestration that can be claimed as a
"carbon credit" is limited to the net amount of change in the total forest carbon pool
from one period to the next. This is referred to as “stock change accounting”. The
second key point is that, even though carbon remains stored in the products produced
from harvested logs (paper, reconstituted boards, veneers, sawn timber etc), this on-
going “capture” is not recognised under carbon accounting rules as applied to the first
Kyoto Pretocol commitment period from 2008-2012. Recognition may occur in later
periods.

In this paper, I will discuss the four main carbon accounting methods currently being
employed in potential CDM projects, the issue of duration and make comparisons
about the methods. Y

1.0 Introduction

The vegetation of the Managalas Plateau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
upland and montane forests. These forests are intersected by many crecks and rivers that
form the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers. Coarse scale analysis of land-
use threats, specics concentration and endemism, catchment pollution, forest
defragmentation and habitat lost places whole plateau ecosystem as High Conservation
Value Forest (Partners with Melancsia (PwM). 2004). Through conservation awareness
programs initiated and run by PwM within the plateau, the villagers have decided to
conserve their forests. The villagers have formed a core group: the Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF), that will work in partnership with PwM to develop
conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2004, a preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Papua New
Guinea and the Department of Environment and Conservation. Samplings (plants and
animals) were conducted over 14 days (11 effective sampling days) in forests around
Itokama Government Station. General observations on biodiversity were conducted
around villages of liokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

This report highlights the vegetation survey. Note samplings were concentrated in one
area representing only a small fraction of the whole proposed Managalas Plateau
Conservation Area.

2.3 Vegetation

Most of the Managalas Plateau is composed of tropical wet evergreen forest. with a
significant percentage of tropical montane evergreen forest. Smaller percemages of upper
montane und freshwater swamp fores! are alsa found.

Lowland forest up to 1.400 m on the north side of the Owen Stanileys is made up of
Pometia, Terminaiia, Celtis. aad Elaecearpus. aww itand forest is made ap of both alluvial
and fill types (Paipmans, 19763. Lowland alluvial forest has a canopy that is multitiered
and irregular. with many emergents. The understory contains 2 shrub-and-herb layer
with 2 variety of climbers. epiphytes, and ferns. The dominant canopy trees include
species of Pometia. Canarium, Anispoptera, Crypiocarya, Terminalia. Syzygium, Ficus,
Celtis. Dysoxvhun. and Buchanania. Other species such as Koompassia, Dillenia,
Eucalpiopsis, Vatica, and Hopea are locally abundant. Dense stands of Araucaria the
tallest tropical trees in the world, are present in scattered locations (Paijmans. 1976).

The Managalas Piateau is predorminantly composed of four major forest types: low
altitude forest on uplands. iower montane forest, low altitude forest on plains and fans,
and savanna. The MPCA js largely covered by low altitude forest on uplands below

=== page 7 ===
1000m, and lower montane forest on high lands above 1000 m. Also, small scattered
forests of low altitude forest on plains and fans which were found to be predominant
below 1000 m.

The vegetation types of the proposed Managalas CA are fragile forests and of biodiversity
importance comprised the low altitude forest on plains and fans, the lower montane
forest, and savanna. The dominant forest types are the forest on plains and fans, and the
lower montane forest which cover more than 75 percent of the MPCA. The lowland
forest and Jower montane forests are predominant and extend to areas where rainfall
exceed 1800 mm per annum, and at higher altitudes with decreasing temperature
respectively (Bleeker, 1983). The lowland forest is structurally and floristically the richest
and typically contains numerous palms, vines and climbers on well drained alluvial
plains. However, in very poorly drained to swampy conditions, sago and pandanus are
found in the understorey.

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic.
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets.of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation appears
irregular. Although the forest type resembles tropical lowland forest observation on
surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are influenced by

topography.

Certain features, characteristic to lower montane formation become obvious at around
700m asl. The presence of Castanopsis accuminatissina and even Lithocarpus and
Dacrydium in the forests at Jarefa and towards the villages of Nibaiba and Kuai indicate
low montane elements. Large woody lianas. plants with compound leaves, cauliflorous
plants, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and lowland hill
forests (Whitmore 1975) become scarce at Jarefa.

By comparison, forest adjacent to Barije River represents typical lowland forest with
abundant plants possessing compound leaves. cauliflory and large lianas. Common
lowland species of Elmerriilia, Aglaia. Dysoxvium, Elaeocarpus, Sterculia. Cryptocarva,
and Terminalia are abundant.

Based on this observation the upland foresis surrounding [tokama can be further classified
into the following types: mixed Castanopsis forest. mixed upland forest and lowland.

6.1.1 Mixed upland forest

On rather flat {eztains mixed forest types dominate with canopy height of 40m. The (orest
is vertically multilayered. Dominant canopy tree species include Cryptocarya, Sloanea,
Castanopsts, Syzygium, Weinmania and Elavocarpus. The ground layer is dense and
largely composed at shrabs of various species.

6.3.2 Mixed Castanopsis forest

On ridges mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy reaching up to 35m tall.
The forest is two-layered: the canopy and the ground layers. Castanupyis acctuininatissima
is the dominant canopy species in this forest pe. Other coexisting canopy species
include Canarium. Ternsiroemia, Cryptecarve. Terminalia and several species of
Syzygium. The ground layer is sparsely vegetated by Pundanus spp.. ferns and creepers
(Figure 7.0).

6.1.3 Mixed lowland forest

Predominant on flat areas near rivers. The forest is multilayered with the main canopy
Stretching up to 40m (Figure 8.0). Dominant canopy species include Cryptocarya.
Syzygium, Elaeocarpus, Slonea, Artocarpus and strangler Ficus. Lower canopy trees
include species of Garcinia, Gironniera, Barringionia and Dysoxylum. The ground floor
is sparse with abundant seedlings. This forest type is probably the dominant type below
700m asl and extend throughout the proposed Managalas Plateau Conservation Area.

6.1.4 Secondary Regrowth

Disturbed forests also form major formations within the area and are represented by early
regrowth, secondary and advanced secondary forests. Overall height range from 15 to
20m. The formation depends on the intensity and frequency of disturbance. Common
secondary plant species that dominate the canopy include Macaranga, Homolantius,
Ficus, Glochidion and Gastonia. The ground layer is densely vegetated by Imperata
cylindrical, Alpinia, Hornstedtia sp., Nephrolepis and various spinny creepers.

7.0 FOREST USE

The local people depend heavily on planis and forest resources for their livelihood. Plants
provide them with basic necessities like medicines, food, poisons, raw materials for house
constiucuon, shelters, canoes, crafts and tools and numerous other minor forest products.
Furthermore, forests collectively act as a reservoir for plants, germplasm base and a gene
pool and, provide refuge for game and other animals. With limited access to essential
Services plant resources thus become a life support base for the local people. It is
worthwhile therefore to record the different plant and their uses of the area. Some plants
and animals used by the locals were recorded during the survey and the list will be
provided in the full report.

Trees and poles are readily available as raw materials for general construction purposes,
but the locals traditionally use few selected species. The heartwood of Fagrea sp. for
instance, provide good posts for houses while secondary species such as Macaranga
aleuritioides, and Homalanthus sp., provide materials for knobs and raflers of houses.
Stems of palm tees and bamboos are conveniently split and spread for purposes of walls
or floors in house construction.

8.0 GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

Several factors were evident from the survey thal support the conservation initiatives
undertaken by the local people.

* The forest types. and the distribution of plant species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmental conditions. !n effect this means that the vegetatina is quite
unique and presents window's of opportuaiies for long teym scientific siudies on this
forest ecosystems. ;

* The apparent lack of regeneration or recruitment of trees 10 larger size classes requires
proper studies.

The implication of past geological events on the present vegetation formations is an
intriguing fuctor and further research would help tc explain its effect and impact on
biogiversiiy.

Due to the lack of proper infrastructure. the people of Managalas rely heavily on
planis and other forest resources for their basic necds. Destruction of these forests
Would reduce ihe resource base of these plants and their products and may affect the
local inhabitants.

The Araucaria hunsteinii trees represent a historical time seate. Dendroclimatology
Siudies in New Zealand have established time periods of similar sott wood species

=== page 17 ===
ry

dating several thousand years back into the past. The remnant trees within the
Managalas Plateau present good prospects to study past climatic changes and their
influences on vegetation.

* Standing forests act as carbon sinks. With respect to global warming, it would be
interesting to know the carbon sequestration potential of these forests by carrying out
appropriate studies.

* Given the uniqueness of the forests and the resources contained therein, outside
institutions, researchers, and tourists would certainly want to visit the area. To prepare
for such influx, the landowners through PwM can draw up sets of conditions and
guidelines that would protect the pristine forest and at the same time generate income
for the forest owners.

9.0 RECOMMENDATIONS

Given the uniqueness of the forests within the conservation area, we highly recommend
that the forest be conserved. The followings are offered for guidance.

* Proper tramping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or resting
sites be identified then design to allow minimal disturbance.

* The pine is a tree of scientific and historical significance. Scattered Stands of these
species should be identified and mapped out. both. within and outside the proposed
conservation area and these areas be protected.

¢ The mixed Castunopsis forest is very sensitive to human disturbances. Conversion of
this forest type io grassland is already a common feature in the Highlands of Papua
New Guinea. ft is strongly recommended that these stands be conserved.

¢ Proper records of plant animal uses be established. This requires someone with good
knowledge of traditional beliefs and riwals to be able to readily access traditional
knowledge.

¢ Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally assess the ecology
of the area. This should also encompass u full botanical reconnaissance survey of the
area. Permanent study plots be established and consistently monitored.

* Establish research collaboration with known research organizations like FRI, Wau
Ecological Institute. Unitech and UPNG. so that research can be conducted in the area
to generate more knowledge on the ecology of the forest communities.

BOOK KEEPING WORKSHOP

Afore Council Chambers

Afore — Ijivitari District

Report Compiled by: Jacob Ramoi - PwM Project Officer
June 2004

=== page 2 ===
1.0: Introduction

The book keeping workshop was facilitated by the Managalas Development
Foundation (MDF) Bookkeeper - Luke Mambe and co-facilitated by Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) Project Officer —- Jacob Ramoi from the 24" - 26" May 2004.

The workshop was conducted at Afore Council Chambers for three (3) days. Only
four (4) basic topics were covered because of the experience and the level of
understanding of the Community Based Organisations (CBO).

The topics were:
1. Basic Principles of Bookkeeping,
2. Record keeping and acquittal of funds,
3. Information about Cashbox and Bank Account,
4. Using a manual cashbook.

Thirty four (34) participants and observers attended the workshop. They set up
their own norms & values and their expectation for the bookkeeping workshop.

This report will briefly summarised the four main topics and the
Sub- topics for the workshop. The four topics have their own aims and objectives
for the participants,

1.1. NORMS & RULES

The participants set up their own nine (9) norms and values as house keeping rules
for them to follow during the workshop.

Ask if you want to borrow something
All question are good

Punctuality

Respect one another

Raise hands to talk

No vandalism

No smoking inside

Unnecessary movement

Equal Participants

1.2. PARTICIPANTS EXPECTATIONS

OM NAM SEP

The five expectations of the participants are;
Financia! Report for board of directors
Assist him in his books (bookkeeping)
Specified Roles & Responsibilities
Learn Basic Methods of book keeping
Transfer to skills.

Nal Ba

2.0: PRINCIPLES OF BOOKKEEPING

The main aims and objectives of this topic are:
> To apply the basic book keeping rules
> Identify the responsible of Treasure & book keeper & Committees

=== page 3 ===
2.1: BASIC PRINCIPLES OF BOOK KEEPING

2.1.1. What is book keeping?

1, Financial records correct (accurate recording)
2. Total amount of money received
- membership
grants
office rents
Bookkeeping is a process of accurately recording income, all money received or going
in and accurately recording expenses (all money paid out) of a group. Simple book
keeping is a CASH BOOK.

2.2.2. Why is Bookkeeping Important?

{a}: Group moncy belong to the member of the groups, the moncy,
the group has does not belong to the treasurer or committee. It
belongs to all members together.

(b): -Know what happen to the money
-Know how much money the group has and how it is used.

(c): Help to use money according to plan
Know how much money is left to spent or already spend
Know how much to spend on other things

(d): Show that a group can take care of money (keep good record)

2.2.3. PARTS OF BOOK KEEPING (8 important parts)

(a) Treasurer/ bookkeeper - looks after money
(b) Finance Committee:
a group that help the bookkeeper /treasurer look after the money.
{c) Cash book — safe
(d) Bank account — Bank keeps money
{e} Cash book — Book where you record Incomes & Expense
() Receipts - Book showing money moved from onc person to another.
(g) Monthly Report - Income and Expense record for one month.

(h) Procedure — good way to do book keeping.

2.2.4. TREASURERS & FINANCE COMMITTEE

A Treasurer and Finance Committee are people who look after group's money.

The Treasure or Finance Officer (Roles & Responsibility)

(a) A treasure is an Individual man or woman who looks after money.

(b) He or she should know how to read, write and work with numbers (add,
subtract, multiply and divide)

(c) Treasurer keeps the Cash box, cash book, receipt and receipt book, he/she holds
the bank documents (if they have a bank account.

{d) He/She records down Income & Expenses

(e} Only treasurer takes money out or puts money in the Cash box.

(} Treasurer has the power to take money out of this account.

(g) Finance Committee gives permission to the treasurers to buy some items (they
set limit).

(h) Treasurer submits monthly report.

(i) Treasurer teachers one or two people to do book keeping.

=== page 4 ===
2.2.5. FINANCE COMMITTEE

(a) Smal! group of people who helps the treasure look after the moncy.
(b) They decide what the treasurer can do and can not do.
(c) They decide how much can be used within the budget.
(a) They ask the treasurer to report to them
Correct Records — Easy to prepare
Incorrect records — Hand to prepare & present.

2.2.6. ADVICE TO TREASURER

(a) Open bank Account

(b) Pay expenses by Cheque is possible

(c}) Withdraw funds from Bank Account for cash box expenses
(d) Issue receipts, keep carbon copy

{ec} Obtain receipts for all money paid

(} No. of receipts in order of payment

(g) Reduce details in the cash book

(h) Pay outstanding / invoice promptly.

(i) Keep cash book with analysis on both side.
(j) Asset register

(k) Keep record of money paid and received

(l) Cash in the Cash Box everyday.

3.0: RECORD KEEPING & ACQUITAL OF FUNDS

Aims and objectives for topic 2 are:
> Appreciate the importance of record keeping and acquittals of funds.
> Understanding and prepare different types of source document
> Understanding the process of acquitting funds.

3.1. FINANCIAL RECORDS.

Record keeping are.
* Records of financial transaction (receipts & invoicc)
* Records of financial for goods & equipment (stocks)
* Records of financial of important documents (contact, agreement)
Financial records means to write down organisations money received and paid out.

Record Keeping helps in these ways:
(1) Control] Cash
(2) Performance of the Organisation
(3) Show other Organisation your performance
(4) Records are also needed for performance

3.2. GOOD RECORDS KEEPING SYSTEM

3.2.1. Elements of Good record system
a) Cheque Accounts

b) Petty cash for small expenses

c) Deposit receipts often

d) Support your entries

=== page 5 ===
3.2.2. BASIC RULES OF PROPER RECORD KEEPING

a) Neat & tidy

b) Written clearly

c) Correction fluid not allowed

d) Proper document to be presented at anytime.

3.2.3. SOURCE DOCUMENTS

a) Receipt
is a document which usually shows the money on organisations receives?
Some organisation use separate receipts for many spend (see also petty cash
voucher) when they do not receive a source document and let the money

recipient sign it.

b) Petty Cash Voucher
Is a document showing the spending of small expenses of the cash box petty

cash?

c) Bank Statement
Is a paper from the bank showing all moncy coming in and going out of the
account during a specific time and balance remaining.

d) Cash sales Register
Shows the total money received and spends from a cash register machine

(used in trade store).

e) Invoice
Is a business document that shows quantity, description, unit price and total
charge to an organisation by a supplier for delivery of goods or services?

f} Cheque butt
This is a small price of paper left in the cheque book after removing the
cheque leaf which shows the details of the organisations spending (date,
amount, supplier, a/c balance.

All sources of documents should be filled because:

Easy to find

Required by law

Donors & auditors to confirm expenses are paid & real.

v

WNWYS

3.2.4: HOW TO RECORD MONEY RECEIVED

When the organisation received money from any source, it is very important to write
a receipt.

This receipt will show:

> That money is given tot the organisation and

» That money has been received

If you have a receipt the problem will be solved, if sometirnes people argue back thal
they gave you more money then that the receipt will show you the fact.

Written receipt should have 2 copies, the original will be given to the person, who
gave the money and the carbon will be left in the book for your copy ~ both copies
will be the same.

5.0. USING A MANUAL CASH BOOK

Aims and objectives for topic five (5) are;

5.1. WHAT IS A CASH BOOK?
A cash book is a book in which cash receipts and payments are recorded.

Cash book namely have a column for:

* Money coming in

* Money going out (paid out)

* Moncy which is left in cash book/ bank account

* Date & description of money

Every time money is recorded on paid out it must be recorded and balance
calculated, this cnable us to know how much moncy is in our cash box or account

at anytime.

§.1.1. Recording money in the simple cashbook.
The following guidelines for recording money in the cash book
(a) all money received or paid out should be written down
(b) when recording money received (income or revenue) the following details are
needed:
- date
- description of where money comes from
- how much money is received
- the new balance

(c) when money is paid out (Expenses}
date

the new balance

(d) you can use one page for a month and than for a new month. You start new
page for one week depending on the amount of transactions.

(e) Balance brought every time you start a new page the last balance on the old
balance should be written at the top of a new page as balance brought
forward.

(f)} Check regular intervals, if you keep cash in the box. Check that the amount
recorded is equal to cash box. If it is not ask yourself why. If you have
forgotten to record some takings — or calculated wrong, you must clear the
balance.

The basic book keeping course conducted by PwM & MDF was to build the capacity
of the Community Based Organisations (CBOs) and the Community Learning
Centres (CLCs} to enable them to understand the basic rules in book keeping; the
responsibilities of treasurers and committees; differences between cash box and
bank account; calculate the balances in the bank account and cash book and to
prepare a more detail cash book.

It was very obvious that the local facilitators could make an impact to their own
community especially trying to explain difficult concepts or components translated
into their dialect.

The Community Based Organisations (CBO) suggested that such trainings should be

addition, it is more sustainable and will cost less to carry out this training.

SUMMARY REPORT

1.0 Introduction

The vegetation of the Managalas Plateau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
hill and montane forests. The forests are intersected by many creeks and rivers that form
the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers. A rich diversity of fauna and flora are
supported by these forest types. Oil Palm development, and subsistence agriculture are
posing great threats to these pristine forests. The villagers within the plateau have decided
lo conserve their forests and are seeking assistance from Partners with Melanesia (PwM)
to develop their conservation initiatives. The villagers have formed a core group; the
Managalas Deveiopment Foundation (MDF). that wil! work in partnership with PwM to
develop the conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2004. preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists. Samplings (piants and animals)
were conducted over i4 days (11 days effective sampiing periods) in uphill forests of
Jarifa near Kam creek. General observations on biodiversity were conducted around
villages of Itokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

This report highlights the summary of the survey. A more detailed repori of the survey

will be provided after thorough synthesis of the data. Note samplings were concentrated
in one area representing only a small fraction of the whole proposed Managaias Plateau
Sonservation Area.

2.0 Plant species diversity

The forests surrownding Janis is a typical uphill forest type situated at an elevation of
approximately 700 to 800m as]. This forest type comprises different cohorts or stands that
are in part influenced by the different landscape formations. On rather flat areas mixed
forest types dominate with canopy height of 40m. Dominant tree species include
Criptocarva, Sioanea, Casianopsis, Svzygiuni, Weinmania and Llaeocarpus. On ridges
mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy reaching up to 35m tali. Castanopsis
accuminatissima is the dorainant tree species in this forest type. Disturbed forests also
form minor formations within the area and are represented by early regrowth, secondary
and advanced secondary forests. The frequently disturbed riverine forest forms a narrow
strip along the rivers.

3.0 Bird diversity.

Summary report to be provided by Paulus Kuimei, Department of Environment and
Conservation. At least 100 species of birds were observed within the viliages of Itokama,
Kuai, Nidaida and the Jarifa forest.

=== page 7 ===
4.0 Mammals and Herpetofauna

Fifty five specimens of rats and bats were collected after 440 net and trapping nights over
11 working nights. In total twenty-three (23) specimens of rodents were captured and
thirty two (32) specimens of bats were collected. After measurements were taken
seventeen (17) bats, all Syconycteris australis were released. Of those, eight (8) species of
rodents were trapped and 3 species of bats were netted. A colony of 5 of the large Forbes
tree mouse were captured when the villagers chopped down the tree they were living in.
The colony of 5 rodents are now kept alive at the Museum of the University of Papua
New Guinea. Details are all given in Table 2.

Although, our netting and trapping nights did not produce any marsupials we observed
three (3) species of marsupials at different times of the survey. That included a juvenile
southern brown cuscus that was kept as a pet after the mother was killed for consumption,
Dorias tree Kangaroo was also kept as a pet by a family after the mother was also
captured and consumed. During the period of the survey, villagers captured three (3)
forest wallabies, which were later consumed (refer to Table 2).

4.1 Wild dog (Canis Familiaris dingo):

The presence of the wild dog was confirmed when a half-crunched bird was left hanging
in the lower shelve of the mistnet in the undercroft of Pandanus trees. Villagers insisted
that this could not have been left behind by domestic dogs but wild dogs.

4.2 Reptilia:

Most of our efforts were concentrated on mammals and not on reptiles and frogs.
However, over the 11 working days our chance - collection and observations resulted in
thirteen (11) specimens of reptiles and frogs. Of those thirteen specimens, three (3)
species of reptiles (2 pythons and a keelbacked snake) were seen. The two species of
pythons were captured by villagers and eaten, while the Keel-backed snake was seen at
the Camp site. The other eleven (11) species (4 frogs & 8 reptiles) were collected with the
help of the villagers and taken as specimens. The frogs comprise of two ground frogs of
the same species, one hylid and one ranid (refer to Table 2).

4.3 Domesticated animals:

Domestic animals were seen in the villages. Of the three, domestic dog, pussy cat and
chicken, dogs and cats can have an influence on the presence of wildlife. Both dogs and
cats are kept as pets but villagers seemed to keep dogs especially for hunting. From our
investigation, it seemed that dogs were kept for hunting more than as pets.

Wild animals were also captured and kept as pets to be sold later of for consumption. A
Doria's Tree kangaroo was kept as a pet after the mother was killed several years ago. In
another house, a juvenile southern brown cuscus was also kept as a pet but later escaped.

5.0 FOREST USE

The local people depend heavily on plants and forest resources for their livelihood. Plants
provide them with basic necessities like medicines, food, poisons, raw materials for house
construction, shelters, canoes, crafts and tools and numerous other minor forest products.
Furthermore, forests collectively act as a reservoir for plants, germplasm base and a gene
pool and, provide refuge for game and other animals. With limited access to essential
services plant resources thus become a life support base for the local people. It is
worthwhile therefore to record the different plant and their uses of the area. Some plants
and animals used by the locals were recorded during the survey and the list will be
provided in the full report.

Trees and poles are readily available as raw materials for general construction purposes,
but the locals traditionally use few selected species. The heartwood of Fagrea sp. for

instance, provide good posts for houses while secondary species such as Macaranga
aleuritioides, and Homalanthus sp., provide materials for knobs and rafters of houses.

Stems of palm trees and bamboos are conveniently split and spread for purposes of walls
or floors in house construction.

6. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

Several factors were evident from the survey that support the conservation initiatives
undertaken by the local people.

e The forest types, and the distribution of plant species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmental conditions. In effect this means that the vegetation is quite
unique and presents windows of opportunities for long term scientific studies on this
forest ecosystems.

e The apparent lack of regeneration or recruitment of trees to larger size classes requires
proper studies.

e The implication of past geological events on the present vegetation formations is an
intriguing factor and further research would help to explain its effect and impact on
biodiversity.

¢ Due to the lack of proper infrastructure, the people of Managalas rely heavily on
plants and other forest resources for their basic needs. Destruction of these forests
would reduce the resource base of these plants and their products and may affect the
local inhabitants.

e The Araucaria hunsteinii trees represent a historical time scale. Dendroclimatology
studies in New Zealand have established time periods of similar soft wood species
dating several thousand years back into the past. The remnant trees within the

=== page 10 ===
Managalas Plateau present good prospects to study past climatic changes and their
influences on vegetation.

Standing forests act as carbon sinks. With respect to global warming, it would de
interesting to know the carbon scauestration potential of these forests by carrving out
appropriate studies.

Given the umueness of the forests and the resources contained therein, outside
institutions, researchers, and tourists would certainly want to visit the area. To prepare
for such influx, the landowners through PwM can draw up sets of conditions and
guidelines that would protect the pristine forest and ai the same time generate income
for the forest owners.

10

=== page 11 ===
7. RECOMMENDATIONS

Given the uniqueness of the forests within the conservation area, we highly recommend
that the forest be conserved. The followings are offered for guidance.

Proper tramping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or resting
sites be identified then design to allow minimal disturbance.

The pine is a tree of scientific and historical significance. Scattered stands of these
species should be identified and mapped out, both, within and outside the proposed
conservation area and these areas be protected.

The mixed Castanopsis forest is very sensitive to human disturbances. Conversion of
this forest type to grassland is already a common feature in the Highlands of Papua
New Guinea. It is strongly recommended that these stands be conserved.

Proper records of plant animal uses be established. This requires someone with good
knowledge of traditional beliefs and rituals to be able to readily access traditional
knowledge.

Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally assess the ecology
of the area. This should also encompass a full botanical reconnaissance survey of the
area, Permanent study plots be established and consistently monitored.

Establish research collaboration with known research organizations like FRI, CRI,

Wau Ecological Institute, and UPNG, so that research can be conducted in the area to
generate more knowledge on the ecology of the forest communities.

undertaken by the local people.

* The forest types, and the distribution of plant species are strongly influenced by the
prevailing environmental conditions. In effect this means that the vegetation is quite

unique and presents windows of opportunities for long term scientific studies on this
forest ecosystems.

* The apparent lack of regeneration or recruitment of trees to larger size classes requires
proper studies.

The implication of past geological events on the present vegetation formations is an

intriguing factor and further research would help to explain its effect and impact on
biodiversity.

Due to the lack of proper infrastructure, the people of Managalus rely heavily on
plants and other forest resources for their basic needs. Destruction of these forests

would reduce the resource base of these plants and their products and may affect the
local inhabitants.

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic,
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation appears
irregular. Although the forest type resembies tropical lowland forest observation on
surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are influenced by

topography.

Certain features, characteristic to lower montane formation become obvious at around
700m asl. The presence of Castanopsis accuminatissima and even Lithocarpus and
Dacrydium in the forests at Jarefa and towards the villages of Nibaiba and Kuai indicate
low montane elements. Large woody lianas. plants with compound leaves, cauliflorous
planis, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and lowland hill
forests (Whitmore 1975) become scarce at Jarefa.

By comparison, forest adjacent to Barije River represents typical lowland forest with
abundant plants possessing compound Icaves, cauliflory and large lianas. Common
lowland species of Elmerrillia, Aglaia, Dysoxylum, Elaeocarpus, Sterculia, Cryptocarya,
and Terminalia are abundant.

Based on this observation the upland forests surrounding Itokama can be further classified
into the following types; mixed Castanopsis forest, mixed upland forest and lowland.

6.1.1 Mixed upland forest

On rather flat terrains mixed forest types dominate with canopy height of 40m. The forest
is vertically multilayered. Dominant canopy tree species include Cryptocarya, Sloanea,
Castanopsis, Syzygium, Weinmania and Elaeocarpus. The ground layer is dense and
largely composed of shrubs of various species.

6.1.2 Mixed Castanopsis forest

On ridges mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy reaching up to 35m tall.
The forest is two-layered; the canopy and the ground layers. Castanopsis accuminatissima
is the dominant canopy species in this forest type. Other coexisting canopy species
include Canarium. Ternstroemia, Cryptocarya. Terminalia and several species of

Syzygium. The ground layer is sparsely vegetated by Pandanus spp., ferns and creepers
(Figure 7.0).

Eucalptopsis, Vatica, and Hopea are locally abundant. Dense stands of Araucaria the
tallest tropical trees in the world, are present in scattered locations (Paijmans, 1976).

altitude forest on uplands, lower montane forest, Jow altitude forest on plains and fans,

2.1 Climate

The climate of the Managalas Plateau is tropical wet, which is characteristic of this part of
Melanesia, located in the western Pacific Ocean north of Australia.

The proposed Managalas Plateau Conservation Area itself has a relatively high annual
rainfall and range from 2000mm to 3500mm., The eastern most part of the conservation
area is slightly drier compare to the eastern part (Figure 2.0). Overall the weighted
average (according to PNGRIS mapping unit averages) annual rainfall is 2,725mm.

Rainfall distribution is associated with the two major seasonal wind patterns of the
region: the northwest monsoons occurring in the months of November to April and the
southeast trade winds occurring in May to October. The northwest monsoon is the wettest
while the southeast trade winds is drier resulting in pronounced dry season (PwM, 2004).

1.0 Introduction

The vegetation of the Managalas Plateau is largely pristine forests comprising of lowland,
upland and montane forests. These foresis are intersected by many crecks and rivers that
form the main catchment for the Bariji and Musu Rivers, Coarse scale analysis of land-

programs initiated and run by PwM within the plateau, the villagers have decided to
conserve their forests. The villagers have formed a core group: the Managalas
Development Foundation (MDF). that will work in partnership with PwM to develop
conservation strategies for the area.

In November 2(4}4, a preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Papua New

animals) were conducted over 14 days (11 effective sampling days} in forests around
ltokama Government Station. General observations on biodiversity were conducted
around villages of ttokama, Kuai and Nibaiba.

This report highiights the vegetation survey. Note samptings were concentrated in one
area representing only a smal! fraction of the whole proposed Managalas Plateau
Conservation Area.

The proposed Managalas Conservation Arca constitutes an area of approximately

The Managalas Plateau is located within the Southeastern Papuan Rain Forests ecoregion.

ABSTRACT

A preliminary survey was conducted in [iokama and surrounding villages of Kuai, and
Nibaiba within the Managalas Plateau, Ijivitari District, Northern Province. The aim of
the survey was to gather baseline information on vegetation types, determine the structure
and assess the plant diversity.

The vegetation survey was carried out in three randomly selected sites, 2 to 4km apart;
Jarefa forest 3km west from Itokama, Kadiakala forest 2.5km northwest from Itokama
and Barije 4km northwest from ltokama. Within each site strip transects of 5 x 50m were
laid out and trees greater or equal to Scm dbh were measured and height recorded.

To get a picture of species number as a function of increasing area, two 20 x 20m plots
were established at Jarefa and Barije forests. Within each plot all species were assessed in
5 x 5m plots and new ones not encountered in 5 x 5m plots were added in subsequent
larger plots of 10 x 10m and 20 x 20m.

Apart from forest sampling general botanical collection was conducted over the entire
area. Plants with flowers and fruits were targeted as these will aid proper identification of
specimens.

Samplings and general observations indicate that a number of forest formations occur in
the area; mixed lowland forest, mixed Castanopsis forest, mixed upland forest and
secondary regrowth. The result from the transects show that high proportion of trees have
dbh <30cm indicating that the forest is quite young.

The Shannon Diversity Index average score is 1.07. This is quite high for such a small
sampling area of 0.O1ha. Species area curve also show increasing species number as area
increases. All in all the Ktokama area has a relatively high species diversity.

It is recommended that the conservation initiatives by the Managalas Development
Foundation in partnership with Partners with Melanesia be strengthen and instrument put
in place to declare the Managalas Plateau as Conservation Area.

A planned 14 days were required by Partners with Melanesians in November 2004, for a rapid
assessment survey on fauna and flora of Managaias Conservation Area,{Managaias
Plateau), Northern Province.The survey in it’s first phase required by Partners With
Melanesian an NGO group for an immediate biodiversity studies in preparation for the area
to be declared a conservation area. However, the stage of it’s declaration is not too soon
without proper biological information’s for it’s support. Two scientist, one field technician
from the University of Papua New Guinea, four final year UPNG Environmental Science
students, and a scientist with the Department of Environment & Conservation, were engaged
to conduct this phase one of the rapid assessment surveys. Main focuses were on birds, and
mammals in vertebrate fauna and plants. Eleven days were actually spent in the field on the
transect-lines, and plot establishments, five days were spent in general observations, and two
were travelling days, Port Moresby ltokama and return.

Three villages (Nibaiba, Kuai, and Jtokama) and their surroundings were covered in either
surveys or the general observations of which seven different types of general habitat or
vegetation types were described, the mid-montane forest, the lower montane forest, lowland
rainforest, secondary vegetation, garden sites(old & new), village sites, and the rivers and
creek habitats. How-ever, studies only took place in six habitats leaving out the mid-montane
habitat due to limited time frame in this phase, hoping to be covered in the next longer phase.

Facilitator Train

Facilitator training alongside materials development are the comerstones of all the
Rainforest Literacy activities.

Facilitator trainings enables the workshop participants, themseives, to identify the
skills and abilities of a good group facilitator. The objective was to develop local
ownership for what facilitator training is all about

A good community group facilitator:

is motivated to try and capture the collective wisdom of the group

is not a bossy, know-it-all type of person

is able to sense different kinds of personalities and is able to draw out opinions
from everyone in the groups

does not feei the need to present his or her own opinions from everyone in the
groups

is able, at the conclusion of the group’s discussion, to put together a summary
statement expressing that opinion that was widely held across the group

should be able to read and write but does not necessarily need any high
educational qualifications

avoids setting himself up in a position of importance at the front of the group, i.e.,

joins the other s in a circle, situation himself at the same level as the others.
Avoids using tables or a podium that separates himself from the others.

is responsible and demonstrates his or her commitment to the group

is able to restrain outspoken members of the group who tend to dominate the
discussion

is mature and respected by the group and the larger community
is creative in using strategies to elicit group participation

is creative in thinking of ways to get the group actively involved in the learning
process

is clever in integrating the use of the radio and the poster into the interactive
learning going on in the community group discussion

is able to restate information from the radio and in the poster in ways that enable
everybody to understand

is able to restate opinion offered by members of the group in ways that honor their
contribution but make it better understood at the same time

is able to steer the group away from confrontation by honoring the contribution of
each member without committing to any.

Is able to effectively manage the administrative aspects of leading a community
group discussion, including the use of the project’s contribution, the development
and presentation of the community’s matching contribution, and the development
of mini-reports that capture on paper the opinion that was generated in the group

=== page 7 ===
Additional strategies, techniques and characteristic of effective facilitators that will be
included in community group facilitator training include:

1) Knows about and draws upon participants, culture, past experiences and interests
as a point of reference when presenting new information;

2) Designs group activities that allow participants to discover answers on their own
or with the support of the facilitator /or other participants;

3) Allows participants to participant interaction to occur;
4) Encourages participants to think and work independently;

5) Encourages participants to pose questions and to initiate interactions on their
own;

6) Creates new and interesting experiences for participants in the group (e.g. does
not use the same strategy over and over again with no variation);

7) Adapts instruction to the individual learning styles and needs of participants;

8) Explains his or her thinking process aloud in simple terms;

9) Allows participants to guess, to develop theories and explanations about a topic or
problem, even if their theories and explanations are not necessarily correct;

10) Prompts the participants to explain how they reached their conclusion (if a good
one) or helps reason through the questions or problems to a good conclusion;

11) Asks the participants to explain his or her reasoning and guides the participant in
order to achieve greater understanding;

12) Gently acknowledges and corrects participants when they are wrong, using
phrases such as “That is a good try, but it is not correct. Let's see if we can correct

it together”;

13) Tracks the progress of each individual participant and provides assistance as
needed.

+. Biodiversity Survey
Q. What is biodiversity survey?

Ans: This name is short for Biological Diversity Survey. It is the study of life and
structure of living things. It includes plants, animals, insects (butterfly), amphibians
(frog), reptiles (snake) etc.

Q. Who will be involved in the biodiversity survey?

Ans: Scientists from University of Papua New Guinea, Other International NGOs
like World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS),
Forestry Department and Forest Research Institute.

Q. Will the local people be involved?

Ans: Yes. It is very important that local people are involved in the survey. Local
people are needed to identify species of plants and animals native to their area.
They will also tell the scientists about their local names and how they use these
species of plants and animals.

1 2 3 & 5

Q. How will the survey be done?

Ans: There are 7 types (taxa group) of surveys:
1. Reptile/Snakes
2. Mammals
3. Plants
4. Amphibians/Frogs

=== page 13 ===
5. Freshwater Fish & Crustaceans
6. Entomological/Insects/Moths (including aquatic insects)
7. Ornithological/Bird

Q. Will these seven types of surveys be done all at once?

A: No. It will cost a lot of money to do all the surveys at once. Depending on how
much money PWM currently has for this survey, PWM is going to do only one
survey which is the Entomological/Insects/Moths (including aquatic insects). The
others will follow later once funding becomes available.

Q. How will the survey benefit the people now and in future?

Ans: The survey will benefit the people in:

Giving information to the local people on the types of plants and animals
they have on their land, in the forest and in the rivers.

Telling the local people the population/figures/numbers of the plants and
animals they have on their land, in the forests and in the rivers; and their
survival on whether or not these species are threatened to die out.

Telling what humans are doing to the habitat of these plants and animals
and what the local people can do to protect them.

Telling the local people other knowledge that they do not know about their
native plants and animals and inform the people on ways to protect these
species.

Elementary children will be able to learn the scientific names of the native
species along side their local names.

When other areas in PNG no longer have the plants and animals, the
Managalas people can be proud and show the rest of PNG what you still
have on your land.

The medicinal value of the plants will be so much that the Managalas area
will be the source of many drugs not known to medical scientist.

The Managalas people will still have for their grandchildren the forest and its
animals. The children will be proud of their fore fathers of what they have
done to their environment and its habitat.

The Managalas people will still have its cultural identity when many areas in
PNG will have lost theirs.

3. Liklik Dinau Moni
Q. What is liklik dinau moni?

Ans: It is a system of allowing people to borrow small amount of money from a
seed source (seed money) to start small businesses, make profit, and repay the
amount borrowed from the seed money with very small interest.

Q. Why liklik dinau moni?

Ans: Liklik dinau moni is easy and flexible with no administrative procedure like the
commercial banks (ANZ, BSP, Westpac) where one is required to have capital
assets or counterpart money in order to get a loan.

1 2 3 4 5

Q. Why is a survey needed before implementing this ‘liklik dinau moni’?

Ans: Before PWM begins this liklik dinau moni, a survey will be carried out to find
out that the money will not be wasted on an activity that will not bring in a good
profit. The survey will also find out other useful information that will determine
whether or not it is worth implementing a ‘liklik dinau moni’ on the plateau.

from around the world in other big countries overseas have proven records of

13. A — Mr Mondiai:

It is scary but true as it happens in many societies. However, we should not be blinded by money and other handouts. Well, what kinds of
things are handouts? Handouts are anything you get without having to work for it. When a politician gives money for a youth or sports group
activity, this is a handout. When the government builds us a road or an aid post, this is another kind of handout. When an NGO gives you a
spade for your work, that's a handout too. You many use the spade to do hard work, but you did not to do the hard work first to get the
spade.

We often hear that handout mentality is bad. Why? It is mostly because handouts tend to make people lazy. Lazy people often do not finish
what they started. People who get used to handouts become lazy in doing things for themselves.

Some people are always trying to get handouts from government, churches, NGOs and companies for their projects. As soon as the
handouts stop, they lose interest in their projects and everything they did starts to fall apart. Usually these people end up getting little
respect from wise people in the community. Why? Because everyone can see what happened!
