When ever a community is given a new road, bridge, aid post or schoo! by the government they are happy. But the infrastructure was given
like it was a handout! A few years later, you can see that local people do not do the simplest maintenance on that infrastructure. They had
no feeling of owning that infrastructure, so that was no feeling to do something to maintain it. Instead, the people expect the government to
do all the maintenance (ref. to Afore/Itokama raod).

This shows that handouts can bring quick results that look very good at first. But in the long run, they collapse, wasting time and money.
Handouts are wasteful!

However, some smart people have thought a lot about handouts. They have decided that handouts are a big problem. They try to resist
taking handouts in their personal lives (ref. to board members and group facilitators). They teach their children the bad things about

handouts, They set an example so that their community will start creating and maintaining its own local infrastructure instead of relying on
outsiders.

Those who stayed away from handouts, usually end up being very happy and proud at what they did by themselves. When you have to
struggle to make or by something, it changes the way you think. You will be more likely to worry about, protect, and look after anything you

had to struggle for. That's why we look after things better when we have to work hard for them, instead of having them given to us as
handouts.

We are all tempted to ask for handouts. But handouts are like the forbidden fruit — they only hurt us in the end. Try to get the handout

mentality out of your head and keep in mind that the main reason we participate in project activities is for the good of our people and not for

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY.

The Namiai Community Development Association (NACODA) Strategic Planning was
very new to most of the participants. After the workshop they all felt that it is a very
useful tool to guide the work of NACODA. The strategic planning workshop looked at
the focus areas and plan for NACODA, through identifying critical issues, tensions and
needs of the organization. The strategic plan also helped NACODA to come up with a
proposal budget for their program activities identified from the strategic planning
workshop.

The Strategic Planning Workshop looked at the New Strategic Direction for
NACODA and help members to sclf-appraise themselves. The participants were
facilitated using participatory approaches, tools and methods and processes

to identify and decide on the following ;

* NACODA’s shared Vision and Mission Statements.
* Core Values and Beliefs
* Goals

« Culture of the organization.

The participants in smaller groups shared experiences and learned from each

other as they go through cultural experiences on how to strategize and plan a

traditional marriage situation and feast for the dead. After the group presentations a brief
summary was done on what is Strategic and what is Planning , its effect on an individual
and organization and what are the consequences if they failed to plan or if the plan did
eventuate.

The participants were briefly introduced to PNG Pre- history Timeline and the
Changing Societies that PNG is going through. Participatory participation was
explained through an “House Building” exercise. The participants were then
taken to look at what is not Development and what is Development. Introducing
the participants to CARGO DEVELOPMENT and the true development, the
INTEGRAL HUMAN DEVELOPMENT.

The participants used SWOT (Strength, Weakness, Opportunities & Threats) analysis to
identify the Strengths and Weaknesses of the NACODA and then they went on to do a
scan of the trends (SWOT- Opportunities and Threats) that are coming from the outside
and affecting NACODA as an organization and upon its individual membership. By
looking at the challenges obstacles and/or issues faced by NACODA and the Managalas
communities internally as an organization and individual membership, family, clan and
the plateau overall. These exercises led the participants to identify and discuss fully the
NACODA Needs. The Trends Scan and the Community Need Analysis helped the
participants identify issues that created tensions within themselves as individuals, the
community at large, NACODA as an organization and it’s relationship with PWM.

3
Strategic Direction ~ Facilitated by Barefoot

Namiai Community Development Association Inc.

Furthermore, the participants together discussed in smaller groups what is currently
happening and what needs to happen to address these trends and community
needs/issucs/challenges/obstacles. The Internal scan, the Trend scan and the NACODA
Community Need Analysis including the comments and discussions raised during recap
and group presentations helped the participants to come up with organizational program
components/strategies- the actual Focus areas. Using SMART (being Specific,
Measurable Achievable, Relevant and Time bound) tools the participants in smaller
groups formulated objectives , identified major activities, then minor activities and
performance indicators to achieve relevant to these objectives. NACODA will at a later
date develop tasks and estimated cost/budget for a possible proposal for its programs to
be forwarded to it’s donors.

Finally the group defined and have in place a new Strategic Direction and plan. This plan
be implemented once funding is available. This executive summary must be read
together with the whole strategic plan if one is not familiar with the concept and
approaches in Participatory Strategic Planning tool.

Background

The socio- economic impact of the Okari nut project on the Managalas plateau became
apparent that communities became organized around it. The establishment of Partners
with Melanesia tasked to organized the Managalas communities around their cultural and
natural resources and further carry out research into Okari nut as a viable non forest
product. There were already threats of large scale logging moving into the plateau. PWM
facilitated communities to be organized into zones created structures like the Combined
Forum Steering Committee Meetings zone boards, clan committees, zone office and
admin support staff and program staff. There are ten zones established on the plateau.
There were few zones that were suspended along the way, while the most organized
zones got incorporated as recognized Legal Entities of their own with IPA. The most
notable ones are zone 1, zone 2- NACODA and the umbrella body on the plateau, the
Managalas Development Foundation.

In 2001 seven years after the overall Managalas Conservation Area Support Project
(MCASP) , PWM held its first Strategic Planning Workshop at Naukanane. The focus
areas identified were, Consensus Building, Training, Gender and Eco- enterprising
became the main focus components of all the programs carried out on the plateau. As
identified in the strategic plan where there were low interest in eco- enterprising
consensus building stopped. The literacy program in the non formal sector was
established prior to the MCASP and strengthened through the formation and
incorporation of the Barai Non-formal Education Association (BNEA). There were many
activities that were not implemented in Gender and the Training components,

The new Strategic direction for NACODA identified the need to further up skill staff
program officers and volunteers and provide gender equality in MCASP on the plateau.

CORE VALUES SUMMARY
The workshop participants NACODA core values are summarized as follows:

* HOLISTIC and INTEGRATED
NACODA believes that for the whole community to benefit , the developmental process
must take into account the Physical, Mental, Emotional and Spiritual development
aspects of an individual. the family, the community and the country.

* PEOPLE PARTICIPATION
NACODA believes that stakeholders and all people must be active participants in any
transformation processes or programs intended to develop their resources and in order to
improve their lives, through what they have within in order to live and upon which their
well being depends.

* EQUALITY AND SOCIAL JUSTICE

NACODA believes in the equal participation of all stakeholders within the whole
population of community elders, adults (women and men), youths and children of all
back grounds and abilities. allow equai distribution of resources and access to services,
The Managalas plateau has its own ethnic groups with indigenous cultures in addition to
ethnic groups that have migrated and settled in the area permanently. As there are
differing cultures, there are different religious groups that are to participate equally and
should not be over looked.

CREATIVE TENSION.

This is the first time a Strategic Plan has been drawn up for NACODA. As such a lot of
critical issues that have plagued the organization since it was established have been
discussed openly. The Strategic Planning workshop re-visited the organization's
Structure. Constitution, and Stakeholders. These have shaped the organization as such.

However, there are still many that need to be continually addressed and discussed at
relevant forums and levels. These issues will continually shape the organization because
they will always be there. These are the Creative Tensions that are unique to NACODA
because of the programs and activities it is involved in as well as the culture of the
organization- how NACODA do things.

The most important tensions are as follows:-

1. Working relationship with MDF
It has been realized that there is a great need for the MDF to implement planned activities
with NACODA.

2. Relationship between PWM and NACODA

There are people who have negative views about the work of NACODA. This will
remain a continuous tension as long as Roles and Responsibilities are not clearly defined.
This tension can only be addressed on a case-by-case basis and will remain for as long as
there is an absent of organization and program plan in operational.

3. Equal distribution of Funds.
Another tension that remains to be addressed continuously is the equal distribution of
funds to the Managalas plateau and especially NACODA for project implementation.

4. Clarity of roles, responsibilities and Functions of NACODA by MDF and PWM
There has been need to clarify the roles, responsibilities and functions. This tensions can
be said to have started from the fact that a fot of the existing stakeholders have had no
say in the establishment of NACODA and what its primary functions are.

5. Legitimacy of the NACODA

The NACODA was incorporated in however ihe Organisations governance requirements
needed to be in place.

There is a great need to carry out awareness on NACODA to the communities in zone
two, especially on the plateau.

4.0 BIODIVERSITY INVENTORY {DISCUSSIONS)

The survey was conducted over twenty working days and nights. A total of 820 tap and 120
net nights and days were utilised in ail the three sites. Although maximum effort was put into
the survey in November 2005 the results were quite unsatisfactory.

At site one, only two species of mammais, Paramelomys mollis, a rat and Syconycteris
australis, the common blossom bat. were captured at 1240m asi. We had anticipated more
than five (5) different soecies of both rodents and bats. The same number was expected of
smaller marsupials and one or two of the larger animals. The reptile composition was also
unsatisfactory. No other svecies was seen excent for the very common Emoia lizards.

Putei, which is site two of the survey also yield the same results. After a total of five nights of
sampling none of rats and marsupials except for a bandicoot was caught by locals, five
species of bats and five of reptiles were captured. This is very unsatisfactory because of the
high number of species which are expected to be present in a lowland rainforest

The same unsatisfactory results were seen at Pongani. We expected more but caught two (2)
species of rats (Rattus exulans, Melomys rufescans), and four (4) bats (Syconycteris
australis, Pranyctimene raptor, Nyctimene albiventer, Macroglossus minimus) from the
nets. Apart from the white bandicoot (possibly Peroryctes broadbenti) that we saw and some
rats (possibly Uromys caudimaculatus, Mottled Tailed Giant rat) that the survey team saw
scavenging amongst the leaf litter in the forest. there were no captures either from the people
or from children as is often seen in other villagers.

Although actual captures were not what we had anticipated, ethnographic information and also
from our observations, we can say that other factors could have contributed to the poor turn-
over of sampling.

Our observations at Putei and Pongani such as diggings in and around ant mounds, at the
base of rotten and fallen tree trunks show that there are Echidnas (ant eaters) and bandicoots

5.2 Social impacis
5.2.1 Hunting Practices

Hunting is still one of the activities thai the villagers take part in from time to fime. During the
period of survey, a female bandicoot with two young joeys was captured and eaten. Onlt the
lower mandible was retrieved for colieciec

Food is abundant. People are well nourished with surplus garden food resources. Wild foods
for human consumption is also abundant except for protein supplements. Therefore hunting for
wild meat seemed to occur on a requiar basis. Pacpie have pigs, dogs, chickens and cats in
the villages. However, domestic pigs and chicken are only consumed during important cultural
occasions, while dogs are kept for hunting and cats as pets to keep house rats away.

People in the area of survey lack protein supplements. Therefore, they will continue to hunt for
wild meat until they can be able to afford protein supplements that are sold in village trade
stores.

5.2.2 Gardening/Subsistence

People in the MPCA are gardeners. Each family has several gardens and food is surplus.
There are so many varieties of food crops, which can cater for their daily supplements.
However, the slash and burn method of gardening and shifting cultivation that they practice
tend to make way for large areas to be left exposed to the disadvantage of smaller ground
animals. Many trees around new gardens are chopped down indiscriminately and ieft to rot.
That was seen in many villages where we walked.

According to the villagers, people are currently making gardens in forested areas, which were
never touched in the last two (2) decades. Gardesing in previously untouched forests at higher
will continue as population increases. Currently with the slash and burn method that these
people use, there will be more open areas. which will affect smalier animais that utilise forest
cover for survival and allow invasive saecies of plants to colonise these areas which may result
in permanent grass patches.

Appendix !i. Equipment and materials used for Biodiversity Inventories
1. Aluminium Traps

Elliot and Tomahawk traps

Thess traps are specificaily built to be laid on the ground to tap smal ground mammals and
marsupials. They can also be used to tran arboreal animals, mostly rats and small marsupials
that spent most of their foraging time up in the trees or above ground.

Sampling of these animals depend on how you place the traps with appropriate baits.

2. Mist Nets.

These are biack nylon nets that are used for sampling birds and bats. Mist nets are tied to wo
(2) poles and placed across waterways, along ridges. open spaces in the forests, across
mouths of caves and in appropriate locations in the sampling site which can maximise catches
The nets are open ali through out the day and also at nights depending on the weather.
Regular visits are made to the nets during the day to check for birds and similarly at nighttime
for bats. Nets are usually ‘closed’ when there are storms.

3. Other items

The dissecting items comprise of needles and threads, cotton wool, scalpel blades, scissors,
plastic bags. bucket, measuring cylinder, scales (different weights), flagging tapes (coloured),
Sticky tapes, ropes, sticks, knives, plastic containers, pencils, note books, rulers, tape
measure, assorted tags, torches, jamps, specimen bags for live specimens and others that
was necessary for sampling.

Chemicals are also utilised to preserve the anima's. The most common chemical is alcohol.
The best concentration/strength at which animals are preserved is 70%. We use chloroform to
allow animals to die slowly without pain and sorinkle borax sait on fresh skins to prevent them
from decomposition. Drying over a normal bush fire consistently helps to dry the skins and
skulls of animals that are prepared as museum specimens.

Enumeration of trees and other vegetation at the Guguavo Ridge in the
Owen Stanley Range of Papua New Guinea.

Kasbeth Evei

Postgraduate Centre, University of Papua New Guinea P O Box 320 Uni PO, N.C.D

Introduction
This survey was basically done to establish the abundance and species diversity of trees
and other plants that occur in the primary forests of Tetebedi area. In Papua New Guinea
(PNG), Montane primary forests are home to many endemic plants and animals.
Likewise, the primary forests at Guguavo ridge is no exception since it contain some of
PNG’s endemic plants and animals.

The Guguavo Ridge upper montane primary rainforest has a sparse distribution of
trees and other forest fiour planis with a 20m visibility. The forest is made up of 80
species of trees ranging from 2m to more than 30m, several species of herbs and vines
(lianas), ferns, gingers, orchids, pandans, palms and bamboos which total up to more than
130 species of plants.

This study enabied us to establish tree density (per m2) and species distribution in
the survey area.

Methods

The survey plot is located on Guguave Ridge some !00km East of Port Moresby and
situated at 1600m above sea level in the Cwen Stanley Range. It is a three hours walk
away from the nearest airstrip of Tetebedi viliage in Cro province.

A 20m X 200m (0.4 ha) sample plot was randomly selected along the ridge. We
marked trees and saplings with the DBH (Diameter at Breast height) of 7cm and above.
We collected leaf voucher specimens for further identification. Cther forest flour plants
were noted as inhabitanis of the foresi area.

Tree height data analysis
Height of trees were categorized inte six height classes; dm-4m =1, Sm-9m =2, 10m-i4m
= 3, 15m-19m = 4, 20m-24m =5, 25m or more = 6.

Results
540 trees were sampled within the 0.4 ha plot. Just over half the trees were between !m

and Si, While nearly 40% were between 10m to iSm andi0% were above 20m. The
highest DBH of the trees was 150cm and the highest iree height was 32m (see
appendix1). There are more than 80 species of trees and another 70 to 80 other plant
species that make up the whole of Guguavo Ridge Rainforest area (see appendix 2).
There were about 2 trees/m2. Altogether, there were more than 130 species cf plants that
were observed. The dominant species of trees include, Cryptocarya, Litsea, Pouteria,
Evodia and Castenopsis.

Discussions

Tropical rainforests make up 7% of the world’s surface area (Swaine, 1965) and contain
more than half of the known terrestrial organisms but yet, the least understood of all the
major vegetation types (Collinson, 1975). Every effort must be made to protect all
sections of the tropica! rainforests of the world, including Papua New Guinea.

As such, the Guguavo Ridge montane rainforest is home to some of the Papua
New Guineas mest endangered and endemic species of plants (Trees and orchids} as well
as anime!s and fungi. Since the site occurs at the top of the mountains, it is vuineradis te
landslides, soil erosion and species loss shouid there be a slight disturbance in the forest
structure. This would then affect the distribution and dispersion strategies of several tree
species since not al! species of trees have the same dispersal mechanism. For example, in
this survey, the Evodia is randomly dispersed while Pouteria and Castenopsis are
dispersed regularly and the Cryptoceryas and Litseas have 2 clumped dispersion ia the
plot.

A good number of timber and non-timber forest products occur within the area
which means that a sustainable forest use practice be encouraged for the region. The
Forest in the long run, will act as a seed bank, sustain all life, retain and recycle nutrients
rapidly and will continue to so for thousands of years (Walter, 1985). Other benefits from
the forests includes poliution indications (esp. SO2) and standing forest biomass will act
as Carbon sinks (absorb carbon dioxide).

Recommendations
The people, especially the older men and woman of the Tetebedi area have an invaluable

ethno biolcgica! and natura! history knowledge of all the naiural resources that surrounds
them. it will be a bonus shouid there be some sort of documentation of these knowledge
in the future encounters.

i would push for a Wildlife Management Area to be established as soon as possible so as
to instill the concept of “public natural resource ownership” for sustainable resource use.
To continue to show up physically every now and then to oversee how things are being
conducted with the people, by the people with a little bit of outside intervention will be
rewarding for all stakeholders.

1.0 Introduction

The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area covers a land area of over 360,000 hectares.
The Managalas Plateau itself is situated within and around the Owen Stanley Range to the
South and West, the Sibuim Ranges to the South-east and Mount Lamington to the North and
East. The Managalas Plateau encompasses a wide variety of vegetation types from alpine
forests at altitudes of 3,800m, to tropical rainforests in the mountains and hills, as well as
savanna grassland and anthropogenic garden areas. The Managalas Plateau is isolated from
most of the urban centers within the Oro Province as a result of poor road conditions, which
are poorly, if at all maintained.

Anthropogenic activity is restricted to mid-altitude valleys as in most parts of Papua New
Guinea, leaving the surrounding mountains virtually uninhabited. More than 15,000 people
from about 150 clans live in more than 70 villages within the Managalas Plateau. Most if not
all of these people enjoy a subsistent livelihood, with much dependence being placed on the
surrounding environment.

Through conservation awareness programs initiated and conducted by Partners With
Melanesians (PwM), the people within the Managalas Plateau have decided to conserve their
forests. Hence, a core group was formed, the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF),
which has worked in close partnership with PwM to develop sound development strategies
for the area. Following on from a preliminary biodiversity survey conducted by a team of
scientists from the University of Papua New Guinea and the Department of Environment and
Conservation, a further study was conducted from the 7” — 26" November 2005, in selected
sites of varying altitude within the Afore District of Oro Province. The survey conducted was
similar to that of the previous year in that it involved surveys on plants, birds, mammals and
herpetofauna.

The objective of the survey was to provide baseline information on the flora and fauna
within the selected sites and to make comparisons of their distribution and diversity at
various altitudes. The information collected and compiled on the flora and fauna will be used
toward the establishment of the Wildlife Conservation Area status for the Managalas Plateau.
In conjunction with this, PwM in its drive to promote capacity building among young Papua
New Guineans has taken on the initiative to facilitate for the training of university students in
field techniques and skills required for biodiversity surveys.

2.0 Methods

There were three sites surveyed, all of which were located within the Afore district of the
Oro Province. The first site surveyed was called Murayane, located at 1240m above sea level
(asl) along the Krerim Ranges, a few kilometers outside of Anatua Village. The second site,
called Putei was 660m (asl) and was located about 5 kilometers outside of Tahama Village.
The third site was a village at Pongani, positioned at 70m (asl). At all the sites surveyed a
total of about 4-5 days were spent in conducting the survey. The day prior to the actual
sampling a general observation of the site vegetation and the landscape was done basically to

to

identify the appropriate spot to place the traps, mist nets and transects for the flora and fauna
surveys.

Flora survey
2.1 Plant sampling

The main objective of the flora sampling was to identify the species diversity and the
structure of the forest within the selected sites of the Managalas Plateau. The main sampling
method used, consisted of the use of a 50m x 50m plot being placed within each of the three
selected sites. Within each of these plots five quadrats of 10m x 10m were drawn and
sampled. This enabled every 10m interval within the 50m x 50m plot to be sampled.

Within each of the five quadrats, the different tree species encounted with a diameter at
breast height (DBH) greater than 5 were recorded together with their estimated heights.
Within the 50m x 50m plot, ten random plots measuring 5m x Sm were also selected and
marked out. From these random plots all the trees and shrubs found were identified and
tallied. This was done to estimate the abundance of tree species within the forest. Thus, apart
from sampling, plants specimens were collected, pressed in paper and taken back to the
UPNG Herbarium for storage and preservation as a record of the species of plants found
within the area surveyed.

Fauna survey
2.2. Bird sampling

Due to time constraints and other difficulties faced with the land geomorphology, the method
used for bird sampling was ‘random mist netting’ rather than the standard line transect
method. Within the random placement method, mist nets consisting of 5 layers were attached
to poles of 2 metres in length and placed at selected positions. The selection of sites for the
placement of the misi nets are done so as to maximize the catch rate in as little time as
possible since we were only allowed to stay in a particular site for about 5 days. In the
random placement method, the sites selected were 10-20m apart. The mist nets were placed
up to 2 metres above the ground. Generally, in instances where it is perceived that more birds
can be caught closer or lower to the ground, the nets are placed closer to the ground, at about
0.5m above the ground. In other instances where it is deemed that the catch can be increased
by placing the nets higher above the ground, then the nets are placed at distances of 1-2m off
the ground. In this case the nets were placed |-2m above the ground with the mist nets
stretching up to 5m above the ground.

The mist nets as stated, consist of 5 layers of netting with an overlapping pocket between
each layer where the trapped birds are supposed to drop into and remain until they are
removed from the net. The netting material is soft so as no to damage the birds whilst they
are held within the net.

The nets were checked at regular intervals in the moming, during the day, in the afternoon
and during the night. This was done so as to minimize the amount or the period of time that
the birds are left in the nets or held in captivity. The birds trapped were then collected and

weighed initially. After the weighing, those birds that were collected as specimens on the
previous trip were released if they were still alive but if they were not, then they were
disposed of appropriately. For any new specimens that were collected, the weights along with
various other measurements of the birds’ features were taken and the details recorded on bird
specimen data sheets provided by Mr. Kulmoi from the Department of Environment and
Conservation (DEC). These data sheets were to be filed at the DEC as a representation of the
bird species that are to be found within the area surveyed. Other methods also employed in
the data collection for the bird species found in the area included; general observations and
biological resource utilization surveys where the local people were interviewed on their
knowledge of what bird species they knew to be present within the area.

The specimens themselves were skinned and stuffed by Ms. R. Singadan to be kept at the
UPNG- NSRC Animal collection also as a representation of the birds’ species to be found
within the area surveyed.

2.3 Mammal sampling.

For the mammals, there were basically two types of methods used to catch them. For the bats
we used the mist nets that were used for the birds also and as for the rodents and other small
marsupials we used trapping system. The mist nets were basically set to catch lower canopy,
fruit birds and bats.

The traps used were of two types, the Tomahawk and the Elliot traps. At times lizards and
snakes are caught in these traps. In the process of trapping, baiting was very important and
necessary to get a good catch. The baits we used were wheat bix, peanut butter, cooked
coconut and at times ripe banana.

The traps were set in quadrats of 50 by 50 m and within this quadrat they were piaced along
transect lines positioned at every {0m intervals. A total of 36 traps were set in the marked out
quadrat.

After the mammals were collected, the desired species were then dissected, skinned, dried
and packed for the UPNG mammal collection. Ms. Rose Singadan did all these and at times
we were allowed to perform these tasks under her supervision.

2.4 Herpetofauna sampling.

The herpetofauna sampling was based on mainly the frogs. However, we came across other
specimens such as snakes and lizards. These specimens were collected, photographed and
preserved also in alcohol and brought to the UPNG museum

In the frog sampling at each of the three camps, the sites we selected were located near
creeks, rivers, ponds, whilst on the land we looked under dead and fallen leaves, beneath the
ground, under dead logs and rotten wood, near roots and old tree barks. Others were found
lying on the leaves and branches of trees ranging from about a few centimeters to more than

three meters above the ground. These areas were located within walking distances ranging
from about ten minutes to an hours walk from the camp.

Some of the frogs were found during the day. However the best catch time was found to be
during the night or from dusk till dawn. It was during these times that all the different
sounds made by the different species of frogs were heard, easily distinguished and recorded
accordingly using a specialized tape recorder.

During the day, the frog specimens collected during the previous night were identified,
photographed and preserved in alcohol. The heart from each frog species collected was
removed and placed into a labeled vial that would be sent overseas for DNA sequencing. The
specimens collected would then be stored in the UPNG Animal collection.

Further information on the species of reptiles to be found within each of the sites were
obtained from the local people via their ethnographic knowledge. Thus, we were able to get a
‘feel’ of what was actually within the area despite our insufficient catch rate.

3.0. Result

3.1. Brief evaluation of the Species found.

The Appendix provides a listing of all the flora and fauna species that were confirmed to be
found within the Managalas Plateau. This conveys the magnitude of animal and plant species
that were found within the site surveyed; yet the Plateau encompasses a vast area and these
species may be doubled or even tripled with further research, bearing in mind that this is only
a preliminary study of the area.

Firstly for the flora sampling in general we discovered that the vegetation at each of the sites
varies according to the different aititude and climate. In that as altitude decreases the plant
numbers and height varies. Hence the Managalas Piateau is observed to have a rich diversity
of plants and from this survey it was site 2, Putei that had the highest diversity of trees.

The bird sampling results showed that there is a vast number of bird species to be found
within the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area. Some of the birds found there include the
Raggiana Bird of Paradise as well as other species of Bird of Paradise such as the Rifle Bird
of Paradise and several species of the Kingfisher Bird of Paradise. These birds are protected
by law and thus add to the conservation status of the area surveyed. There was observed to be
a general trend of increase in species diversity with decrease in altitude and the Bird of
Paradise species were observed to be rather common in the sites surveyed.

As for the mammals the most common species found were mostly of bats and rats. Bats
being the Synconycteris australis (Common Blossom bat) from the Chiroptera family while
the rats being the Paramelomys mollis and Rattus exullants both from the family of Muridae.
Cuscuses were also observed in two of the sites (1 and 2), which we surveyed. Southern
brown cuscus and Dorias tree kangaroo from the family of Phalangeridae and Macropodidae
respectively were the common cuscuses sighted.

4.0 Discussion:

4.1. Experiences:

It was a great opportunity to have been part of this biodiversity survey team. We learnt so
much during this training. Not only did we put the theoretical skills we learnt in school into
practice, but the general expectations of what is required in order to carry out biodiversity
surveys.

4.1.1 Flora sampling encounters and experiences

Through observations from all three sites, distinct differences could be seen in the types of
vegetation. Each site was located at various altitudes and so each was exposed to different
environmental factors such as temperature and soil type. In site 1, Murayane, mosses and
ferns were more abundantly distributed. This was seen to be typical of areas of high
altitudes. With site 2, Putei, the common vegetation features included buttress roots and
cauliflorous plants. These features are found mostly in lowland rainforests. As for site 3,
Pongani, the area was identified to be that of flood plain.

In terms of the skills acquired from the flora survey, it was learnt that one of the most
important tools in conducting a survey is selecting an appropriate sampling technique. Plants
unlike animals are immobile however it is impossible to count every single species in an area
so using the right method, such as the line transect, can give a more realistic account of the
whole forest vegetation. In collecting the required data, we learnt to use a dbh tape to find the
diameter of trees at breast height. We also learnt to estimate tree heights during the sampling.
The identification of trees was another vital skill required for the field and as beginners we
learnt to distinguish a few trees species. But apart from the above, simple observations were
learnt to be another important feature especially in trying to understand the distribution of
certain species. Hence, the overall experience from the flora survey was very worthwhile
and it taught us just how much diversity there are in the number of tree species in Managalas.
This experience also helped us all to enhance much of what learnt from our various Plant
Biology courses.

=== page 9 ===
4.1.2 Bird sampling encounters and experiences

On general observations alone, it can be stated that there was a general trend of increase in
the diversity of bird species with decrease in altitude. That is, the bird species diversity
increased as we moved form the higher altitude site down to the other two sites of lower
altitude. The bird species diversity at the first site was minimal with only a few species being
able to adapt to the conditions at such high altitude. The second site showed an increase in
the bird species diversity in that some of the same birds from the first site were caught along
with several other new species. In the second site we were able to catch two different species
of Kingfisher Bird of Paradise, and they were observed to be rather common within the area
surveyed. At the third site, we also caught a different species of Kingfisher Bird of Paradise
along side this we had the opportunity to see a female Raggiana Bird of Paradise. It was an
exhilarating experience to be able to feel and have a ‘hands-on’ encounter with these
magnificent birds.

Skills learnt in the bird surveys and mist netting includes general observations and listening
for birdcalls that were used for identification of species not caught but observed to be within
the area surveyed. We were also taught how to put up the nets and also how to select the sites
in order to obtain a maximal catch. We also learnt how to remove the birds from the nets
efficiently so as not to cause too much harm and discomfort to the trapped birds. We also
acquired skills on how to take proper measurements of the birds’ identifying features and
characteristics and on how to fill out the proper forms as required by the Department of
Environment and Conservation. In addition to all these, we were also shown techniques on
how to preserve the specimens for future reference.

4.1.3 Mammals sampling encounters and experiences

Mammals are only a small part of the whole living kingdom. To have a better understanding
of mammals it is very important to study their environmental lifestyle and morphological
structures. For species identification one has to carefully study the morphological differences
that lie between species of rats or bats or any mammals in general, It is of significant
importance that our diverse mammals’ species must be conserved not only for scientific
research purposes but also for our future generation to appreciate the various mammal
species the Managalas Plateau has in abundance.

In carrying out this mammal sampling during these three weeks, we had the privilege to learn
so many things. We were mostly putting into practice what we have learnt in school (biology
courses) while other skills learnt were totally new to us but may be of vital importance to our
future careers. We practically carried out line transecting and set traps at 10m by 10m
marked out intervals of the 50m by 50m transect. It is important to set traps in quadrat mark-
outs or transect for statistical analysis, retrieving traps afterwards and population calculations
(Density- an appropriate unit for species distribution or population count). We learnt also that
the different species distribution is influence by so many factors such as the climatic
condition, vegetation type. the production time of the forest, the natural hazards that occurred

=== page 10 ===
in the past years and urbanization factors. So in carrying out a Biodiversity assessment all
these factors must be taken into consideration. In that way one can really understand why
some species can survive in one part of the environment/vegetation while others cannot.

Apart from transecting we also leamt how to prepare mammal species for specimen
collection. We did skinning, dissecting and packing of specimen mammals. Each of us had a
turn to prepare animal specimen for species collection and preservation.

We also leamt that it is important to be open-minded when working in a group and out in the
field. To attain good survey results we have to be patient at times and better still, have a
good relationship with the locals.

All in all it was a very good learning experience for us despite some short falls on the way.

4.1.4 Herpetofauna sampling encounters and experiences

We were privileged to have traveled into the lower montane forest (1* camp), the lowland
rainforest (2" camp), and the secondary vegetation and savanna grassland (3° camp) to
locate the different species of frogs in the Managalas Plateau. The frogs from our experience
had proved to be important as indicator species of the general conditions of the environment
amongst other fauna and flora in any type of rainforest. We say this because in a forested
conservation area, such as the one we surveyed, there was an abundance of frog species, as
we were able to find twenty- five (25) species. The fact that we collected these many species
in such a short period of time proved that the rainforest is quite healthy when compared to
some areas of similar vegetation that had a lesser number of species. We had collected these
many species in such a short period and had proved that the rainforest is quite healthy
whereas in some areas that we had seen and heard stories of had lesser number of species as
low as two.

In a healthy forest, the canopy is maintained to shade the forest floor in which maintains the
moisture or water content of the forast floor microclimate. The frogs at best prefer to keep
their surface tissues wet. Due to the fact that frogs have a very thin epithelial layer, it has to
be kept moist to allow for effective diffusion of substances between cells. This dampness
adaptive characteristic has suited the frogs to a life in water and had thus evolved the
mechanisms to prevent death as a result of excessive water loss to the environment. In the
Managalas we found six different species of Litoria sp. and three Hylophorbus sp. and
majority had maintained two and single species. This diversity of species showed high
genetic diversity and a general importance to conservation and further studies.

5.0 Recommendations:

As part of our observations during the course of the survey, we believe that the following
suggestions and recommendations can be used to better facilitate for the scientists involved
in the survey as well as to obtain better results in the surveys conducted.

There should be proper liaison with the local people so as not to cause any disputes
within their communities. The people going into the communities should be sensitive
to the traditions and customs within each of the communities and not try to enforce
their ideas on the people. Their has to be prior ground work done so that there is
ample discussion with the people and they are aware of all that is to happen in their
community in advance. If there are any existing disputes among people within a
community, then alternate arrangements have to be made to sort out the problem
before the surveying team arrives so as not to disrupt the sampling schedule of the
researchers.

There should be greater awareness to better educate and familiarize the local people
with the importance of forest and wildlife conservation and how this can be beneficial
to them now and also for their future generations. They have to be made aware that
the decisions they make has local as well as global implications in they are in a way
contributing toward the controlling of global issues such as global warming and the
heating up of the earth's atmosphere.

Timetables have to be flexible to account for any unforeseen circumstances that may
happen along the way. We believe that the actual sampling time should be at least a
week (7 days) long to allow for maximization of the catch rate for the mammals
especially. Traveling time should also be taken into account and given enough
allocation.

The surveys should be arranged at different times of the year to capture the different
seasons that take place during the year so as to have a better understanding of the
species distribution and seasonality. For instance, this year’s survey was conducted
during a time when most of the forests were not in fruiting season and this may have
contributed to the very low catch rate that was observed for most of the mammal and
bird species that are known to inhabit this part of the country. Thus, we recommend
that the survey for next year be put to the middie of the year to get a better
understanding of how the seasons may affect animal behavior and distribution.

6.0 Conclusion

All in all, we can say that this has been an exciting and very educational trip for us as we
were able to see what actually happens in the field and develop some skills that may be
helpful to us in whatever field we may be employed in. The training provided in the field was
complementary to what we learnt in school whilst also giving us much needed practical
experience in biological field surveying.

|. Introduction.

Two facilitators (John Ericho, Abane Haefa) were contracted to carry out the week long
meeting/workshop at Serefuna in the Managalas Plateau from the 19" — 25* December 2005. At the pre-
meetings with the Partners with Melanesians (PwM) the terms of reference was issued and a briefing was
given and questions were raised to ensure everyone was on the same wavelength. The two facilitators
met and presented a tentative outline of the programs to PwM staff to comment and improved the
program outline. The team was transported by hire transport to the Itokama over the Owen Stanley
Range. After about an hour and half walk the team arrived at our destination.

In this report a brief background is presented, followed by a brief description of TOR, a list of the team
members, a brief description of methods used, and the issues to be addressed. Then discussion points
are captured and presented followed by next steps and a summary at the end.

ll. Background.

Partners with Melanesians (PwM) are a national NGO established about 20 years to work closely with the
people of the Managalas Plateau. The Managalas Plateau is described below in the Terms of Reference
background information as follows.

Managelas Plateau is a raised valley lying between 600 to 1000 meters of altitude above the coastal
plain of Oro Province and is situated south of Popondetta and North of Port Moresby. It stretches
between the Owen Stanley Ranges to the south and west, the Sibium Ranges and Mt. Lamington and
the Hydrogrphers to the north ands east. it encompasses 380 000 ha, comprising areas of alpine heights
of 3 800 meters, montane and hill forest, savanna, anthropogenic grassland and gardens. The
countryside is very mountainous and ridges. rivers, and water falls make up the scenery. About 12-15000
people of approximately 150 clan groups are living in 40 village communities. Clusters of sub-clan
groups, around which most social and economical activity is organized today, effectively fall into ten
cultural zones.

People in Managalas are subsistence farmers and grow their own food of yam, taro, kaukau and other
garden produce. The Plateau also boasts cash crops which includes; coffee, vanilla and peanuts and
okari nut. Most of these have not been sold out due to lack of proper roads and air transport costs being
too high. While the opportunity exist to develop economically. Logging and oil palm development lurks
precariously in the background threatening menacingly to overtake the Plateau in the guise of economic
development. Thus the beginning and inception of the Managalas Program by PwM is to arrest that
threat. The Managalas Program includes three main programs. These include: the Consensus building,
the Capacity Building and the Conservation Program. The Consensus building program embarked on
mobilizing and organizing the Managalas communities into 10 cultural zones each zone incorporating a
community based organization (CBO). It was envisaged that the MDF will develop into a well trained and
organized organization to work with each of the CBOs to help realize the vision of developing, “A
peaceful and self reliant communal society living in harmony with nature’. This was the Exit Strategy
envisaged years ago. The Consensus building program has nearly completed this task. The Capacity
building project also worked hard to develop the capacity of the MDF and CBO Board and Management.
These two projects are ongoing and are nearing the completion stages. The Conservation project is
continuing with mapping and inventory work and this needs more emphasis and focus as it has the
possibility of being derailed by socioeconomic development requirements.

INTRODUCTION

The Island of New Guinea fauna consists largely of frogs. According to Richards (2002), the 250
frog species were documented from New Guinea, more diverse compare to other countries. ‘This
is because New Guinea has a constant warm and wet environment that provides humid habitats
and cool temperature at widely different elevations (0-3600m asl) (Richards 2002).

Frogs and other amphibian make up the important component of New Guinea ecosystem and
occur at high densities. They provide important source of food to other organisms and for many
local people (Allison, Bickford et al. 1998).

One aspect of identifying diversity of plants and animals species is to understand and make
broader ecological assessment of biodiversity (Richards 2003). For example Orsak, Easen et al.
(2001), illustrated Lepidoptera, especially moths were chosen because it was used as a general
biodiversity indicators.

This study was intended to document frogs of Managalas Plateau, within approx. 3600 hectares
of virgin forest. Papua New Guinea has difficult mountain terrain which is inadequate to conduct
studies in many interior areas.

Frogs collected at Managalas will contribute to our knowledge of frog fauna in Papua New
Guinea.

The main objectives of Herpetofauna biological survey were to:
1. Document the number of frog species found at 3 elevations at each sites.
2. Identify species abundance and diversity, enable proper management and promote
conservation in sustainable way.

METHODS

A month biological survey was conducted at Managalas plateau, Oro Province from g* 24°
November. I conducted frog survey at night by search and visual encounter survey. I detected
frogs by their advertisement calls and recorded their calls using a tape recorder. I also did
thorough search on the forest floors, turning over logs and going along streams and search
rugged mountain and steep hill slopes.

At daytime | took photographed of all new frog species in life. | took several body measurements
of frogs and fixed the specimens in 10% formalin and later store them in 70% ethanol. I also
took tissues for future DNA study.

For the purpose of this report, | identify and named frog species according to their morphological
characters. Proper identification of specimens will be given with scientific names and the
specimens will be stored at Natural Science Resource Centre (NSRC) at University of Papua
New Guinea.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Species Diversity and Abundance

A total of 110 individual frog specimens was collected of which 27 species was documented
during the survey from 4 families (Table 2).

Managalas has a promising high diversity of frog fauna. The frog assemblage at Managalas is
comprised of common frogs and few rare frog species especially smaller frog species from
family Microhylidae. It is true Managalas has wide selection of habitats that is good for frogs.

Compare number of species collected at 3 elevations. More species was collected at site 2,
followed by site 1 and site 3. This does not mean there are less number of species at sitel and
site 3. High diversity of frog call was heard at site 1 and site 2 but were scattered in camp 3. Few
of the species were widespread and abundant at all 3 sites. The reason some of the species were
not collected because of some nights had continuous heavy rain (Figure2).

There were significant differences in the number of individual specimens collected in 4 families.
The family Microhylidae has about (90%) of individual specimens collected at site 1 and site 2,
Hylidae (23%) and Ranidae (14%). The Myobatrachidac has the poor representative of
individual frog collected (1 %), Figure 2.

In addition, the difference indicates that some frog species can be found at different elevation.
For example Ranidae and Myobatrachidae were found at lowland (site 2 and site 3) compared to
Microhylidae and Hylidae. It be can demonstrated that frog species in a family can only found at
an elevation, are limited and have habitat preference, (e.g. Albericus sp, a montane frog), (see

Frog family and species in brief

Hylidae: Common name Tree Frog. Several species collected were very abundant, calling early
hours of the evening during and after the rain, two Litoria species were collected down hill on
small trees about 1.5m-<3m above ground along the stream at Site 1, (1200m). Other 3 Litoria
species were collected during the rain. Litoria sp3. was collected at stilled old pooled water, ~
2m-5m on the tree. Litoria sp2 and Litoria sp4 both collected on the forest floor next to the
stream. Nyctimystes species is the only species in different genus, distinguished by large eyes
and a membrane when close. A specimen was collected in the day along a fast flowing river
upstream, Site 1, (1200m) and other specimen collected at camp 2, (660m) on forest floor, closed
canopy. Litoria thesaurensis and Litoria infrefranata are lowland species live in open pooled
and swampy area; the call of LZ. infrefranata was heard adjacent to the main road next to the
village Site 3 (~50-70m).

Microhylidae: Most frogs in this family dwell on the forest floor and above ground on tree leaves
about <Im-15m or more. Microhylids were abundant, several calls heard were very difficult to
capture. Al/bericus sp was the only specimen collected at montane forest, Site 1, down hill on
leaves of small shrub trees about >1m adjacent to the stream. 3 Austrochaperina species were
abundant, captured on the forest floor at the lower montane forest, Site 1, (1200m) and some
frogs were brought during day time by local assistances. In addition, Hylophorbus species were
found abundant on the forest floor at Site 1 and Site 2. The Oreophryne (arboreal sp.) abundant
at Site 1 calling above ground about 1.5m-2.5m on tree leaves, it was also collected at Site 2 but
only one individual specimen was collected in Site 3. On the other hand Oreophryne (nr
hypsiops sp.) were abundant at Site 2 but was absent in Site 3, only one specimen was collected
near Anatua village 3m on the coconut palm (~800m). Cophixalus species was abundant at Site |
and Site 2 including Site 3 (~1200m-70m). The species is small compared to other species and
often hard to locate on forest floor. Sphenophryne sp. and Xenorhina sp. are two species
captured in Site | and Site 2. Sphenophryne sp. is not so abundant in Site 1, (1200m) 2
specimens were collected in the day on the ground under the tent during the rain. It was different

CONCLUSION
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) has extremely high diversity of frog fauna.

There was a significance differences in frog species collected at 3 sites. Some species of frogs
collected live and are found only at certain elevation and habitats, (e.g. Albericus sp) was found
in montane forest, other species do well in high and low elevation, e.g. Oreophryne (arboreal sp).
Some species lived only in low elevation (¢.g. Platymantis papuensis).

The data showed high species diversity in family Microhylidae at site 1 and site 2, The other
family Hylidae, Ranidae may likely show increase diversity. In addition different frog species
forage different habitats. For example, Hylidae are tree frogs and are common along streams,
rivers and live above ground on trees.

SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION

1) Actively carry out awareness program to educate resource owners the importance of
research and conservation.

2) Clearing large areas for gardening increase temperature within surrounding environment,
this practice in future provide good habitat for other introduce animals, ¢.g. Bufo marinus
(introduced toad), easily finds its way in hot temperature. Many frog species become
disadvantage when their habitats and environment change and will from the heat.

3) Develop long term monitoring and research into special plants and animal species. Such
long term monitoring guide good forest management and promote sustainable
development and is vital for decision makers in future.

I wish to THANK Partners With Melanesian (PWM) invited me to take part in Managalas
Biological Survey, namely Vincent Manukayasi (project Manager), Anoia (Field Officer), Roy
Garawa, Bradley Dabadabab and Dickson Darebo. I want to extend my thank you to Rose
Singadan who took me on board to do Herpetofauna, Pais Piskaut (UPNG), Paulus Kulmoi
(DEC) and Hapo, Jacinta, Florence and Jane (4" year UPNG students) including local field
guides for their assistance in the field. I am very grateful to the landowners and communities of
Managalas who accepted us with great heart, these communities include Anatua, Taham and
Pongani. Further to cookers, you fed us with plenty to eat and finally to people who helped carry
our cargos going through rough and tough walking to 3 camp sites. THANK YOU. You
contributed to the success of the survey.

Your wise decision in protecting the forest and wildlife will support you TODAY and for your
children in FUTURE and country Papua New Guinea (PNG).

1.0 INTRODUCTION

The Managalas Plateau Proposed Conservation are is situated in the south eastern part of the
Southern Papuan region in the |jivitari District - Oro Province. The Proposed Conservation
Area constitutes an area of approximately 300,000 hectares and is located on a Plateau now
known as the Managalas Piateau.

The area is predominantly wet tropical rainforest and surrounded by the Owen Stanley
Mountains to the west, lowland rainforest extending to the coastal areas to the west

Composition and diversity of animals are relatively unknown in any literature in the Managalas
proposed Conservation Area although there have been studies (unpublished reports) done by
individual researchers in other parts of Oro Province and in neighboring Provinces (Milne Bay
and Morobe Province), that this Province share Provincial boundaries with.

Unpublished information that are collected from collection trips are likely to be kept at UPNG
Natural Science Resource Center and PNG National Museum where specimens of Birds,
Mammals, Reptiles and Frogs are deposited. However, other additional information are often
kept as individual field notes by the researcher and in institutional reports.

However, we can make assumptions from scarce published information that. the area may
contain a higher ievei of biodiversity than other neighboring areas. The area is abundant in
wild food resources and vast areas of the MPCA are covered in a variety of vegetation types
from secondary re growth/old gardens 'o open areas of grasslands, swamps which are often

waterlogged during rainy seasons, lowland rain forests at 500m asi to montane forests
reaching more than 2000m.

4.0 BIODIVERSITY INVENTORY (DISCUSSIONS)

The survey was conducted over twenty working days and nights. A total of 820 trap and 120
net nights and days were utilised in all the three sites. Although maximum effort was put into
the survey in November 2005 the results were quite unsatisfactory.

At site one, only two species of mammals, Paramelomys mollis, a tat and Syconycteris
australis, the common blossom bat, were captured at 1240m asi. We had anticipated more
than five (5) different species of both rodents and bats. The same number was expected of
smaller marsupials and one or two of the larger animals. The reptile composition was also
unsatisfactory. No other species was seen except for the very common Emoia lizards.

Putei, which is site two of the survey also yield the same results. After a total of five nights of
sampling none of rats and marsupials except for a bandicoot was caught by locals, five
species of bats and five of reptiles were captured. This is very unsatisfactory because of the
high number of species which are expected to be present in a lowland rainforest.

The same unsatisfactory results were seen at Pongani. We expected more but caught two (2)
species of rats (Rattus exulans, Melomys rufescans), and four (4) bats (Syconycteris
australis, Pranyctimene raptor, Nyctimene albiventer, Macroglossus minimus) from the
nets. Apart from the white bandicoot (possibly Peroryctes broadbeoti) that we saw and some
rats (possibly Uromys caudimaculatus, Mottled Tailed Giant rat) that the survey team saw
scavenging amongst the leaf litter in the forest, there were no captures either from the people
or from children as is often seen in other villagers.

Although actual captures were not what we had anticipated, ethnographic information and also
from our observations, we can Say that other factors could have contributed to the poor turn-

over of sampling.

5.1 Species of Conservation Value

within the conservation area. Others are found only in one area or more than one area. Only
two, Doria’s Tree Kangaroo (Dendrolagus dorinus), and Boelen’s python, Morelia boeleni
are protected by the the Flora/Fauna Act. Of the two, Boelen’s python is a “poorly known
species.”

Doria's Tree Kangaroo is widely distributed in the Southern Papuan region but it is a protected
species according to the Red Book of Protected species in PNG. There are ten (10) species of
Trees Kangaroos in the World and eight-(8) are found in New Guinea. Doria's Tree Kangaroo

5.2 Social impacts
5.2.1 Hunting Practices

Hunting is still one of the activities that the villagers take part in from time to time. During the
period of survey, a female bandicoot with two young joeys was captured and eaten. Onit the
lower mandibie was retrieved for collected.

Food is abundant. Peopie are well nourished with surplus garden food resources. Wild foods
for human consumption is also abundant except for protein supplements. Therefore hunting for
wild meat seemed to occur on a regular basis. People have pigs, dogs, chickens and cats in
the villages. However, domestic pigs and chicken are only consumed during important cultural
occasions, while dogs are kept for hunting and cats as pets to keep house rats away.

People in the area of survey lack protein supplements. Therefore, they will continue to hunt for
wild meat until they can be able to afford protein supplements that are sold in village trade
stores.

5.2.2 Gardening/Subsistence

People in the MPCA are gardeners. Each family has several gardens and food is surplus.
There are so many varieties of food crops, which can cater for their daily supplements.
However, the slash and burn method of gardening and shifting cultivation that they practice
tend to make way for large areas fo be left exposed to the disadvantage of smaller ground
animals. Many trees around new gardens are chopped down indiscriminately and left to rot
That was seen in many villages where we walked.

According to the villagers, people are currently making gardens in forested areas, which were
never touched in the last two (2) decades. Gardening in previously untouched forests at higher
will continue as population increases. Currently with the slash and burn method that these

=== page 46 ===
peopie use, there will be more open areas, which will affect smaller animais that utilise forest
cover for survival and allow invasive species of piants to colonise these areas which may result
in permanent grass patches.

5.2.3 Outlook on People’s lifestyle

The overall outlook on the lifestyle of the peopie is generally like those of other people in rural
areas of PNG. The basic resources for human sustenance are available, food, fresh and clean
water, clean air. firewocd and other resources for human survival. Generally the people are
healthy and enjoy a good village lifestyle.

The project area has an airstrip, which is serviced by PNG Airlines, Health Center, A
Community Top-Up School, pius various churches (Anglican, SDA, and United Pentecostal
Church) and other agencies that act on behalf of the government.

5.2.4 Logging and Mining Activities

Managalas Proposed Conservation Area is Resource rich. The area is abundant with food
resources. which are sufficient for the people. Natural (wild) resources are also abundant that
is; wild animals, forest products etc which people utilise. There are other viable resources
(Coffee, Vanilia, Garden foods, Bete! nuts etc) that people can sel! for extra income but
currently these are consumed at the village level and therefore they are not economically
viable.

However, if this trend continues and the pressures of external economic activities are inviting,
people may redirect their attention to alternative sources of generating economic activites that
are beneficial to sustain their immediate needs (eq.. Children’s Education, Schoo! fees. Medical
fees, Family commitments. Travel/Entertainment requirements and basic numan needs).

Very common examples and experiences gained from other parts of the country show that
mechanised clear-fell logging and mining activites are often inviting. They bring in cash
incomes although short-term and very destructive for peogie in rural settings whe have been
basically left neglected by their respective governments for too long. Therefore, a main road is
what the Managalas people need quickiy.

A proper road network linking all the main villages to each other, to Afore Sub District
Station and to Popondetta, main town center for Oro Province is what the people need
most. It is a major setback for all the people who live in the Proposed Conservation
Area.

Until this problem is resolved in the next 5 to 10 years, Conservation Efforts, deliverance
of Basic Rural Services and Developmental activities will continue to progress at a very
slow pace in Manaala in comparison to other areas in Papua New Guinea.

Bird-life of the Conservation Area.

The avian species within the Managalas Conservation Arca represent a wide variety of species from
Passerines to Non-Passerines. It has a very high species diversity and good distribution of bird species in

disturbed natural vegetation have species composition of the common indicator species like the friar birds,
parrot species, starlings, fly-catchers and the Raggiana bird of Paradise. The lowland vegetation also have
a wide variety of species distribution, which includes some good number of important and protected bird
species that can be found available in this vegetation type. Species identified common indicator species at
crown canopy levels under canopy levels, shrub layers, and the forest floor, where species including, the
pigeons (Ducula spp) the fruit doves (Ptilinopus spp), the hombill (Aceros plicatus). The cockatoos
(Cacatua galerita and Probosciger aterrimus), the parrots of different species, the fly-catchers, the honey-
eaters, the robins, King bird of Paradise (Cicinnurus regius), the magnificent rifle-bird of Paradise (Ptiloris
magnifcus), scrub fowl, brush turkey, followed by less indicator bird species.

The high mountain bird species confines themselves due to habitat types and the sources of feed available,

Discussions
(a) possible threats to bird lives of the conservation area.

In references to sites covered from phase 2 bird biodiversity surveys, there were no major threats
encountered to justify possible threats to bird lives of the area. Commercially involved activities were
discouraged by the loca] landowners of the conservation area, except for mini projects, like the growing of
coffee trees that generate little cash income and subsistence cash cropping. The small coffee gardens
already established at each villages sites may have little impact of the available bird species, but clearing
for new garden sites may have some effects to some species having their habitats permanently destroyed,
displacing them seeking possible refuge in the nearby vegetation’s. Magagals Plateau has a very rich soi!
profile and if the local people can clear secondary vegetation’s for new gardens, much of the rainforest will
continue to remain good biological grounds for not only the birds, but all the fauna species in the area.
Much of the higher elevations ranging from 1000 meters above sea level and beyond remain naturally, a
biological habitats for many species, and these encourages high species diversity.

It was good to know that local people from the sites visited, have been practicing traditional methods of
catching birds. The idea of conservation within the plateau have developed high feelings between the local
landowners and Partners With Melanesia. This trend have continue without having the conservation area
concepts declining and having the area ceveloped for other commercial activities. Bird species density will
decline when landowners are not too happy with the conservation concepts, which will lead to more natural
habitats destroyed for cash cropping and other activities. Close participation’s of conservation programs
must be regular and informative to avoid any possibles threats.

Recommendations

Managalas Conservation Area may be recognized one of the first type of conservation area in Papua New
Guinea if declared at a later stage. It’s rich biodiversity have encouraged local landowners who have deep

Small agro-forestry projects may be viable and be encouraged to sites where there will be less destruction’s
with no valued fauna and flora species. To maintain the valued richness of biodiversity of this conservation
area, I would recommend for these few ideas be exercise.

1. Management and planning of each individual, clan and village lands for smal! agro-forestry projects, to
avoid loose of any important species in the area.

2. Where possible, all identified important species at each zones of villages be made known to them for
protective measures. Not only that information’s, but other biological information's that the villagers
have to know.

3. Rehabilitation programs of three species planting in grasslands, secondary vegetation’s and other man
made clearings to maintain species diversity, which includes the host plant for Queen Alexandra’s

4. Some important fauna species were recorded through interviews with the local people to be available
in high mountainous areas, that the use of helicopter wil] be more appropriate in future biodiversity

5. The two phases of bird results, so far covering zones 1,2 and 7 in November 2004 and November

ABSTRACT

In November, 2004, a rapid vegetation assessment was conducted near Itokama and
the surrounding villages of Kuai and Nibaiba. In November, 2005, a phase 2 survey
was conducted as an extension of that survey. The overall aim of the survey was to
gather baseline information on vegetation types, determine the structure and assess the
plant diversity within the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area.

The vegetation survey was carried out in three selected sites, Kierim lower montane
forest, Tahama forest and Pongani forest near the coast. Within cach site plots of
50x50m were demarcated. Within the plot, strip lines of 5 x 50m were marked out at
10m interval. The strip line was subdivided into 5x10m subplots and trees 25cm dbh
were measured and heights recorded.

To account for shrubs, herbs and saplings, at least 5 quadrats of 5 x 5m were randomly
placed within the demarcated plot and all species enumerated.

Apart from forest sampling general botanical collection was conducted within the
vicinity of each site. Plants with flowers and fruits were targeted as these will aid
proper identification of specimens.

Samplings and general observations indicate that a number of forest formations occur
in the proposed conservation area; lower montane forest comprising of mixed
Castanopsis forest, low altitude forest on plains and fans, monsoonal or dry evergreen
forest and patches of savanna grassland towards the coast. The results from diameter
measurements in all plots showed that high proportion of trees have dbh <30cm
suggesting that the current forest types are quite young. However, there are indications
that there was a period of suppressed growth that has some bearing on the current
forest structure.

The Shannon Diversity Index average score is 1.50. This is higher than the first survey
at Itokama. Species area curve also show increasing species number as area increases
from mountain to the coast. All in ali the Managalas Conservation Area has a very

high species diversity.

It is recommended that the conservation initiatives by the Managalas Development
Foundation in partnership with Partners with Melanesia be strengthen and instrument
put in place to declare the Managalas Plateau as Conservation Area.

1.0 Introduction

In November 2004, a preliminary biodiversity survey on the plants, birds, mammals
and herpetofauna were conducted by a team of scientists from the University of Papua
New Guinea and the Department of Environment and Conservation. In November
2005, phase 2 study of the survey was conducted. The survey covered larger forest
areas ranging from lower montane forest to ficod plain forest near the coast. The
overall aims of the survey are 2 fold:

1. to assess the general plant diversity of the Managalas Proposed Conservation

Area (MPCA).
2. assess the diversity of vegetation types and their formation occurring within
the MPCA area,

This report highlights the results and observations of the phase II vegetation survey
conducted over a period of 20 days.

2.0 Managalas Plateau

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area constitutes an area of approximately
300,000ha and is located on the Managalas Plateau in the Isivitari District of Oro
Province.

The Managalas Plateau is located within the Southeastern Papuan Rain Forests
ecoregion. This lowland and montane ecoregion is made up of the Owen Stanley
Range and surrounding lowland and coastal areas in southeastern PNG (Figure 1.0).

A detail description of the cnvironment settings of the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area is given in Partners with Melanesia Report (2004) and summarized
in Piskaut (2004).

3.3 Pongani

Pongani is situated near the coast at 9° 04’ 18.9"S and 148° 31’ 31.0” E, at an

4.0 Methods

The methodology employed here slightly differ from previous survey where strip
transects were taken randomly. Here plot of 50m x50m was demarcated in each site.
In each plot, belt transects of 5 x 50m were laid out systematically at 10m interval. To
get an overall picture of the plant biodiversity of the area, the strip transects were
subdivided into quadrats of of 5 x 10m (50m’*). In each quadrat all trees 25cm dbh
were enumerated. Parameters measured include diameter at breast height (dbh), height
and identification of species at least to genus level. Diameter and height were
measured to elucidate the structure and dynamic of the forest.

Note strip transects only account for tree species. To assess the species density within
the 50 x 50m plot, further 5 x Sm quadrats were laid randomly and all herbs, shrubs,
creepers, climbers and saplings enumerated. At least 5 quadrats were laid out.

General botanical collections were also conducted over the survey period and plants
samples pressed and transported to the UPNG Herbarium for further identification,
and storage.

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic,
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation
appears irregular. Although the forest type resembles tropical lowland forest
observation on surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are

influenced by topography (Piskaut, 2004).

At Anatua there appeared to be some distinct zonation. The lowland forest gradually
grades into montane forest above 1000m asl. However, certain features characteristic
to lower montane formation become obvious at around 700m asl. This is similar to the
vegetation pattern observed at Jarefa and the surround hills. The presence of
Castanopsis accuminatissima, Lithocarpus, Podocarpus and Dacrydium in the forests
indicate low montane elements. Large woody lianas, plants with compound leaves,
cauliflorous plants, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and
lowland hill forests (Whitmore 1975) become rare or scarce above 1000m.

The forests at Tahama represent typical lowland forest with abundant plants
possessing compound leaves, cauliflory and large lianas. Common lowland species of
Elmerrillia, Aglaia, Dysoxylum, Elaeocarpus, Sterculia, Cryptocarya, Anisoptera,
Hopea and Terminalia are abundant.

At Pongani, a diversity of vegetation types coexists. These include flood plain forest.
lowland hill forest, monsoon forests and savanna grasslands.

In general the vegetation within the sites surveyed so far can be classified into the
following types; mixed Castanopsis forest, low altitude forest, savanna and monsoon
forest.

6.1.1 Low altitude forest

Predominant on flat terrain and near rivers. The forest is multilayered with the main
canopy stretching up to 40m. Dominant canopy species include Cryptocarya,
Syzygium, Elaeocarpus, Slonea, Pometia pinnata, Artocarpus and strangler Ficus.
Lower canopy trees include species of Garcinia, Gironniera, Barringtonia and
Dysoxylum, The ground floor is sparse with abundant seedlings. This is the dominant
vegetation type on the Platcau and include the mixed upland forests.

Canopy species dominance varies locally. For instance, at Jarefa. the forest comprises
of mixed canopy tree species. At Tahame and toward Afore and even to Pongani. the
forest is dominated by dipterocarps (4nisoptera and Hopea).

6.1.2 Mixed Castanopsis forest

On ridges and mountains mixed Castanopsis forest predominates with canopy
reaching up to 35m tall. The forest is two-lavered; the canopy and the ground lavers.
Casianopsis accuminatissima and Lithecarpus are the dominant canopy species in this
forest type. Other coexisiing canopy species include Cararium, Jernsiroemia,
Cryptocarya, Terminalia and severa! species of Syzygium. The ground layer is
sparseiy vegetated by Pandanus spp., ferns and creepers.

6.1.3 Savanna grassiané

This vegetation occurs in patches from the flat coastal area to the foothills. The
dominant tree is Eucalyptus confertiflora that forms the main canopy. The ground
cover is dominated by /mperata cylindrical (Kunai grass). Patchy occurrences of
savanna indicate that the area from Pongani towards Afore were once dominated by
grassland. In the absence of fire the vegetation has reverted to forest.

6.1.4 Monsoon forest or dry evergreen forest

Monsoon forest occurs at Pongani. This vegetation type is very similar to the
monsoonal forest along the southern part of New Guinea and is an indication of
pronounced dry and wet seasons. The overall canopy height is reduced and range from
10 to 15m. Common plant species that dominate the canopy include species of

6.2 Forest structure

The forest structures are similar in all sites as indicated by the diameter class
distributions (Figure 3.0). That is the current forests are younger. There is lack of
recruitment into the higher size classes. However, the proportion of trees >50cm
further indicate that the original forest was impacted upon by natural disturbance
events in the recent past. According to the locals the drought period of 1997/98 did
affect the forest on the plateau.

6.3 Plant species diversity

The species diversities of the areas surveyed appeared similar with slight variations
that could be attributable to the sampling error. Overall, a total of |.22ha was sampled
with 289 species enumerated. This number excludes other species not present in the
plots. This is suggestive of very high species diversity. The overall species diversity
score for all sites is 2 with the Tahama forests having the highest diversity. This figure
is quite high considering the small area sampled. It is envisaged that this figure will
increase if a permanent tha plot is established in each site.
