Paul Konia! NTFP/Managatasi- survey 2005/07

By: Paul P Konia.

Recommendations & Assumptions:

Common Name: Kopi/Kofi (Tok Pisin)

English: Coffee

Local Dialect: Kofuke

Scientific Name: Coffea Arabica- Family: Rubiaceae

Background:

Around the birth of Jesus Christ, coffee was reportedly first discovered growing in
Ethiopia by a sheepherder named Khaldi. Whenever he moved his sheep into one
particular pasture, the sheep would start acting extremely lively and erratic after
eating the “red cherries” on a particular bush found in that pasture. Tentatively,
Khaldi tried eating a few of the beans himself and experienced the same reaction.
The local area monks heard about Khaldi and this “devil’s fruit” but soon they too
were eagerly sampling it so they could stay awake for their prayers. Arab traders,
during a trading expedition, decided to bring back some beans to their homeland
and began to plant and grow their own beans. Soon they began to boil the beans and
produced a drink called “qahwa” (meaning “unable to sleep”). The drink gained
popularity until around 1453 when the Ottoman Turks introduced the beans to
Constantinople and in 1475 the world’s first coffee shop; “Kiva Han” was opened in
the city. The “coffee craze” developed to a point where women could even divorce
their husbands if they failed to provide the women with a daily ration of coffee. The
mere existence of the plant was a closely guarded secret in the Moslem countries

=== page 2 ===
when an Arab named Baba Budan started the actual spread of this delicacy to the
outside world illegally. Baba Budan smuggled some beans to Mysore, India where
descendants of these first smuggled plants can be found to this day.

In 1600, Italian traders brought some of the beans to Pope Clement VIII who was
urged to ban the drink as “unholy” because it came from Moslems that were “Non
Christians” but he surprised them by “baptizing” it instead. Now “coffee” was an
acceptable beverage for Christians. A few years later, Dutch traders smuggled out a
coffee plant from the port of Espresso to the island of Ceylon and to their East
Indian colony of Java, source of coffee’s nickname today. In 1713, the Dutch
unwittingly gave a coffee bush to Louis XIV of France that, from which, in 1723, a
French naval officer, Gabriel Mathicu do Clieu, stole a seedling and took it to
Martinique. Eventually, 90 percent of the world’s coffee spread from this one plant.

Jamaican Blue Mountain Coffee:
In 1728 Sir Nicholas Lawes, then Governor of Jamaica and owner of Temple Hall

Estate, brought the first coffee plants to Jamaica. First, cultivation started in the
foothills of St. Andrew but soon plantations extended deeper into the fertile Blue
Mountains. The coffee industry has experienced many ups and downs from those
early days until today.

From 1800 to 1840, Jamaica produced 70,000 tons per year making her the largest
producer in the world. Then, in 1838, came the abolition of slavery. This spelled the
end to many coffee plantations, as newly freed farmers began planting and clearing
all the available hillsides to earn a living and to have land to live on. By 1891, the
coffee industry was in general disarray so legislation was passed to provide
“instruction in the art of cultivation and curing by sending certain districts,
competent instructors.”

The effort to increase quality was largely unsuccessful as the largest buyer in those
days was the Canadian market and they resisted it as being unacceptable. Finally, in
1944 the Jamaican government established a Central Coffee Clearing House where
all coffee for export had to be processed. This cleaning and grading process was a
giant step in the improvement in the quality of the Jamaican coffee being exported.

Following the devastating hurricane of 1951, there were only three Coffee
Processing Plants (called “pulperies”) remaining in operation in the Blue
Mountains. In an attempt to regulate the growth that was sure to follow, the Coffee
Industry Board was formed to establish guidelines in quality, cultivation and
processing. The Coffee Industry Board is still an active force today and garners
some of the credit for the resurgence of Jamaican coffee. In 1973, the three coffee
processing plants at Mavis Bank, Silver Hill and Moy Hall along with a new comer,
Wallenford, registered the name “Blue Mountain Coffee”.

A few years ago, the Twyman family’s Old Tavern Estate Coffee won the legal right
through the Jamaican courts to also sell its superior product under the “Blue
Mountain” name.

=== page 3 ===
Jamaica is famous for producing some of the finest coffee found anywhere in the
world. What makes this little island such a prime spot for growing a world-class
coffee? As in real estate, it’s “Location, Location, Location” and in this case, that
location is the Blue Mountains. Coffee plants need to be well watered, well drained
and experience periodic coolness during some stages of development. To be called
“Blue Mountain Coffee”, it must be grown at altitudes between 2,000 and 5,000 feet
in the Parishes of Portland, St. Andrew and St. Thomas and, most importantly, be
grown on the estates of; Mavis Bank, Silver Hill, Moy Hall or Wallenford. Coffee
grown elsewhere in the Blue Mountains or anywhere else in Jamaica cannot be
called “Blue Mountain Coffee. Blue Mountain coffee is exclusively made from the
Arabica Bean. The Arabica bean is more fragile to grow but is considered more
flavorful and has less caffeine than the Robusta Bean grown in many parts of the
world.

Small growers like James Dennis in the District of Section are finding success in
selling their production directly to discriminating tourists as most of the “official”
Blue Mountain Coffee is currently exported to Japan. First they must harvest their
beans and then sun dry them on bamboo racks before roasting them over a smoky
wood fire. They weigh and package the beans in plastic bags for sale to passing
tourists and locals. Want your coffee ground? They will pour the roasted beans into
an old hollowed-out log and have someone pound and pulverize the beans using a
stout, tapered hardwood branch with a flat surface on the end.

More small growers, like James Dennis, along with the officially recognized and
established “Blue Mountain Coffee” growers known as JABLUM (Jamaica Blue
Mountain) are growing and producing what is regarded as the “Best Coffee in the
Caribbean” and quite possibly the “Best Coffee in the World”.

Coffee was introduced to Papua New Guinea in the late 1940s thus in the late 1960s
it was taken up to Afore and the Managalas plateau by the colonel administration to
be grown as a cash crop.

The Managalas plateau has almost over 700 farmers who grow more than 800 000
coffee trees that can produce about 8000 bags annually at an average weight of 360
000 (45kg per bag) kilograms. In monetary terms, the current coffee buying price at
the plateau is K2.00 which means that the revenue going in annually will be about
K720 000.00. Moreover, if coffee is sold at factory door price in Goroka which
stands at K4.50 per kilogram, then farmers of Managalas plateau would have
collected K1, 62000.00 annually.

Plant Description: The coffee plant is a woody perennial evergreen dicotyledon that
belongs to the Rubiaceae family. It has a main vertical trunk (orthotropic) and
primary, secondary, and tertiary horizontal branches (plagiotropic). Two main
species of coffee are cultivated today. Coffea arabica known as Arabica coffee
accounts for 75-80% of the world's production. Coffea canephora, known as
Robusta coffee, is more robust than the Arabica plants, but produces an inferior
tasting beverage with a higher caffeine content. The coffee plant can grow to

=== page 4 ===
heights of 10 meters if not pruned, but producing countries will maintain the coffce
at a height reasonable for easy harvesting.

A common tended, planted or cultivated medium-large tree with distinctive lateral
branches, deciduous green to red leaves and fruits with hard corky pink/ purple
shell that is cut open in to equal halves.

Plant Development: Three to four years after the coffee is planted, sweet smelling
flowers grow in clusters in the axils of the leaves. Fruit is produced only in the new
tissue. The Arabica species is self-pollinating, whereas the Robusta species depends
on cross pollination. About 6-8 weeks after the flowers are fertilized, cell division
occurs and the fruit remains as a pin head for a period that is dependent upon the
climate. The ovaries will then develop into drupes in a rapid growth period that
takes about 15 weeks after flowering. During this time the integument takes on the
shape of the final bean. After the rapid growth period the integument and
parchment are fully grown and will not increase in size. The endosperm remains
small until about 12 weeks after flowering. At this time it will suppress, consume,
and replace the integument. The remnants of the integument are what make up the
silverskin. The endosperm will have completely filled the cavity made by the
integument nineteen weeks after flowing. The endosperm is now white and moist,
but will gain dry matter during the next several months. During this time the
endosperm attracts more than seventy percent of the total photosynthesis produced
by the tree. The mesocarps will expand to form the sweet pulp that surrounds the
bean. The cherry will change color from green to red about thirty to thirty-five
weeks after flowing.

Root System: The root system can extend 20-25 km in total length and the absorbing
surface of a tree ranges from 400 to 500 m*. There are main vertical roots, tap
roots, and lateral roots which grow parallel to the ground. The tap roots extend no
further than 30-45 cm below the soil surface. Four to eight axial roots may be
encountered which often originate horizontally but point downward. The lateral
roots can extend 2 m from the trunk. About 80-90% of the feeder root is in the first
20 cm of soil and is 60-90 cm away from the trunk of the tree (Mavolta, 195-196).
However, the greatest root concentration is in the 30 to 60 cm depth. The roots
systems are heavily affected by the type of soil and the mineral content of the soil.
To be thick and strong the root system needs an extensive supply of nitrogen,
calcium and magnesium. During planting the main vertical roots are often clipped
to promote growth of the horizontal roots, which then have better access to water
and added nutrients in the top soil.

Leaves: The elliptical leaves of the coffee tree are shiny, dark green, and waxy. The
leaf area index is between 7 and 8 for a high-yielding coffee. The coffee plant has
become a major source of oxygen in much of the world. Each hectare of coffee
produces 86 Ibs of oxygen per day, which is about half the production of the same
area in a rain forest (source: Anacafe).

Harvesting: Each year coffee is harvested during the dry season when the coffee
cherries are bright red, glossy, and firm. Ripe cherries are either picked by hand,

=== page 5 ===
stripped from the tree with both unripe and overripe beans, or all the beans are
collected using a harvesting machine. These processes are called selective picking,
stripping, and mechanical harvesting, respectively.

To maximize the amount of ripe coffee harvested it is necessary to selectively pick
the ripe beans from the tree by hand and leave behind unripe, green beans to be
harvested at a later time. In Brazil, harvesting the same tree several times is more
cost prohibitive than separating and discarding the unripe or overripe cherries.
Therefore, Brazil typically harvests using the stripping method when 75% of the
crop is perfectly ripe. Stripping is feasible and cost effective in Brazil due to the
uniform maturation of Brazilian coffees. In stripping the beans are pulled from the
tree and fall to the ground where they are caught by sheets. The beans are removed
from tree debris by tossing the coffee in the air allowing the wind to carry away
sticks and leaves. The coffce is then put in 60 L green baskets, which is the
measuring tool used by coffee producers to determine wages. Some estates, such as
Fazenda Monte Alegre in Sul de Minas Brazil, have a computerized system to
determine wages, which accounts for the amount of coffee collected from each
person, the difficulty of the harvesting conditions, and the production of the region
being harvested. About 12-20 kg of export ready coffee will be produced from every
100 kg of coffee cherries harvested.

Processing: Irrespective of the harvesting method, green coffee beans and overripe
coffee cherries inevitably end up mixed with the perfectly ripe cherries and must be
separated. Over ripe coffee cherries, undeveloped coffee cherries, sticks and leaves
float in water. Ripe coffee beans and green coffee cherries are dense and sink.
Therefore, the first separation step takes place by separating the floaters from the
sinkers. The floaters are usually sent directly to the patio to be dried and are then
slated for internal consumption. The ripe and green cherries can be sent to the
patios to be dried using the natural (dry) process or can be sent to the pulping
machines.

The first stage of pulping is used to remove the green cherries from the ripe
cherries. In the pulping machine the internal pressure is monitored to push the
coffee against a screen with holes only large enough for a coffee bean (not cherry) to
pass through. Since the ripe cherries are soft they break and the seed is released
fitrowgbethelnesries.arc hard and cannot be pulped. Instead of passing through the
screen, the green beans pass to the end of the barrel system and are separated from
the ripe beans. The pressure inside the barrel controls how many cherries will be
pulped. A very high pressure will cause all of the cherries including the green beans
to be pulped. It is necessary to continuously monitor the pressure so that about 3%
of ripe cherries are not pulped and are removed with the green cherries. This
margin of error ensures that no green cherries are mistakenly pulped. The pulp
and beans are then separated by centrifugal force and a barrel screen system.

The beans covered in the slippery mucilage can be sent to the patios to dry as
pulped natural coffees or can be sent to fermentation tanks. The fermenting tanks
are used to remove the mucilage before drying. The pulped beans are put into
cement tanks with water and are allowed to ferment for 16-36 hours. On the way to

=== page 6 ===
the fermentation tanks another density separation can occur. The highest quality
coffees are the most dense and should be separated and fermented in a different tank.

The fermentation time depends on a number of factors including the amount of
coffee fermenting, water temperature, and humidity. The mucilage is made up of
pectin materials including protopectin (33%), reducing sugars including glucose
and fructose (30%), non-reducing sugars such as sucrose (20%), and cellulose and
ash (17%) Protopectin is not water soluble and will hydrolyze to pectinic acid in the
fermentation tanks. Hydrolysis of the protopectin and degradation of the pectin by
enzymes is the process that occurs to remove the mucilage during fermentation
(Wrigley, 455). Currently, the best way of determining the end of fermentation is to
feel the beans to determine if the beans are still encased in mucilage. If the beans
are fermented for 36-72 hours stinker beans develop. Lactic, acetic, and propionic
acids are produced in this process and are believed to prevent the traditional
fermentation taste by inhibiting mold growth that regularly occurs during drying on
i wratidlin formichcavidmianks the beans are moved to drying patios and dried to 1 1-
12% moisture content. A small portion of the lot is hulled and milled by a mini-
huller. Three hundred grams of coffee is classified for defects (100 grams is often
used), and the percentage of each screen size is determined. Then, 200-300 grams of
coffee is roasted in a sample roaster and cupped to determine quality. Ideaily no
lots will be mixed until the coffee has been classified and cupped. The coffee
remains in pergamino until shipment time to help protect the flavor and aroma of
the coffee.

Before shipment coffee must be dried from approximately 60% moisture content to
11-12% moisture content. Coffee is typically dried on large patios made of asphalt
or cement and then transferred to mechanical dryers. The coffee on the drying
patios is shifted every 30-40 minutes and is shaped into long rows of no more than 5
cm in height. Next to cach row is open ground, which is warmed and dried by the
sun, The coffee is then shifted onto the dry portion of the patio, and the section
where it was previously is now allowed to dry in the sun. This helps accelerate the
drying process and prevents fermentation and moldy beans from developing. This
method is widely used in Brazil, but less widely used in Guatemala or Costa Rica
where the coffee is more often piled perpendicularly to the old piles. To dry coffee
solely by patio drying it takes 6-7 days for washed coffees, 8-9 days for pulped
naturals (semi-washed), and 12-14 days for natural (dry-processed) coffees. This is
why coffees are typically dried on a patio until they reach a moisture content of 15%
and are then transferred to mechanical dryers. Once the coffee reaches 25%
moisture or less it can be piled at night and covered with cotton cloths to allow the
coffee to breath. If it rains these piles can also be covered with plastic. Coffee should
not be covered with burlap sacks since this will impart a distinct burlap flavor and
aroma to the coffee.

In a study done in Kenya, the report highlights that there are six stages to drying

¢o fin drying. Moisture 55-45%.

2) White Stage drying. Moisture 44-33%.

3) Soft Black stage. Moisture 32-22%.

4) Medium Black Stage. Moisture 21-16%

=== page 7 ===
5) Hard Black Stage. Moisture 15-12%

6) Fully dry coffee and conditioning. 11-10%.

In this study it was discovered that sun drying for stage three is mandatory for
coffee quality. It also reported that as long as the temperature was between 40-
50°C--which means a bean temp of 35°C--then the coffee quality will not be
seriously compromised during the other stages.

The final two stages (15-11% moisture) in just six hours at 40°C in a mechanical
dryer. There are several dryer systems available. Many older dryers are converted
grain dryers that are not as efficient as the new horizontal barrel dryers. The new
dryers are designed to mix the coffee evenly to ensure uniform drying. Drying by
using mechanical dryers accelerates the slowest part of the drying process (15-11%)
and helps prevent fermentation. In some environments that have a high humidity
the entire drying process must take place in mechanical dryers. Mechanical dryers
should never be set higher than 40-45°C and this question should be asked before
buying any coffees that have been mechanically dried. At higher temperatures the
germ is killed and the flavor potential of the coffee is ruined. At extreme
temperature the bean crystallizes and when smashed with a hammer will break like
glass.

The best, but least utilized method of drying coffee is by using drying tables. In this
method the pulped and fermented coffee is spread thinly on raised beds, which
allows the air to pass on all sides of the coffee. The coffee is mixed by hand and the
drying that takes place is more uniform and fermentation is less likely. Most coffee
from the Managalas Plateau is dried in this manner and it is the commonly used
drying method used widely in Papua New Guinea. It is sometimes known as Solar
Drying. Solar Dryer is good during rains and at nights. A drying bed is built with a
shelter over it with plastic sheet. The sides and ends of the bed are properly covered
and coffee parchments are spread on the bed to dry. Parchments are turn regularly
for sun to dry all sides. It takes about 3 — 4 weeks for the parchment to dry properly.

Diseases

Coffee Leaf Rust:

Coffee leaf rust first destroyed Brazils crop in 1970. Since then, it has spread to
every coffee growing country in the world. The disease was first observed in Sri
Lanka in the 1860's. Many countries, including Sri Lanka and Ethiopia, replaced
much of their arabica coffee with disease resistant robusta coffee. The disease is
spread from spores from lesions on the underside of the plant by wind and rain.
Rust is prevented by spraying with copper-based fungicides at 3-5 kg/ha at 4-6 week
intervals during the rainy season. In PNG, this disease was discovered in the 1980's.
Efforts by the Coffee Industry Corporation have successfully curbed this disease.

Coffee Berry Disease:
Coffee berry disease was first discovered in Kenya in 1920 and is caused by the

virulent strain of Colletotrichum coffeanum the fungus lives in the bark of the coffee
tree and produces spores which attack the coffee cherries. Spraying has been
determined to be the best way to avoid the coffee berry disease. Captafol and

=== page 8 ===
copper-based fungicides have been effective. The Kenyan coffee hybrid Ruiru 11 is
resistant to both coffee berry disease and leaf rust.

Bacterial Blight:
Bacterial Blight (Pseudomanas syringae py. garcae) is a disease that occurs where wet

and cold conditions prevail.

Nematodes:
Meloidogyne exigua, M. incognita, M. coffeicola, Pratylenchus brachyurus, and P.
coffeae are the most common species of root-knot nematodes. All arabica cultivars

are susceptible to nematodes.

Leaf Miner:
The leaf miner (Perileucoptera cofeella) occurs mainly in Brazil. Coffea stenophylila is

the only coffee cultivar resistant to the leaf miner

Traditional use:
There are no traditional uses of coffee recorded on the plateau because this crop was

introduced.

Potential as a NTFP:

Largely depends upon processing and access to markets. In particular, handling and
storage of beans and reliable cost effective transport to domestic markets (sce route
proposed on transport). The major technical processing problem is the beans
instability at ambient temperatures and humidity and its tendency to either rot or
over dried, eventually loosing it correct moisture when tested at the laboratory.

Coffee is feasible to store in most places on the plateau. The best alternative is to dry
the beans using the common technique of solar drying or sun dry. Solar drying is
appropriate because of the plateau’s climatic conditions of cloud cover and
associated rain most days. It should not prove too technically difficult to introduce
appropriate thermal dryers in to the area for down stream processing (making
green beans) — a number of designs are there and supported by the PNG Coffee
Industry Corporation and other local based organizations. However, experience
elsewhere has shown that unless their introduction must be accompanied by
comprehensive management training (in particular quality control) they are
unlikely to be successful. There is currently a standardized system for packaging
and storage in Goroka, the country’s leading coffee producing province.

Irene, you have a very clear idea of the problems with coffee on the Managalas plateau in the way you
have presented our case.

The main cause of our problems here is Market Inaccessibility, poor road conditions in the zones to Afore
where it leads to the coast. Because of the poor road condition in the zones, there is no truck coming in to
pick up the coffee from the farmers. Added to that is the very low price paid to the farmers at the road
side (point of sales — normally in the villages). We don’t think it is poor processing methods, but it has
something to do with storing the coffee over long period of time due to no buyers coming into the villages
as the road is poor. As the coffee beans are stored over time, the beans get mouldy from the cool tropical
humidity and the coffee beans go bad.

On another note, PWM feels very reluctant to introduce into the plateau community a new cash crop, as it
might have other negative impacts that may lead to added problems, so PwM feels, that we should utilise
what cash crop that is already there (coffee) where the people are knowledgeable about it.

Decreasing coffee retums has led to the abandonment of the coffee plots and to the trend that locals turn
to less sustainable manners in order to gain a new income (such as logging, oil palm plantations and
mining)This in turn leads to risking the anticipated conservation effects of the Managalas Community
Conservation Area Project. [See map of threats)

Executive Summary

Partners With Melanesians in pursuit for the Proposed Managalas Community Conservation Area
Project has been working with the Communities on the Managalas Plateau for the last 15 years
and has assisted the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) and successfully established the
ten (10) Community Based Organisations (CBOs) on the Managalas Plateau to enhance its
programme activities and to mobilize community collaboration and participation through as
sustainable approach to development options and encourage a self-reliance community economic
base.

The role of PWM is facilitating the core-programme activities and assist in eco-enterprising
activities for the local communities. The current eco-enterprise activities are Okari nut (Tropical
Almonds) Marketing Research and Sales, Vegetable Sales and Researching on Coffee and other
potential non-timber forest products, PWM also charters Third Level Airlines to transport market

produce to Port Moresby for marketing.

The soil and the climatic conditions of the Managalas Plateau have proved to be very conducive
for Arabica Coffee. The area is known for its coffee and for the last ten years there has been
drastic setbacks due to very poor road conditions that alienated the area from possible markets
and other basic government services. According to a survey carried out in December 7" — 15th,
more than 300 tonnes of coffee are destroyed every year due to market inaccessibility. That has
put the local communities under immense economic pressure,
as the economy of this nation has been in the doldrums for more than a decade.

This is a threat to the proposed Managalas Community Conservation Area Project as the
communities might succumb to the options provided by big industrial development especially,
mining, logging and Oil Palm due to the economic pressure mounting as a result of the
Government’s User Pay Policy whereby the essential government services are now payed for
and money is a big player in the game.

PWM after a thorough assessment of the whole situation identified that coffee is one of the best
eco-enterprise options for the Managalas People. Even though the domestic prices are not good,
yet compared to other local products, coffee is the winner, yet it is losing because of some of the
issues this proposal aims to address.

The idea of starting Managalas Organic Coffee Project (MCOP) was established under the PwM eco-
enterprise drive for alternative development options for the Managalas communities. Coffee was there
long before the Managalas Conservation Area Support Project was established and the local people of the
Managalas Plateau are well acquainted with it and they often refer to it as “Coffee em Bun blong of

Managalas"

Last year when the NC-IUCN’s funding for the NLRPA program come in, the Management decided that
PwM will concentrate the Marketing Budget Line for coffee marketing research because PwM saw Coffee
to be a more viable produce from the plateau and given the worst economic conditions, coffee still comes
out the winner in comparison to other potential alternative produce from the plateau.

Whilst pursuing Coffee Marketing research which includes sample testing and grading done last year and
this year with our assessment of the fluctuations of the domestic pricing and local buying rates on the
plateau by interested parties, quality control, organic certification, rehabilitation programmes, and the
location of the Oro Coffee mill PwM also saw the need for a separate and specific funding for the MOCP so
that these issues can be addressed to enable the success of the project and the benefits reaching the local
communities.

a proposal for Managalas Organic Coffee Project. It was on Erick’s invitation that I developed a proposal
for the MCOP that was initially submitted last year August. However, DOEN Foundation wanted more
information about the Managalas annual production which we initially stated on the proposal as 60 tons

around late November 2004, Edwin and I conducted a survey, which we established our findings in our
report to be extremely higher (around 950-1500 tons annual Managalas Production). I furnished an
updated report and send it together with a re-submission of our proposal to DOEN.

2. Give a brief summary of the development of the project from the start until
today, stressing the last year.

The project continued the past year (2006) with substantial amounts of time and money spent
on planning for both the organisations Five Years from 2007 to 2011, and an Exit Strategy
for Manugulus Development Foundation, the local partner. This caused a shortfall in our
budget for the year since these activities were unbudgetted for.

Under the Conservation Component, a substantial amount of resources and time was put into

Counterpart funding from IUCN enabled further charters for produce coming off the Plateau.

With the Consensus Building Component. after a reorganization of the component in 2005, work
commenced on the production of material and training of Literacy Co-ordinators and Facilttutors.
However, duc to our planning process. which took up most of our time, the Consensus building
process has now been deferred to start in early 2007 with the MDF AGM.

A new Project Officer for MCASP was recruited and bused on the Plateau tor a while. but due to
differences between the Project Officer and the MDF staff, he was recalled to Port Moresby and
worked from there.

Likewise, a series of excursions were carried out into three (3) possible sites for expansion in
Tetebedi. Musa and Enga. The trip to Enga was aborted due to transport dilficulties. Based on these
excursions, the organization will then decide which areas it should work in, in the future, as part of
our expansion program.

Furthermore, networking amongst the different NGO's, CBO's and community groups within Oro
Province, was another activily that took prominence during the year. Likewise,

3. How has the development on the national and local levels influenced the project
activities during the last year?

=== page 3 ===
‘we

The development in areas of politics and the national cconomy has not been helpful for the
implementation of the program. Powerful political and cconomical interest groups are now speeding
up the exploitation of the country’s natural resources in order to put the country’s economy back on
track. The recent government has declared tax breaks for companies interested in developing the oil
palm industry. Oil palm is now Papua New Guinea's largest agricultural foreign exchange carner,
ahead of coffee. International financial institutions and other funding agencics are now providing
funds for the Oil Palm companies. This model offers the companies a beter and more profitable
alternative [rom the conventional large-scale plantations owned by the company. Conversely, growers
do not own shares in the companies.

Time bas become critical as the logging companics are encroaching in buffer areas just to the
northeast and southwest of the plateau. Clan groups who have involved in the consensus building
process over the years, to date are vocal about ensuring sustainable development of the plateaus
according to locally defined guideline.

However, the majority of rural communities in PNG are by no means poor. With the exception of
areas degraded or polluted by large mines, logging. agriculture or fishery projects, the customary land
tenure system has enabled local communities to have free and casy access to land, clean water and the
abundance of natural resources for the decent quality of Tile.

The granting of oi! palm, logging and alluvial mining licenses to foreign developers in the province
will have tremendous impact on the rural communities. This is a set back for the program if these
projects impact on the natural environment on the Plateau. Government services such as roads,
schools and hospital are Jacking in most rural areas and development such as oil palm, logging and
alluvial mining will contribute to environmental and social impact on the rural communities.
Conversely, the local people do not own shares in the companies.

The project continues to face major transportation problems due to the state of the road linking
Popondetia to Afore thence to Itokama. While the road works were completed in 2005, a major
problem has been the bridge over Pongani River. which has collapsed. It is anticipated that as more
work is carried out in the area of eco-enterprise, there will be a major push by the communities on the
Plateau to have their roads fixed.

Likewise, the airlines that service the Plateau are unpredictable. We continue to Lace major setbacks
when the planes do not fly into the Plateau and while it is understandable [rom our point of view. the
local communities blame us for delaying activities and workshops.

Another positive for the MCASP has been the eventual involvement of both local level government
and provincial government in the activities of the project. We have likewise been fortunate to have
started a relationship with Conservation Melanesia and Dadacol. both have been points of contention
for many years. We have also been fortunate to have started a working with the Provincial AIDS
Commiltice who have supported us with transportation from Popondetta to the Managulas Plateau.

=== page 4 ===
B. Implementation of the project

I. Have the project activities been implemented as planned?

Unfortunately, duc to the pressing need for a Strategic Plan for the organisation, many of the pkinned
activilies Were not implemented and pushed back to 2007. A lot of time was spent working with stafl
and various stakeholders to draw up a strategic plan and an exit strategy for the MCASP as requested
by the Managalas Leaders during the previous years Leaders Summit.

The Consensus Building Programme was faced with delayed printing of material and this has also
been pushed back to this year 2007,

2. Have there been any changes in the implementation of the project? (Details to be
given in the work plan report)

A series of workshops were conducted which brought together stall and board members ol the
organisation as well as various stakcholders to discuss the work of the organisation and then develop a
Strategic Plan for the next five years. The workshops began with a Reflection Workshop at Motupore
Island: a Strategic Panning Workshop at Sivarai Namona, and a Staff Retreat at the Bluff Inn Motel.

This all culminated in the drafling of relevant documents. programmes and plans which will now be
used by PWM and MDF to implement various project activities within the next five years,

Towards the end of the year, a workshop was conducted under ODW Rainlorest Literacy to provide
training tor new CBO staff on the CB Process to prepare them for implementation this year. PWM has
now successfully merged the work of the ODW Rainforest Literacy with the CB Process utilising the
same personnel to carry oul both the Clan Group Discussions during the Literacy programmes in the
villages. This will then lead on to the Zone Forums and the Combined Forum towards the end of the

year.

While we had originally planned to visit two sites for the expansion of our project Lc. Musa and
Elem, we managed to visit Tetebedi as well which was a bonus. On the other hand, the visit to Elem
was abandoned when the Team could not get into the area after travelling half way there to Mt Hagen.
This trip was accomplished during December/ January by the Executive Director and the Project
Officer.

3. Have the changes, if any, resulted in any reallocations on the budget?

There was reallocation of funds with approval from RFN. with major reallocations occurring within
our programme budget to cater for the series of workshops that had not been budgeted for initially.
This necessitated a redirection of funds from planned program activities to cover a major part of this
expenditure, however, at the end of the year there was still a shortfall of over K60,000.00

4. To which extent have the expected results been achieved?

The past year has unfortunately been very slow for the organisation in terms of the implementation of
the planned activities. However, this was compensated for by the development of a Strategic Plan and
Exit Strategy which has now given us direction to move forward over the next five years. This has
been an ongoing issue of contention, in that there did not seem to be any guide or direction for the
organisation to follow until now. The Workplan and Budget for 2007 reflects this development.

=== page 5 ===
5. To which extent has the purpose of the project been fulfilled?

The program had been conducted widely through out the Managalas Plateau all year round. Ficld staff
have been carrying out regular fickd patrols to respective zones to assist management of each
community-based organisation with technical advice. Many of the communities involved have already
demonstrated considerable initiative in organising themselves to develop a sustainable development
plan for their areas.

These clan groups have had considerable experience collaborating with one another and with other
outside agencies and organisations on other local development initiative. The proceeding of

Training workshops to date make it clear that communities believe in their social and economic well
being is dependent on sound, long-term management of their resources. In effect, communities are
learning to build on existing social capital and to expand it for use with new eco-enterprise activities.

Communities are now becoming aware of the importance of managing their environment sustainably
and taking major roles to help themsclves as the result of the training and awareness. Every effort ts
being made to ensure that an opportunity to participate in eco-enterprise activity follows the initial to
provide greater awareness and participation with the communities. For instance, zone 10 is currently
under negotiation for Forest Management Area (FMA) to tie up deal with landowner for exploitation
of the rich forest resource. The negotiation is still continuing and this will depend on the landowner to
decide between conservation and development,

Individual CBO's and their Zones are now independently seeking technical and financial assistance
from other sources. Zones | and 2 have now basically become self-reliant in terms of project planning
and implementation.

Managalas Development Foundation, the local partner in this project, is now been given the tools to
develop to be independent and to work on their own as has been agreed Ww during the meclings and
workshops in 2006, MDF will have on board a Project Co-ordinator from outside of the area who will
assist them implement the Exit Strategy.

6. Please explain the deviations, if any, from the purpose and the expected results
according to the work pian.

A major deviation has been a relocation of funds towards the planning process. While many training
activities were not carried out due to this process, it is not a cause for worry as we now better
understand the situation and have planned relevant training activities to cater for this deviation,

Another change has been the need to move the Consensus Building Program over to the new year,
This has been an ongoing problem because of the printers and the studios that have been developing
the Rainforest Literacy material. We are now looking al other service providers who can produce on
lime.

7. How has the co-ordination of the project regarding local, national and
international co-operation, including field visits, functioned?

The program had been well accepted by the local communities so much so that people from the
acighbouring communities continuously ask for assistance to start something similar in their areas.
Interest continues to grow amongst CBO's, NGOs, government agencies and other interested parties
who have interest in both community development and environmental work,

=== page 6 ===
6

Local co-operation between MDF. CBO's and communities is quite good. They have shown keen
interest in participating and supporting the project. The project is working alongside other CBO's
programs because all of these organizations complement each other.

With complimentary funding from other donors, the work at the ficld level is proceeding with much
interest by the affected communities. the relevant government agencies and the MDF stall and Board,

A major problem faced by many NGO's including ours is the perception that we are the alternative
service delivery mechanism and therefore we should be catering for all the community needs. Local
staff continue to use their local knowledge and standing to make unreasonable demands on the
organisation. This should be addressed in the new year with the implementation of the Exit Strategy.

MOU’s have been drafied by our Lawyers to enable relationships between PWM and MDF. the LLG
and the Provincial Government for collaboration within the project area. This should be negotiated

and signed in the next year.

C. Other Considerations

I. Are there any specific internal or external conditions that have influenced the
implementation of the annual work plan?

a) There were a number of internal conditions that influenced the implementation of the anoual
workplan. These include staff reluctance to implement these program activities on specific
date as planned due to financial disagreements. Lack of major contribution and cqual
participation from all sectors of the communities. including in-kind contribution have had
serious and negative impact over the project due to the pervading cargo mentality, Although
this is a natural and common concern throughout rural areas in Papua New Guinea, the
Managalus people have taken advantage of the financial situation to demand almost
everything to be paid for before they will do anything.

There also continues to be a breakdown in effective teamwork between the Field and CBO stalf
on the onc hand, and PWM project and support staff on the other hand.

b) The major external condition, which affects the implementation of the project, is
communication and transportation difficulties given the remoteness of the project. Training
workshops and community meetings continue to be delayed due to poor weather and road
conditions, The road Jink from Afore to ttokama has been covered by bush and deteriorating
road condition has resulted in less and less produce transported to urban markets for sale.
Road and transportation difficulty has affected program implementation and can be very
trying for project staff who have to travel in these conditions to do their work. This is also
compounded by the lack of a reliable air transport system and rising cost of airfares.

2. Is it probable, after the fast year’s development, that the project will reach its
goals or is there a considerable chance for changes?

A lot of lessons have been learnt from the project over the years. The project has offered so many
good things such as awareness, trainings, exposure of national issues, exchange of ideas, and
collaboration of partners NGOs and government agencies, This last year has seen a number of events
which will have lasting impact on project implementation, especially with the recruitment of a [ull-
tcum ol staff in the Port Moresby PWM Office who are now able to plan, coordinate and implement
the programs based on the contract,

=== page 7 ===
This year will sce resurgence in community involvement and contribution due to he experiences of the
community with the MOCP’s contribution to their economic well-being. Likewise, the Consensus
Building Program which is now amalgamated into the main MCASP activities, will enter another
phase of involving children and schools in learning traditional knowledge and practices through our
traditional learning centres.

Training programs have been conducted to develop the capacity of field staff to carry out activities
with minimum supervision and also to transfer skills to other community members. It is also the aim
io maintain the staff base so that there are no gaps when technical project stall leave the organization.

A reorganisation of the MDF Board and recruitment of reliable and qualified MDF stall will see a
new and community oriented MDF in 2007, with the appointment by the PWM Board of a Project
Co-ordinator from outside the Managalas Plateau.

3. How has the last year’s development affected the probability of the project's
continuation after the professional and economic support from the REN has
been phased out?

It is anticipated that the project will attempt to seck funds exicrnally to continue, in the event that
funding from REFN is no longer available. This is in light of the fact that considerable amount of
resources and time have been invested in mobilizing the Plateau community to the extent they have
become a community that is ready to tackle issues affecting them. They have become an example of
organized communities in PNG that are now resourced to work together for their own well-heing,

At least for the foreseeable future, this is unlikely to happen. but steps are been taken to address this
eventuality. We anticipate with the MOCP coming on board and a push for diversification of MDF's
funding base, this will be a start of an independent organization to take over when PWM moves oul of
the Plateau

4. Please evaluate the project’s relevance and foundation according to national
plans and priorities during the last year.

The program is relevant at this stage during the economic hardships that are faced in rural
communities in Papua New Guinea. Current scenario is that investors are harvesting natural resource
at an alarming rate. In so doing. investors do not comply and failure to produce proper environmental
impact and reconstructive planning prior to government granting operational licenses. In the course of
harvesting the natural resources, socio-economic problems have risen to new heights; hence the only
option to prevent such rising issues is to encourage community development projects and actively
mobilizing communities to deal with issues for themselves,

The national government and international government donors have recognized the program as
significant. It is likely that after the end of project funding period, some of these organizations will
help in the funding of the project. This is because the program is also in line with poverty alleviation.
The program is in line with government priorities and public plans that encourage idea of “bottom-up
planning” for the Local Level and Provincial Government Reform System (PGRS) and the Education
Reform Sysiem (ERS) program in Papua New Guinea. The program equips rural communities with
wider thinking capacity and to produce well-framed plans for development.

D. Audit report

PWM’s account will be audited and the financial report will be sent to RFN by April 2006.

1. DESCRIPTION OF THE ENTERPRISE

The Managalas Organic Coffee Marketing project is a joint undertaking between
Partners with Melanesians (PWM) and the Managalas Development Foundation
(MDF), a Federation consisting of 16,000 highlanders organized in 10 cultural
zones living in a 360,000 hectares conservation area inside the Managalas
Plateau of Oro Province, Papua New Guinea.

The project will organize the marketing of organically grown Arabica coffee by
setting up a local company jointly owned by Partners with Melanesians (PWM)
and other local Non-Government Organization and the Coffee Farmers of
Managalas Plateau. Capitalization of the Company will be done on an equity
sharing basis with PWM investing K428,000 and the Farmers putting in shares
through their existing coffee trees and gardens.

Arabica coffee in the form of Parchment, green beans and ultimately an organic
certified blend produced by the Project will be sold both locally and exported to
outside markets. The development of these products will be done over a period
of 3-5 years time (CY 2006-2009).

The project objectives are:

a) To improve the capability of the Farmers to produce good quality
organically grown coffee by providing them adequate technical
extension services in coffee production and post harvest technologies;

b) Increase the Federations (MDF) capability to self manage their
organization and eventually the operations of the Project;

c) Provide a balance to conserving the ecosystem of the Managalas
Plateau and at the same time derive economic benefits from non-timber
forest products (NTFPs) found therein;

d) Provide an alternative trade system that can give the Managalas
Farmers fair prices and cost efficient services in marketing and
increasing value added to their coffee crops under a more equitable
profit sharing arrangement.

The Project will also have as a secondary objective of testing this model for other
coffee growing areas of PNG to replicate. The replication value of this mode! will
create a significant impact on the coffee industry of the country which is
dominated by small growers (80%). MOCP can also serve as a model eco-
enterprise system in developing other non-timber forest products (NTFPs) both in

=== page 14 ===
3. Product Description
3.1 Product Description: Managalas Organic Coffee

Coffee grown within the Managalas Plateau is mostly of the Arabica variety

( Catemoor and Biue Mountain - Coffea Arabica). The rich voicanic soils of the
Plateau, an even rainfall distribution and cool climate (elevation: 900-1,000
MASL) allows a good coffee growing environment.

Farmers usually plant at distances between 1.5 x 2.0 meters to as close as 1m x
1m. Shade trees (Albizzia Falcataria. Leucaena Leucocepala and several
species of local pine trees - Casuarina) are used to moderate the sunlight
intensity to a desired level of 25 — 40% shade.

Among the cultural practices common to growers are quarterly weeding or under
brushing and pruning once every 2-3 years. Chemical fertilizers and pesticides
are unheard of among farmers; relying on the natural richness of the soils and a
balanced forest environment, Managalas coffee is as organically grown as can
ever be defined by any certification standards. The remoteness of the place.
difficulty in transport and high costs of chemical inputs pius the unfamiliar use (or
even knowledge of) of synthetic inputs are contributory factors to maintaining an
organic based production regimen among farmers in the Plateau.

Coffee cherries are ripened on the trees and handpicked when they reach cherry
red stage; the cherries are then depulped using a manual coffee depulper and
fermented for 6-12 hours. The fermented parchment coffee is washed
thoroughly and sun dried in elevated platforms or spread out in mats to dry for 5-
7 days. Parchment coffee is normally dried up to a level of 20-30% M.C. The
haif dried parchment coffee is then placed in jute sacks and sold to buyers, For
those areas where buyers are in frequent, the beans are further dried up to a
lower level of between 12% - 14% M.C. at which stage they can safely be stored
without undermining quality of the beans.

An average farmer in Managalas has around 500 trees in his garden. Yields can
vary between 1.5-2.0 kgs/tree of Parchment Coffee equivalent depending on the
amount of care he gives to the plants.

3.2 Sustainability of Maintaining an Organic Based Coffee Production and
the Environmental Impact of Coffee Production in Managalas
Coffee growing in Managalas or elsewhere in PNG enjoys popularity due to its

high economic returns and low production costs. The current world market and
prices for coffee is on the upward trend: particular to organically grown coffee,

13

=== page 15 ===
prices are very lucrative — reaching levels of $ 21 - $75/kg/of roasted beans in
specialty markets that cater to health and organic products.

The scenario that PWM/MOCP wants to create in Managalas is to balance the
ecological/biodiversity conservation of the plateau with the economic utilization of
NTFP’s within. This concept of ecoenterprise albeit new to Managalas has had
mixed results in other countries where it has been tested. Best practices and
lessons learned in the other experiences can be of much value to this project so
as not to repeat errors and maximize on good practices learned elsewhere.

The MOCP objectives of setting up a marketing support system to improve price
and market access among the Managalas farmers is a strategic economic
intervention but could create potential downsides that unless anticipated and
addressed could become a potential threat to the Plateau and the success of the
project itself.

Some of the possible scenarios that can impact on the conservation of
Managalas and the production of organic coffee:

1. Anticipate that with an efficient marketing system in place and good prices
given to farmers, there will be an increase in interests to expand areas to
coffee — this could mean opening new fields and cutting old growth forests.

2. In Migration. Previous experience in the Philippine setting (Kalabugao,
Impasugong, Bukidnon) witnessed the destruction of the Kalabugao Plains
ecological balance and the eventual loss of forest cover due to in migration
from people wanting to have a piece of the coffee trade. A similar thing
can happen in Managalas especially when road access is improved and
ingress is easy.

3. introduction of chemical inputs. In the belief that using synthetic fertilizers
and pesticides will increase productivity, people will begin to use them —
and lose the distinction of an organic marque; disturb faunal harmony and
potential water quality loss are possible side effects.

4. In road of more traders, buyers and new products. While competition is
always healthy for business, unrestricted and unqualified entry of new
players can create chaos to prices(Price war);pressure to farmers to
produce; “pole vaulting” or non compliance to contracts and agreements.
Introduction of new crops, products (alcoholic beverages for example) can
slowly erode a community's cohesiveness.

5. The development of a cash economy based on NTFP’s (coffee, buay.

vanilla and other products) in Managalas can create shifts in the needs and
wants among the community members. This shift from subsistence

i4

=== page 16 ===
economy (home grown food and self sufficiency) to a cash economy for
over the counter items also creates changes in community relationships
and needs to be anticipated to counteract cultural degradation.

3.2.1 Recommendations and Insights:

PWM and the Partner Communities and Farmers have to formulate a joint policy
on a Forest Land Use Management Pian particularly on the matter of NTFP
utilization and agricultural development. The effects of open agriculture to the
biodiversity of Managalas have to be considered in the management plan of the
Plateau. Slopes, habitats, watershed areas and old growth seed trees have to
be protected. Growth cycles and allowable extraction rates of NTFPs and their
management practices need to be established before full utilization is
undertaken. An option that can be studied is to test crop combinations (multi-
cropping systems) that can optimize the use of current agricultural lands and
produce year round cash flows to farmers without (them) resorting to opening
new gardens. An example seen in the area is a combination of coffee-vanilla-
buay for cash crops and a multi-crop garden for sweet potato, plantain,
sugarcane, papaya and vegetables (squash, taro, yams and greens). The soil in
Managalas is very fertile and has a good carrying capacity for a multi-cropping
system.

As an example of the above scenario: If a househoid ts allowed 2.0 hectare for a
garden — one (1) hectare will be planted for food crops and another hectare
planted to a multi crop system of coffee-vanilia-buay for cash crops. The
hectarage that will be used for agriculture within the Plateau will only be 5,332
hectares (2,666 household population x 2.0 hectare each household). Out of a
total area of 360,000 hectares, this is only 1.5% of the total Conservation area.
This development to agriculture would be highly insignificant in affecting the
ecological balance of the whole plateau and in maintaining the sustainability of
the Plateaus productivity and maintaining ecological integrity; even with a 2.6%
annual population growth.

Another concern that has a big strategic value to the Managalas Plateau is its
road system. While currently in a sorry state of disrepair, this very status might
be contributory to people not going there. All these will change however when
economic development happens in Managalas. The increased productivity in
Managalas will eventually necessitate the building of a good road system. In
migration, entry of other players in the trade of coffee, farm and forestry products,
new ideas and tastes for new products will eventuaily change the cultural
environment of the villages as well as the surrounding physical environment.

The entry of chemical agricultural inputs in particular could undermine the very
reason of the project -- the production of organic products and conservation of
the Plateau. It is near impossible to prevent changes and development to
happen but in the present state of things, PWM, MDF, CM and other allied

15

=== page 17 ===
developmental NGOs operating within the Plateau can exert efforts to direct the
kind of changes and type of development that can occur in Managalas by
planning its development in advance.

The role of the road system passing through Managalas from Afore to
Popondetta plays a very critical and strategic value to this directional planning for
the Plateau. It is the only road_system existing that allows entry and exit to the
area outside of using light planes.

PWM, MDF, CM and other groups operating in Managalas can present to
government (en banc) a proposal! to operate and manage this road system.
Build, operate, maintain and get exclusive transport franchise to the Managalas
roads in exchange to its conservation and management. Through some degree
of control to these road systems, the group can indirectly influence the
development of the conservation area.

Addressing the concerns on the cultural integrity of the communities can best be
done through an open communication and adequate information, education
campaign. Strengthening existing social and political structures within the
Plateau cements bonds of unity and creates a mechanism of solidarity capable of
answering issues, problems and concerns that will arise in the course of
development and change. 16,000 votes in the Plateau can aiso be a very
strategic political argument to use among the local and national bureaucracies, to
use as leverage for assistance for the Plateau.

4.0 Description of the Market

4.1 The Local Market (PNG)

There are 26 plantation processors and 40 processors listed in the CIC coffee
directory of PNG. All the processors buy parchment coffee and green bean and
also extend toll services by processing parchment coffee to green bean for a fee
(usually 0.25 toea — 0.30 toea/kg).

Interviews with five companies in Goroka showed very positive responses from
the owner/managers with regards to the plan of MOCP to market Managalas
coffee to them. Some of the feedbacks:

1. Most companies are operating at half capacity only — for lack of coffee or
the mills were over designed;

2. One company (Kongo Coffee) is paying a K 1.00/kg premium above
factory door prices just to get quality beans and is willing to extend that
premium to MOCP for quality beans;

3. All five interviewed offered to buy and/or process parchment coffee and
pay good prices for volume and quality;

4. One Company (Arabica’s Limited) wants to buy organic coffee beans and
offered to process MOCPs organic coffee and share market. Their main
problem for their organic coffee line is supply of organically grown beans
and the reliability of organic origin; An indicator that organic coffee
production enjoys premium prices is the fact that they (Arabicas limited)
still earn margins even with a very high cost of transporting coffee by small
plane from the interior highland areas. (K 2.60/kg).

5. All five were willing to cooperate in extending technical assistance to
MOCP to ensure good quality and prices;

6. Two processors (Yondu Coffee, Kongo Coffee) are doing private
extension services to coffee growing communities to promote good post
harvest drying and improve production. Both companies see the vaiue of
coffee as a means to developing village communities and want to
collaborate with efforts that go beyond just buying parchment coffee.

4.2 Export Market: Europe, Japan, US

Organically grown coffee enjoys lucrative markets in the developed countries in
Europe, U.S. and Asia, particularly Japan. To earn an organic marque however
needs the requirements of a certification body and standards. Each market has
a specific organic certification protocol and these have to be considered when
trying to enter into a specific market. Linkages with Fair trade groups and
ecoenterprise networks with the intended country markets can be of help in
facilitating product entry and distribution. A specific buyer in Holland — Travocca
has had initial discussions with PWM as potential buyer for organic coffee.

17

=== page 19 ===
Attached are lists of potential Markets for Organic Coffee in the U.S., Europe,
Japan (Annex ___). Certification groups for coffee can also be contacted for
organic certification (Annex ___).

4.3. MARKETING PLAN

The Project will purchase from the Managalas farmers Parchment Coffee, then
process the parchment into green beans and sell the processed green beans to
local bean processors and roasters either in Lae, Goroka or Hagen through
auction.

Three stages of coffee marketing will be done over a period of three (3) years:

Year 1(CY2006)_—- MOCP will purchase parchment coffee from the 10
cultural zones and process them into green beans for
sale to processors and coffee roasters in Lae, Hagen
and Goroka by auction

Year 2(CY 2007) - Parchment coffee will be processed to green bean
and sold to local processors and roasters; 30% of
the processed green beans will be exported as
organic green beans

Year 3(CY 2008) - 50% of the processed Green bean will be sold to local
buyers, and 30% will be exported as organic green
bean; 20% will be processed into roasted ground
coffee and packaged as organic coffee under
MOCP's brand name for sale to end users (local and
export)

4.3.1 Location

The enterprise will be located in the Oro Province. Purchasing of the Parchment
Coffee will be done within the Managalas Plateau. Buying of parchment coffee
will be done through the 10 cultural zones; 6 Zones are selected for assembly
points: ltokama, Serefuma, Koruwo, Siribu or Ogonomo, Koino and Kawowoki. A
central assembly point of the product will be set up in the Afore Station where the
coordination of the coffee trading operations will be done. Through the station in
Afore, a communication system, purchasing and grading office and storage
facilities will be set up. Shipping and bulk storage will be done in Popondetta
through the wharf in Oro Bay. The Port of Oro Bay can ship the products to
either Lae and eventually to Goroka or Hagen. The Port in Lae is also the main
shipping point for export and export documentation.

=== page 20 ===
The CIC Popondetta Coffee Plant:

There is an existing coffee processing plant in Popondetta that is non-
operational. The mill is owned by the Oro Province under the Department of
Agriculture. Most of the machineries and facilities are intact but needs repairs
and rehabilitation. Based on interview done with CIC, the original intent of the
plant was to service the needs of the coffee growers of Managalas. However.
since the plant was located in Popondetta (243 kms away) instead of within
Managalas, the plant became inaccessible to individual farmer growers and
eventually lost patronage with them. Buyers and traders also did not patronize
the use of the plant since it will just duplicate their work of processing the beans
which they can do by shipping the parchment to Lae, thus putting additional costs
to them.

The Coffee Plant is presently being offered for tender by the Department of
Agriculture. PWM can present a proposal to the Provincial Government with the
backing of the Managalas farmer Communities to take over the ownership and
management of the mill. A proposal to buy out the mill over a period of 5 years
and use it to process coffee from Managalas would have advantages to the
project. Costs can be reduced (instead of toll processing the parchment to other
mills) and quality of the beans can be better controlled. The need for a
warehouse and storage facilities prior to shipping to Lae is solved without
incurring costs for building. It can also serve as a central office for the project.

4.3.2 Main Customers (Target Clients)

The main customers targeted by the project will be the processors/roasters in the
major coffee growing areas — Western Highland Plateau, Eastern Highland
Plateau, Simbu, Morobe, Eastern Sepik, Enga and Southern Highland Plateau.
Coffee processing and buying however is mostly centered in Goroka and Hagen
with transshipments done through the port of Lae. There are 40 existing
processors in the Goroka-Hagen area with 5 companies that do roasting for local
and export markets.

The five (5) companies interviewed alone represents a market of 240,000 50 kg.
green beans/year. (Yondu — 60,000 bags; Airport coffee — 60 bags; Arabicas
coffee — 80,000 to 150,000 bags; 80 tons/year of Organic coffee; Kongo — 60
tons/year organic coffee; 70,000 — 100,000 bags green bean/year).

The volume of coffee needed from these five companies alone represents a
parchment equivalent of 320,000 bags or 16,000,000 kgs of dry parchment.

The 1997 data on coffee production from all the provinces of PNG recorded a
supply of 1,075,403 60 kg. bags of green beans. The data source was from

4.3.3 Total Demand and Market Share

Projecting the current production capacities of the Managalas coffee growers, the
latest survey by PWM shows that there are 700 farmers who grow more than
800,000 coffee trees that can produce about 8,000 bags or 360,000 kgs in 45 kg
bags of parchment.

Assuming the whole production of Managalas is marketed through the MOCP,
this volume represents a mere 0.4% of market share (4,500 bags green
bean/1,075,403 bags total demand). Comparing the markets demand versus the
volume of Managalas coffee production, it should not be a problem selling
Managalas coffee to processors since it represents only a very minor percentage
to their total demand (0.04%).

The key to Managalas getting a good share of the market ts by maintaining a
high standard of quality and this feedback was validated with interviews from the
processors themselves.

4.3.4 Selling Price

Selling price is a function of supply and demand for a particular period in time.
However, factors such as quality, reliability, volume and access to supply can
improve selling prices.

Three methods can be used to determine selling price “comparative method” -
by using benchmark buyers prices (example in Goroka or Hagen) or through a
“what the market will bear method” by way of an auction system. MOCP can use
whichever method suits it best and gives a better quote.

Coffee however is a traded commodity and usually buyers follow the index used

by the commodity market, so a similar system may have to be adopted by
MOCP

5.3. Projected Volumes Targeted

The MOCP will operate within the 10 cultural zones of the Managalas plateaus.
From a recent survey done by PWM on coffee production on the plateau the total
projected volumes available is 2,401,271 trees from 899 hectares. These figures
are derived from PWM's data, where 30% of the farmers numbering 646 were
interviewed for the survey.

From the study, the following data were used to project the volume of Parchment
coffee available:

1) Average trees per farmer is 520

2) Range of number of trees is 150-1,900 trees/farmer

3) 646 Farmers (30% of total population estimated) owns 720,493 trees

4) Coffee yield per tree is between 1.5 — 2.0 kgs. berry/tree

5) Recovery of Parchment coffee from cherry is 20% by weight

6) Total number of farmers in the 10 zones is estimated at 2,153 Farmers
owning 2,401,271 trees from 899 hectares.

The total volume of Parchment coffee computed from the above data is between
720,381 kgs. (low yield of 1.5 kgs. cherries/tree) and 960,508 kgs. (average yield
of 2.0 kgs. Cherries/tree).

For the purpose of this plan, the lower figure of 720,381 kgs. will be used to
represent 100% of the total volume of parchment coffee produced in the
Managalas plateau.

The projects share of the market is estimated at 30% on the 1“ year (Volume:
216,114 kgs. dried Parchment); 50% on the 2™ year (Volume: 360,190 kgs. dried

Introduction

The first Consensus Building Workshop for the year was conducted from 20" — 24”
February 2006 at Noukonane Village. It was attended by MDF, CBOs and active
stakeholders in the then Rainforest Literacy Program, now Consensus Building Program.

The workshop ran for five days. Day one was spent in a slow but heartwarming welcome
by the Noukonane Elementary School and an introduction of what was to happen during
the week. Day two was spent entirely on issues for the Managalas Conservation Areas
Support Project (MCASP) as a whole. Even before the workshop began, informal
discussions with participants indicated a community desperate for information on the
outcomes of the Managalas Leaders Summit held on 19° — 22" December 2005 at
Serefuna village, particularly, the three-year (2006 — 2008) Partners With Melanesians
Inc. Exit Strategy Plan. The Partners With Melanesians Inc. (PWM) Exit Strategy was
viewed as a ‘wake-up call’ by the Managalas community who are very much dependent
on PWM as the alternative service provider. The communities very much held the mis-
leading perception that PWM is a Managalas owned-organization and all funds should be
spent on the Plateau other then secing PWM as a National Non-Government
Organization, free to choose what they want to do in line with its (PWM’s) vision and

mission.

Thus the workshop accommodated for stakeholders to be engaged in this dialogue. This
perception was evident when a day was exhausted on reflecting on what worked well and
did not work well for the MCASP over the past 17 years since the project began in the
Managalas in 1987. Instead of leaving the people dissatisfied that nothing will be done on
issues that did not work well for MCASP, the afternoon session was constructive with
lively discussions, converting the disadvantages into positive outcomes which the
participants thought should be addressed in the MCASP program components and should
form parts of the PWM Exit Strategy Document. Some of the positive outcomes which
participants thought communities are able to do themselves as ‘community contribution

=== page 23 ===
introduction

This design guide describes how to design materials for the Consensus Building Multi-
Channel Learning Program. Materials to be developed using this Design Guide
include:

Series of four interactive radio broadcasts

Newsletter in two languages

Flip Chart with a Poster and facilitator instructions with graphic symbols
Facilitator's Guide

Key Word elementary literacy flyers

Who is the Donor?
RFN — Rainforest Foundation Norway
Overall Goal of the Program

The overall goal of the program is to create a multi-channel “system” of leaming that
enables women and less literate families to integrate conservation and development.

Target Audience

The target audience is women and less literate families on the Managalas Plateau.
The learning will take piace in many settings. However, the main forum for the radio
broadcasts will be clan groups, women’s groups, youth groups, sports groups and
elementary schools.

Learning as Dialogue

“Learning as dialogue” means that learning occurs through a dialogue process that
benefits all parties, both the facilitator and the participants. All parties bring their
knowledge and experience to the table and all parties learn from the dialogue process.
Learning as dialogue is a different educational model than the typical European
educational model. Learning as dialogue reflects traditional core values much more
than European core values, as shown in the table below.

Process Traditional value European/American value
Communication: | Inclusive Exclusive

Shared Private (knowledge as power)

Contributing Persuading

Participating Debating position

Listening and being heard in turn | Dominating the floor

Creating a mutual vision Winning, being right
Ownership: Share Accumulate

Collective Individual

Use relationships to accomplish | Relationships get in the way
goals
Leadership: | Assume responsibility and look | Give orders he. |
5 after the group

In the Consensus Building Multi-channel Leaming Program, facilitators bring
information to the group, then put it on the table. Participants also bring their insights
and ideas to the discussion. Through that “mixing” action, plans are developed that
allow the group to move forward. Mistakenly, facilitators think they have something to
give to people who need it. Actually, the discussion is the heart of the learning.
Everyone learns together and everyone's ideas change in the process. The learning
materials must be designed to accommodate this type of learning.

=== page 25 ===
Multi-channel and Distributive Learning

Multi-Channel Learning

Multi-channel learning means that several media and several settings are used to get
the information to the learners. Following are examples from the Consensus Building
Program of multi-channel learning.

Multiple media used in the Consensus Building multi-channel learning:
Radio broadcasts

Newsletter :

Flip Charts with Symbol-coded posters

Literacy flyers

Facilitator guides

Multiple settings used in the Consensus Building multi-channel learning:
e Clan groups
Women's groups
Schools
Trade store walls and church and house walis, etc. (for the poster)
Literacy classes
Other settings where information is informally discussed (community space,
family homes, etc.)

There are two advantages to using multiple media and multiple settings:

1) Learners receive the same educational messages in several different formats
and places. Through repetition with fresh media and settings, they are more
likely to remember the messages and see how they relate to their lives.

2) Everyone has their own leaming style. For example, if you leam better by
reading, multi-channel learning provides reading materials. If you learn better
by looking at pictures, symbols and graphics are provided. If you learn better
by listening to people speak and/or talking about.the issues yourself, the
dialogue will be most powerful for you. In other words, multi-channel learning
anticipates the variety of learning styles that individuals possess.

Distributive Learning

Distributive learning is an instructional strategy that reinforces educational content by
distributing it in several locations repetitiously. This way, the learners are reminded of a
learning objective again and again so they are more likely to remember it. Also,
distributive learning works well with multi-channel learning because different media and
settings are used to reinforce specific learning objectives. This way, for example, the
learner can learn how important it is for women to participate in decision making from a
newsletter article, a radio broadcast interview, and a group discussion. Refer to
section, “Distribution of Learning Objectives” for distributive learning in Consensus
Building.

=== page 26 ===
Interactive Radio

Interactive radio instruction (!RI) program consists of three kinds of participants:

1) Radio actors
2) Group facilitators (audience)
3) Group members (audience)

During IRI broadcasts, radio actors interact with the group members and the facilitator,
and the facilitator and group members interact with each other. Radio actors ask
questions, provide activity cues, and encourage the group members and group
facilitators to participate during the broadcast. Radio actors give instructions to the
group facilitator. The facilitator follows directions given by the radio actors, then
organizes discussion and other activities with the group after the broadcast. Group
members often respond to questions, respond with a familiar phrase, or do some other
activity such like hand claps as directed by the radio actors.

Radio
Actors

Character Development

All main view points in the community should be represented by the drama characters.

For example:

Character #1) a young person who has visited the city/town who has
forgotten village values and represents the view of the developer
and short-term interests

Character #2) Avvillage elder who represents traditional values

Character #3) An individual who has balanced traditional values with
progressive values

=== page 27 ===
Active Learning

Active learning means the learners are active, not passive. !n other words, they
participate in activities with the teacher/facilitator and with each other. They do not sit
quietly in their seats for the information to be “dumped” into them. In active learning the
teacher will often pair students to work with each other, or conduct group activities.

This engages the students and makes them more interested in the activity. They will
tend to remember information better and look forward to the next learning session. It
also gives them some control in their leaming which helps them to improve
independent thinking and problem-solving skills.

Active learning is when leamers do something, as opposed to passively receive
information. Following are examples of active learning activities:

entertaining, and participatory. The audience should be involved by answering
questions posed by the radio actors, repeating of familiar phrases, or physically
responding to cues with activities hand claps, familiar phrase responses, pointing, etc.
Humor, used in double meanings, word play, and silly sound effects, also keep learners
engaged, if used with taste and cleverness.
