Introduction

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area encompasses about 360 000 hectares of pristine
rainforest in the Managalas Plateau, Ijivitari District, Oro Province. The area is bordered by the
Owen Stanley Range to the southwest and the Sibium Range to the southeast. Popondetta town
and the famous Kokoda Trail are situated north of the proposed conservation area.

Like most areas of NG, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora, but at
the moment is poorly documented. Biologists from the University of PNG have carried out two
previous surveys but the truc biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete. This is evident
from the diverse frog fauna sampled during this survey, because frogs are a good indicator of a
rich and a vibrant environment.

There are about 250 frogs recognised from NG. This number increases at a fast rate because new
species are discovered and described every year, some remain undescribed in museum
collections throughout the world (e.g. American Museum of Natural History, British Museum of
Natural History, Bishop Museum, South Australian Museum). More than 50% of NG frogs
comprising the one family Microhylidae reproduce out of the water. Therefore the wet and
humid environmental condition of the whole Managalas Plateau provides an abundance of habits
for these frogs. However, no previous attempts have been made to quantitatively document this
rich component of the plateau before the previous two surveys by members of this team.

This report summarises the results of the herpetological survey conducted during Phase III of the
Managalas Plateau from 20" May 2006 to 5" June 2006.

Methods

Frogs were detected at night by locating calling males and by visual encounters. Efforts were
equally distributed along rivers and streams for aquatic frogs, and away from water bodies for
non-aquatic frogs.

Some frogs were identified in the field, and voucher specimens were also collected for further
confirmation and storage at the UPNG Natural Science Resource Centre.

Snakes and lizards encountered were also captured and specimens collected for preservation.
Three snakes Furina tristis, Stegonotus modestus and Tropidonophis statisticus were brought to us by
local people.

Survey sites

Numbumare, Aiare village along Musa River.
Altitudinal range: 547-600m.

GPS location: 09° 19° 50°* S, 148° 13° 50” E

Dakara, Umwate village
Altitudinal range: 778-800m
GPS location: 9° 16’ 27°° S, 148° 14° 50" E

The vegetation of both sites are typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs are well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp. palms
and Calamus spp.

Results

A total of 15 species of frogs from three families were recorded. Of these 47% of the species are
of the family Microhylidae, a normal observation for other parts of NG where microhylid frogs

usually dominate. The other families, Ranidae and Hylidae constitute 26.5% of the total species

each. Six species of snakes and three species of lizards were also documented during the survey,
although less time was diverted for snakes and lizards (Table 1).

Local information mentions the presence of Green Tree Python (Morelia viridis), Death Adder
(Acanthophis sp) or probably NG Ground Boa (Candoia) because the later two snakes
superficially resemble each other. Local informant also mentions the presence of large green
frog, which could be Litoria infrafrenata. These animals were not encountered so are not
included in the species accounts.

Mantophryne lateralis

Medium sized frog with brown colour on the back with black longitudinal strip along the side from

Discussion

Frogs are secretive animals and hide during the day but come out during the night to feed, mate
and carryout their other essential biological functions. Daytime encounters are usually
accidental, or when one actively looks for them in likely hiding places. Therefore sampling has
to be done during their active periods so that maximum encounters can be made. Heavy rains
also trigger higher frog activity but some species of the subfamily Asterophryninae may call
during the day.

Diversity Patterns

Diversity at generic and specific levels is high for microhylid frogs in the Managalas Plateau
(Figure 1). This is expected because elsewhere in NG. microhylid frogs usually dominate the
Anuran fauna. For example, Richards (2002) recorded 30 microhylid frogs, 19 hylid frogs and 5
ranid frogs from the Kikori Basin. Richard’s survey was conducted for three years covering

=== page 14 ===

=== page 15 ===
altitudinal range of 40-1300m. It is expected that the number of frog species in the Managalas
Plateau will increase as more surveys are conducted covering all altitudinal ranges of the plateau.

Some species documented at Nabumare were not recorded from Dakara and vice versa, but this
is an artefact of environmental conditions and sampling period. Dakara was much dryer than
Nabumare, so the number of species encountered at Nabumare was higher than for Dakara
(Table 1). At the moment this comparison does not mean anything at all, because a long term
sampling with a lot of rainy periods will reveal the truc diversity of frogs from the two sites. But,
there is some similarity between the two sites, with the presence of four ranid species,
Hylophorbus sp and Mantophryne lateralis at both sites. The three Nyctymystes species collected
along the Musa River were not encountered along smaller creeks, suggesting these species
preferred larger fast flowing rivers compared to smaller creeks.

The six snakes and the skink lizards documented during this survey should be indicative of a
more diverse component of the Managalas fauna. Additional efforts directed towards these
components of the fauna should be prioritised during future surveys.

New Species

A sizable frog fauna (47%) of the surveyed sites are undescribed, including a small skink lizard,
suggestive of many new species yet to be documented. As the survey moves higher to over
1000m new species, especially hylid frogs that prefer fast flowing mountain streams would
undoubtly be discovered. The three Nyctymystes frogs, a genus endemic to NG appears to be new
to science, but further analysis will be done to confirm this.

Environment and Conservation Considerations

Frogs are sensitive to environmental change and are a good indicator of the status of an
environment. In a pristine environment free of pollution, the diversity of frogs at the family,
generic and species levels are usually high. Most of the environment of NG is still under pristine
conditions, except probably around the vicinity of large mining/industrial areas and cities. By
comparing past frog diversity to future diversity should large scale environmental degradation
activities occur, the status of the environment could be determined by assessing the decline in
diversity of frogs.

The environment in the Managalas Plateau still remains intact providing numerous microhabitats
for many animals to utilize. The consequences of clearing forests for large scale agricultural
activities, logging or mining operations would be loss of habitat for many of the rich biota. These
include the Bird-wing Butterfly, Tree Kangaroos, Cuscus, Bandicoots, and a host of many new
species of frogs yet unknown to science.

All these rich biota are the traditional rights and heritage of the Managalas people. Everywhere
in PNG, people are close to their forests and depend on it more than 90% of the time and would
not sustain a good living should the forests go, especially in rural areas where government
services are lacking. A comprehensive list of forest products depended upon by the Managalas
people is out of the scope of this report, but suffice is to say that, wood, food, building material,
Okari nut, bamboo, rattan, Pandanus are some of the things that come to mind. If NEC approves
the Managalas conservation area, the forest will continue to provide for the current generation
and those to come in the future.

1.0 INTRODUCTION

This report presents the findings from the third Managalas Biodiversity Survey, which was conducted
from 20" May 2006 — 05° June 2006. The Managalas plateau is proposed for conservation, which if
approved by the National Executive Council (NEC) will become a Wild Life Management Area
(WMA) in Papua New Guinea (PNG). A team of biologists from the University of Papua New Guinea,
and Department Environment Conservation were involved in this survey. The survey covered both
flora and fauna diversity. Fauna survey included mammals, frogs, reptiles, snakes, birds and bats while
flora compiled plants data.

In this survey, two areas were sampled, one at a lower altitude while another at a higher altitude. The
rationale was to determine the species composition of a typical coastal lowland vegetation and a typical
coasta! mid montane forest. The main focus of the survey was to determine the species composition of
the area surveyed which would indicate various important species in the area.

The first survey site was Nabumare of the Aiari area, which is surrounded by lower montane forest.
The soil type is mainly black loamy volcanic and is rich in debris from leaf litter on the forest floor.
This site has an altitude of about 547m above sea level (as!). The people in the area are very friendly
and their population is about 200 from the 2002 national census although they live in a very large land
area. This population excludes the children who were born after the census. At the moment there is no
functional goverment services in the area although they have an Aid Post and a Community School.
There are no stuff to serve the people, as the geography is so rugged and mountainous that no body
from outside is willing to go. “Even if they went, they would retum after a couple of weeks” was a
remark made by the councillor of Aiari village. The people have initiated an airstrip and is completed
but they have no funding to obtain the necessary equipment to get the airstrip registered and
functioning to be able to have small planes landing. An important service to the people and will
certainly have an enormous impact in the lives of the local people.

The second survey site was Dakara, which is located within the vicinity of the Umuate village. The site
has an altitude of about 778 m asl and is mostly surrounded by a typical mid montane forest. The
vegetation is a bit similar compared to the first site except that it is at a higher altitude. The soil is
mostly black loamy volcanic with lots of plant debris. Umuate village is situated between Itokama
airstrip and Aiari village (first survey site). The people in Umuate go to Itokama for various services
such as medical treatment as well as sending their children to attend primary school there. The
population in the village is estimated to be between 100 and 200 excluding infants.

1.1 GENERAL BACKGROUND OF MANAGALAS PLATEAU

The Managalas area is in the Oro Province of Papua New Guinea. It is quite remote and is isolated
from other parts of the Oro Province as well as PNG at large. It is situated between Owen Stanley
Ranges to the southwest and Sibium Ranges to the southeast. The pleateau is mostly rich in volcanic
soil from the famous Mt. Lamington’s eruption in the 1940's, which is located to the northeast.
Managalas has an altitudinal range of 500m -- 1800m asi and encompasses an area of 300,000 hectares.
It bas an extreme rich flora and fauna biodiversity, which has not been documented yet. There are
about 150 clan groups, which are divided into ten zones, which make up the bulk population of more
than 15, 000 people.

2.0 METHODOLOGY
2.1 SURVEY SITE

This survey was conducted in two different sites within the Managalas Plateau in the Oro Province.
Managalas Plateau encompasses a total area of 300,000 hectares and is situated between the Owen
Stanley Range to the southwest and the Sibium Range to the southeast while Mt Lamington and the
Hydrographers to the north and east. It has an altitudinal range of 500m to 1800m as}.

The first survey site was located at Nabumare in the Aiari area at 09° 19’ 51.4” S and 148° 13'50.1" E
and ranges from 547m to 600m elevation. Nabumare is a half to one-day walk from Itokama airstrip
and passes through another village called Umuate. The survey site is surrounded mostly by lower

The second survey site is a half days walk from Nabumare (first survey site), which is located at
Dakara area of Umuate Village. It is also a half days walk from Itokama Airstrip and has an altitudinal

2.2 POPULATION AND SOCIAL STRUCTURE OF THE AIARI AND UMUATE PEOPLE

At these sites the local people have a special relationship with their environment. Their forest is intact
and contains large amount of unexploited flora and fauna biodiversity not known to the rest of the
world. The people were exposed to the outside world in the 1960's when the Summer Institute of
Linguistics (SIL) was introduced into the Itokama area. This implies that their understanding of the
world around, pattern of social structure, leadership and their interactions with the environment is
unique,

Aiari and Umuate villages are in Zone 4 and zone | respectively of the 10 zones in the Managalas
Plateau, ljvitari District. The local people in these areas have a number of bases in the form of houses.
The permanent houses are built in the main village while temporary garden huts are built in the forest
near the garden for shelter. Moving around has become part of their lives ever since and is considered
to be very important in both the social organization and the subsistence of the local people. The local
people inter marry, usually from other groups in the other villages. Most married couples live on the
husbands land. Their real social life is centred around hunting, gardening, house construction and
gathering wild nuts during its season.

The Aiari and Umuate areas are both not densely populated as in Aiari there are about 200 people
while Umuate has about 100 — 200 people.

2.3 PLANT SAMPLING TECHNIQUES

A 50m x 50m plot (total area of 2500m’*) at compass bearings was set up and a peg with coloured
flagging tapes were placed at each comer to demarcate the four comers of the plot. A 50m transect was
run through the centre of the plot and pegs were placed at 10m intervals along the transect. All trees
with DBH of Scm and or more Im away from transect line on both sides were identified and recorded.
Each tree species with DBH recorded had its estimated height recorded as well. Voucher specimens
were collected for taxonomic identification and deposited at the UPNG Herbarium.

Five quadrats (Sm x 5m) were placed within the established 50m x 50m piot at random compass
bearings and random number of steps. Ali plants (herbs, shrubs, palms, pandanus, lianas, trees and
grass) of 0.5m or above within the quadrats were enumerated. Voucher specimens were also collected
for taxonomic identification.

A general collection was also done from both survey sites to determine the type of plants that comprise
these areas.

5.0 DISCUSSION

5.1 People and their relationship with plant biodiversity

Papua New Guinea’s forests are among the richest in the world and its biodiversity plays a major role
in the lives of many rural Papua New Guineans. Most people (85%) in PNG depend on forest resources
to sustain their livelihoods.

The Aiari and Umuate people have a special relationship with their forests. The forests have become
part of their lives from which they extract various natural plant resources for their needs. They depend
on the forest plants for food (wild fruits and nuts), medicines, raw materials to make tools and
weapons, to build houses and fences, for rituals and magic, for arts and crafts and many more. Thus,
plant biodiversity has enhanced the people's general understanding in the uses and their status in the
community. This has led the people to believe that they have respect for the forest they dwell in and the
resources they extract for their use. This relationship has mutually and equally benefited the people as
well as the environment they live in.

5.2 Plant Biodiversity and Conservation

The proposed area is very rich in plant biodiversity with little disturbance. The forest is intact and has a
greater potential to offer to the people of Managalas and PNG many various products. However, the
forests are also vulnerable to treats from logging, mining, growing population etc. Many PNG forests
have already been exploited by logging and mining companies and have left the forest owners no forest
to dwell in freely, or no long term benefits to the resource owners.

This may happen to the Managalas forest if it is not protected from exploitation of such nature in the
future. Therefore, the proposed idea of conserving Managalas for future generation is important and is
crucial for all stakeholders (landowners, conservation NGO's, Government) to cooperate and work
together to protect Managalas proposed area. Conservation will bring in various benefits to the local
people both directly and indirectly. For instance, tourists will be attracted to come into the area to see
Bird Wing Butterflies of Oro. Bird wing butterflies will disappear if the host plants are destroyed in the
forest. There is also potential for drug discovery in this forest because drug discovery program has now
increased in Papua New Guinea and such forest has a potential to offer for drug discovery.

5.3 Vegetation and species of concern

The vegetation in the Managalas area ranges from a lower coastal forest to mid montane forest to a
higher altitude forest and there are some transitional forests in between which comprise species of both
vegetation types. This implies that a good representation of species of both lower and higher altitude
occurs there. In this survey and the gencra! observations that were made, species such as Gyrinops
(eaglewood), Castanopsis (strong wood for house construction), orchids (ornamentals), Terminalia
(okari nut trees) and Aristolochia (host plant of Bird wing butterflies) are found in the area. These are
important species of concern which if not conserved will disappear and the future generation of Oro
and PNG at large will not sce for instance Birdwing butterflies and will not have okari nuts to eat and
enjoy.

6.0 SUMMARY

This survey shows that both survey sites are extremely rich in plant biodiversity. However, first survey
site comprises more species than the second site. These sites were only a small portion of the proposed
Managalas Conservation Area. In both sites only a few different species occurred in each otherwise the
Species composition was quite similar (refer to appendix 3). The various new species found in each site
were subjected to preference of the altitudinal range. There is a greater family diversity in Nabumare
than in Dakara which results in the more diverse plant groups in Nabumare. A complete species list of
the area is important and is desired to assess the important species that occur there. After taxonomic
identification of the voucher specimens a complete florai list will be provided for the area.

Introduction

The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) covers an area of over 360 000 hectares.
It is situated in the south eastern part of the Southern Papuan Ecoregion in the ljivitari District,
Oro Province. It lies between the Owen Stanley Range to the southwest, the Sibium Range to
the southeast and Mt Lamington to the northeast. The area is comprised of 40 villages with
approximately 16 000 people scattered throughout the plateau. The approximate population size
within the study sites is around 100 individuals. The area is abundant in forest resources and vast
areas of the MPCA are covered in a variety of vegetation types from secondary regrowth,
montane forest to open grasslands. Higher altitude forests exist beyond 2000m.

Partners with Melanesia (PwM), is a national NGO which focuses its work on the Managalas
Plateau. PwM in its conservation programme aims at protecting the undisturbed environment by
carrying out awareness and in the process of establishing a conservation area.

From May 20" to June 4” 2006, PwM engaged UPNG scientists to carry out the third phase of
an on going biodiversity survey in the Managalas Plateau. The main objective of UPNG Post
Graduate student being part of this survey was to gain experience in field techniques and to
render assistance to the experienced field scientists. The information compiled on the flora and
fauna will be used toward the establishment of the Managalas Wildlife Conservation Area.

Methodology

Different sampling techniques are used for plants and animals in the field. A one hectare plot or
a line transect may be used for plant sampling. Mammals are usually trapped or spotted by spot-
lighting using visual encounters at night, while other vertebrates such as frogs, snakes and lizards
are captured during the animals’ active periods. Birds and bats are usually enumerated with the
aid of mist nets. and some times by visual encounters using binoculars. Local information is
some times useful and may be utilized. The sampling methods used in this survey are detailed
below.

Study Site Description.

Two sites were surveyed during this trip. The first site was at Nabumare, located at 09° 19°50”
S, 148° 13°50” E at an altitudinal range between 547-600m. It is in the lower Musa area towards
Aiare village. The second site was at Dakara, located at 09°16°27°°S, 148°14°50°°E at an
altitudinal range between 778-800m. 11 is about half an hour walk from Umwate village.

The vegetation of both sites are typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs are well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Flora Sampling

A 50m x 50m plot was established using compass bearing. At the 25m mark. a line transect was
placed across the plot for enumerating all plant species. Trees with a diameter at Breast Height
(DBH) equal to or greater than Sem were recorded within Im on either side of the line transect.
Tentative identification and height of each tree were all recorded. Five quadrates measuring 5m x
5m were also marked out randomly within the 50 x 50m plot and plant species contained in each
quadrate were enumerated. Voucher specimens of all plants within the plot were collected for

Fauna Sampling

1. Mammals

Mammals were sampled using Tomahawk and Elliot traps, while mist nets were used for bats.
The Elliot and Tomahawk traps were alternatively placed every 10m interval in a 50m x 50m
plot previously marked out. At site 2 Tomahawk traps were placed along Kuman and Pingi creek
for water rats. Baits used included roasted coconut with peanut, ripe banana and tinned fish.
Species caught were later skinned and dried for preservation at the Natural Science Resource
Center, UPNG.

2. Birds

Birds were sampled using mist nets erected at about 30cm above ground level to 10/15 meters.
Visual identifications were done for birds too high for nets. Bird identifications follow Beehler er
al (1986) and Coates (1990). Local informants were also utilized for birds not encountered but
were known to exist in the survey areas. Calls were used to identify nocturnal birds,

3. Herpetofauna

Frogs were captured with naked hands as they are harmless. The frogs were found close to
streams, rivers and further inland - terrestrial frogs. Frogs collected were either hiding on/under
leaf litter, exposed on vegetation while others burrowed into the topsoil 10-15cm deep and they
had to be dug out. Frog capture was maximized after rainy periods. During the periods where no
rainfal] occurred, few species were calling higher up in the canopy layers. Hence, the favorable
times or periods of collecting frogs are usually during wet weather conditions.

Although less time was spent on sampling snakes and lizards, some specimen were also
collected. The local people brought others in.

Appendix 2 (Tables 1-4) provides a full list of plants and animals found within the two survey
sites, Figures |-4 are pictures of some of the animals sampled at the two localities surveyed.

Mammals

Twenty species of mammals from seven families were sampled from the two sites (Table 2). The
families Muradie and Chiroptera had more species than the other families (Figure 1). Figure 1
depicts species distribution in each family and Figure 2 shows the species count from the two
sites, Nabumare and Dakara. All the mammal species found in Nabumare also occurred at
Dakara, including 30% more species that were not encountered at Nabumare. This could explain
species prevalence and endemism at higher altitudes.

Discussion

The preliminary results from the two sites were rich in the diversity of plant and animal species
sampled (Appendix 2), The Managalas Plateau encompasses a vast area and the number of
species documented so far may double with further surveys. There was a slight difference
observed in the general make up of the biota of the two sites sampled. Nabumare had more
species of animals than Dakara. The different species distribution is influence by factors such as
the altitudes, climatic conditions, vegetation types and the production time of the forest. Dakara
was at an altitudinal range of 778-800m, which is higher than Nabumare, at 547-600m. The
vegetation of both sites were typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs were well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Apart from our experience in participating in a biodiversity survey, we gained first hand
experience on various field methods that were used to sample the animals and plants. These
included trapping methods, transects for plant sampling and mist netting for assessing birds /
bats. Frogs sampling requires a lot of patience and effective hearing ability. We saw that it was
normally during the rainy period that the catch rate was maximized.

From this trip we were able to experience some unexpected problems that may arise in a
biological survey .We learnt that to collect good results one had to be patient at times, be open-
minded in any discussions and good public relations with the local people. These would avoid
problems such as loss of sampling time, loss of specimens due to domesticated dogs, and the
general lack of understanding from the local people.

Recommendation

The following recommendations have been done after the survey.

1) Study sites should be confirmed and everyone in the area be informed of the survey
team’s arrival. No last minute decision for survey site location.

2) More awareness is required in the potential survey sites. There has to be prior ground
work done so there is ample discussion with the people and they are aware of all that is to
happen in there in advance.

3) Campsites should be restricted to survey team and field guides (or cooks) only,

4) Experienced personnel from PwM should always accompany trainees out in the field.

5) PwM should continue to engage students in such training because it helps in the capacity
building of our country’s up and coming young scientist.

Conclusion

We can say that this has been an exciting and very educational trip for us as we were able to see
what actually happens in the field and develop some skills that may be helpful to use in whatever

In general observations of Managalas Plateau Conservation Area, the two biodiversity surveys conducted,
first in November, 2004 and the second in November, 2005, provided us with affair idea of the area, at

three species of neurotoxin homo-batrachotoxin, a chemical defense from the birds, the crested pitohui, the
hooded pitohui, and the misty pitohui.

ABSTRACT

In November. 2004, a rapid vegetation assessment was conducted near ltokama and
the surrounding villages of Kuai and Nibaiba. In November, 2005, a phase 2 survey
was conducted as an extension of that survey. The overall aim of the survey was to
gather baseline information on vegetation types. determine the structure and assess the
plant diversity within the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area.

The vegetation survey was carried out in three selected sites, Kierim lower montane
forest, Tahama forest and Pongani forest near the coast. Within each site plots of
50x50m were demarcated. Within the plot, strip lines of 5 x 50m were marked out at
10m interval. The strip line was subdivided into 5x10m subplots and trees 25cm dbh
were measured and heights recorded.

To account for shrubs, herbs and saplings, at least 5 quadrats of 5 x 5m were randomly
placed within the demarcated plot and all species enumerated.

Apart from forest sampling genera! botanical collection was conducted within the
vicinity of each site. Plants with flowers and fruits were targeted as these will aid
proper identification of specimens,

Samplings and general observations indicate that a number of forest formations occur
in the proposed conservation area; Jower montane forest comprising of mixed
Castanopsis forest, low altitude forest on plains and fans, monsoonal or dry evergreen
forest and patches of savanna grassland towards the coast. The results from diameter
measurements in all plots showed that high proportion of trees have dbh <30cm
suggesting that the current forest types are quite young. However, there are indications
that there was a period of suppressed growth that has some bearing on the current
forest structure.

The Shannon Diversity Index average score is 1.50. This is higher than the first survey
at ltokama. Species area curve also show increasing species number as area increases
from mountain to the coast. All in all the Managalas Conservation Area has a very

high species diversity.

It is recommended that the conservation initiatives by the Managalas Development
Foundation in partnership with Partners with Melanesia be strengthen and instrument
put in place to declare the Managalas Plateau as Conservation Area.

6.0 Discussion
6.1 Vegetation

Forest formations in the proposed Managalas largely reflect the geology, topographic,
edaphic and climatic conditions in the area. Within the Itokama area the forest types
display very unique sets of features. In a broad sense, the general forest zonation
appears irregular. Although the forest type resembles tropical lowland forest
observation on surrounding hills shows that undifferentiated stands occur and are

influenced by topography (Piskaut, 2004).

At Anatua there appeared to be some distinct zonation. The lowland forest gradually
grades into montane forest above 1000m as]. However, certain features characteristic
to lower montane formation become obvious at around 700m as!. This is similar to the
vegetation pattem observed at Jarefa and the surround hills. The presence of
Castanopsis accuminatissima, Lithocarpus, Podocarpus and Dacrydium in the forests
indicate low montane elements. Large woody lianas, plants with compound leaves,
cauliflorous plants, and species of Myristica which are typical features of lowland and
towland hill forests (Whitmore 1975) become rare or scarce above 1000m.

6.2 Forest structure

The forest structures are similar in all sites as indicated by the diameter class
distributions (Figure 3.0). That is the current forests are younger. There is lack of
recruitment into the higher size classes. However, the proportion of trees >50cm
further indicate that the original forest was impacted upon by natural disturbance
events in the recent past. According to the locals the drought period of 1997/98 did
affect the forest on the plateau.

6.3 Plant species diversity

The species diversities of the areas surveyed appeared similar with slight variations
that could be attributable to the sampling error. Overall, a total of |.22ha was sampled
with 289 species enumerated. This number excludes other species not present in the
plots. This is suggestive of very high species diversity. The overail species diversity
score for all sites is 2 with the Tahama forests having the highest diversity. This figure
is quite high considering the small area sampled. It is envisaged that this figure will
increase if a permanent Jha plot is established in each site.

4.0 BIODIVERSITY INVENTORY (DISCUSSIONS)

The survey was conducted over twenty working days and nights. A total of 820 trap and 120
net nights and days were utilised in all the three sites. Although maximum effort was put into
the survey in November 2005 the results were quite unsatisfactory.

At site one, only two species of mammals, Paramelomys mollis, a rat and Syconycteris
australis, the common blossom bat, were captured at 1240m asl. We had anticipated more
than five (5) different species of both rodents and bats. The same number was expected of
smailer marsupials and one or two of the larger animals. The reptile composition was aiso
unsatisfactory. No other species was seen except for the very common Emoia lizards.

Putei, which is site two of the survey also yield the same results. After a total of five nights of
sampling none of rats and marsupials except for a bandicoot was caught by locals, five
species of bats and five of reptiles were captured. This is very unsatisfactory because of the
high number of species which are expected to be present in a lowiand rainforest.

The same unsatisfactory results were seen at Pongani. We expected more but caught two (2)
species of rats (Rattus exulans, Melomys rufescans), and four (4) bats (Syconycteris
australis, Pranyctimene raptor, Nyctimene albiventer, Macroglossus minimus) from the
nets. Apart from the white bandicoot (possibly Peroryctes broadbenti) that we saw and some
rats (possibly Uromys caudimaculatus, Mottled Tailed Giant rat) that the survey team saw
scavenging amongst the leaf litter in the forest, there were no captures either from the people
or from children as is often seen in other villagers.

Although actual captures were not what we had anticipated, ethnographic information and also
from our observations, we can say that other factors could have contributed to the poor turn-
over of sampling.

5.2 Social impacts
5.2.1 Hunting Practices

Hunting is still one of the activities that the villagers take part in from time to time. During the
period of survey, a female bandicoot with two young joeys was captured and eaten. Onit the
lower mandible was retrieved for collected.

Food is abundant. People are well nourished with surplus garden food resources. Wild foods
for human consumption is aiso abundant except for protein supplements. Therefore hunting for
wild meat seemed to occur on a regular basis. People have pigs, dogs, chickens and cats in
the villages. However, domestic pigs and chicken are only consumed during important cultura!
occasions, while dogs are kept for hunting and cats as pets to keep house rats away.

People in the area of survey lack protein supplements. Therefore, they will continue to hunt for
wild meat until they can be able to afford protein supplements that are sold in village trade
stores.

5.2.2 Gardening/Subsistence

People in the MPCA are gardeners. Each family has several gardens and food is surplus.
There are so many varieties of food crops, which can cater for their daily supplements.
However, the slash and burn method of gardening and shifting cultivation that they practice
tend to make way for large areas to be left exposed to the disadvantage of smaller ground
animals. Many trees around new gardens are chopped down indiscriminately and left to rot.
That was seen in many villages where we walked.

According to the villagers, people are currently making gardens in forested areas. which were
never touched in the last hve (2} decades. Gardening in previously untouched forests at higher
will continue as population increases. Currently with the siash and burn method that these

INTRODUCTION

The Island of New Guinea fauna consists largely of frogs. According to Richards (2002), the 250
frog species were documented from New Guinea, more diverse compare to other countries. This
is because New Guinea has a constant warm and wet environment that provides humid habitats
and cool temperature at widely different elevations (0-3600m asl) (Richards 2002).

Frogs and other amphibian make up the important component of New Guinea ecosystem and
occur at high densities. They provide important source of food to other organisms and for many
local people (Allison, Bickford et al. 1998).

One aspect of identifying diversity of plants and animals species is to understand and make
broader ecological assessment of biodiversity (Richards 2003). For example Orsak, Easen et al.
(2001), illustrated Lepidoptera, especially moths were chosen because it was used as a general
biodiversity indicators.

This study was intended to document frogs of Managalas Plateau, within approx. 3600 hectares
of virgin forest. Papua New Guinea has difficult mountain terrain which is inadequate to conduct
studies in many interior areas.

Frogs collected at Managalas will contribute to our knowledge of frog fauna in Papua New
Guinea.

The main objectives of Herpetofauna biological survey were to:
1. Document the number of frog species found at 3 elevations at each sites.
2. Identify species abundance and diversity, enable proper management and promote
conservation in sustainable way.

METHODS

A month biological survey was conducted at Managalas plateau, Oro Province from g* ~~ 2°
November. I conducted frog survey at night by search and visual encounter survey. I detected
frogs by their advertisement calls and recorded their calls using a tape recorder. | also did
thorough search on the forest floors, turning over logs and going along streams and search
rugged mountain and steep hill slopes.

At daytime I took photographed of all new frog species in life. I took several body measurements
of frogs and fixed the specimens in 10% formalin and later store them in 70% ethanol. | also
took tissues for future DNA study.

For the purpose of this report, I identify and named frog species according to their morphological
characters. Proper identification of specimens will be given with scientific names and the
specimens will be stored at Natural Science Resource Centre (NSRC) at University of Papua
New Guinea.

Managalas has a promising high diversity of frog fauna. The frog assemblage at Managalas is
comprised of common frogs and few rare frog species especially smaller frog species from
family Microhylidae. It is true Managalas has wide selection of habitats that is good for frogs.

Compare number of species collected at 3 elevations. More species was collected at site 2,
followed by site 1 and site 3. This does not mean there are less number of species at site] and
site 3. High diversity of frog call was heard at site 1 and site 2 but were scattered in camp 3. Few
of the species were widespread and abundant at all 3 sites. The reason some of the species were
not collected because of some nights had continuous heavy rain (Figure2).

CONCLUSION
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) has extremely high diversity of frog fauna.

There was a significance differences in frog species collected at 3 sites. Some species of frogs
collected live and are found only at certain elevation and habitats, (e.g. A/bericus sp) was found
in montane forest. other species do well in high and low elevation, ¢.g. Oreophryne (arboreal sp).
Some species lived only in low elevation (¢.g. Platymantis papuensis).

The data showed high species diversity in family Microhylidae at site | and site 2. The other
family Hylidae, Ranidae may likely show increase diversity. In addition different frog species
forage different habitats. For example, Hylidae are tree frogs and are common along streams,
rivers and live above ground on trees.

SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION

1) Actively carry out awareness program to educate resource owners the importance of
research and conservation.

2) Clearing large areas for gardening increase temperature within surrounding environment,
this practice in future provide good habitat for other introduce animals, ¢.g. Bufo marinus
(introduced toad), easily finds its way in hot temperature. Many frog species become
disadvantage when their habitats and environment change and will from the heat.

3) Develop long term monitoring and research into special plants and animal species. Such
long term monitoring guide good forest management and promote sustainable
development and is vital for decision makers in future.

Date of Survey: 23-27 August 2006
Location: East of Managalas

Introduction:

As part of PwM’s attempt to alleviate poverty and to improve local livelihood in the
Managalas Conservation Area, under the [UCN funding, this survey was carried out.

Survey location:

The rice survey was carried out in almost all parts of the Managalas Plateau. The survey area
as was divided into two parts. The Eastern part which covers villages and zones starting from
zone 5, at Siribu, Ugunomo, through the zone 6 (Dea, Tabuane, koino, Numba, Kaira, Sila,
Kavoki and A fore was carried out by myself.

hh
Starting from Koruvo (Zone 4) up to Kaitavna, Tahamo thrpugh to Serepuna, Kokoro,
Buamfu, Anatua, koe, Itokama and Nokunane Villages was carried out by PwM’s Eco-
Enterprise Coordinator (Doradora Sogaye).

Farmer Information:
Managalas people have not yet gone seriously into rice forming. The survey indicated that
only few farmers have actually tried out planting, but on a very small scale.

During the course of this survey, the list of interested farmers names was collected.

We also noticed there was lack of knowledge on farming methods. From few rite plots
observed, it became obvious that we found the following:

a) None of the farmers had attended any formal training on rice farming

b) Harvested rice (from few farmers) had not been properly consumed- no proper
milling equipment and all harvested grains got spoilt

c) Current farmers admitted they got their rice seeds from friends and trukai rice
Industries at Popondetta.

SOAP & CANDLE MAKING WORKSHOP

=== page 2 ===
Introduction
The 1° workshop on soap and candle was conducted in at Koene in zone 6 from

3‘?-7" October 2005. The follow up on this workshop was originally planned and
scheduled on the 22" May to 2™ June 2006, but then it was postponed to 26"
June —7"" July 2006. Due to the problem with the trainer's wife as a result the
trainer could not make it on time as mentioned above.

Finally we managed to complete the said workshop held recently at Manena
village from the 26-27" July 2006.

Manena resting place is a newly established place with three buildings over the
Bareji River. Before the workshop, Manena resting place was officially declared
opened by the trainer Mr. Keosai Damboro. However this workshop is one of its
first kinds to be held and seeing the outcome as indicated by the number of
participants attending this meeting, I would recommend more of this workshop
in the near future.

Objectives

The objective of this workshop is to:
e) To train Managalas people on how to make oil, soap & candle
f) To educate 7 impart knowledge to the locals about rural
technology/methods of making soap etc. using locally available
resources

Workshop Outline
The process and steps in which this workshop was conducted include:
1, Scraping & drying of coconuts
2. methods of making soap
3. materials needed for making soap
4. steps in making soap

Below is general outline & explanation on per the workshop for future
training if required;

-Scraping & Drying of coconuts

-gathering of drying coconuts-right type of coconuts are those with red eye/spot
for this workshop [we have used 137 coconuts

-scarping of coconuts must be verb fine

-drying of scrap coconuts takes about 3-4 days out in the sun

SOAP & CANDLE MAKING WORKSHOP

How to install & use of press machine
* oil press machine is mounted on to a timber to a height
where the you can easily reach the handle and easy to
press
* the right height is up to the level of the belly button. If it is
very high you will find it very to reach the handle and
press

How to Use the oil press machine
* put a handful of dried coconut through the panel into the
machine
* then pull the handle down to press-if the handle is nard to
pull down-loosen or slacken wheel by using the bar to
create space to allow waste out
* repeat the same process until enough oil is collected

Methods of making coconut oil

There are two ways of making coconut as illustrated the trainer:
1. boiling of coconut cream
2. or by using oil press machine

Steps in Boiling

scrap coconut into a bow!

add coconut or rain water & squeeze to produce cream

strain the cream into the clean pot/container

close the lid and place in the sun for up to 2 hours

after 2hours you will notice cream coming up to the top & only water

remain at the bottom

Use cup to separate the cream into a separate /another clean pot

7. now boil the cream to obtain oil

8. oil will be ready when you see bubbles coming out from the bottom of the
pot

9. remove the pot from the pot & leave it aside to cool down

10. fill the oil in the container ready for use-them make soap oil & candle

Vie why

»

The Use of Oil Press Machine
The second method of making oil is by using the oil press machine

.. the steps:
1. scrap dry coconuts
2. dry them by spreading on the canvas/iron roof sheet above the ground
3. at every land half hours stir/turn
4. drying time is 3-5 days depending on the weather condition

5. when the scraped coconuts are dried up...now they are ready to be

Materials/ingredients you must have in order to make soap include:
7 cups of water (3.5.litres)

6 cups of coconut oil (same sized cups as above)

1 cup of caustic soda

2 plastic buckets

2 cups (empty cups)

a pair of hand glove

soap tray

clear plastics

face/mouth musk (cover nose & mouth)

,

WONAMRWNE

Making soap include:

«the Steps

put 7 cups of water into the buckets

add 6 cups of coconut oil into the same bucket then

stir until water and oi! are evenly mixed (then leave it for 20-25 minutes)
add 1 cup of caustic soda into the bucket with water & oil

stir for 2 hours until the bucket is cold

now it is ready to make soap...pour into the soap tray

and let it to dry

after it is dry cut them using the mark on the soap and let them to dry
properly for about a week. When use are sure completely dry remove it to
do your laundry, wash or even to sell it for money

PAM OVMFS WNP

Three things extracted from them to make soap including dry
coconuts are:

a) dry coconuts

b) jethropa &

c) animal grease

9. Achievements
A total of 40 participants attended the workshop, including participants from
zones 7, 9, & 10. About 137 dry coconuts were used in the workshop and
produced about a quarter bucket of coconut oil; out of the one-quarter bucket of
oil, 83 pieces of laundry soap and two bottles of candle were produced. The soap
was distributed to all participants an s samples including one for the trainer &
PwM Eco-enterprise Officer.

Manena community members want more training to be conducted at their

complaints.

meals for us. Not forgetting all the big men & elders for the village.

=== page 1 ===
Managalas Proposed Conservation Area
ORO Province

Students Report on the 3™ phase of the Biodiversity Survey
in the Managalas Plateau. .

June 2006

Report Prepared for the Partners With Melanesian Inc., Port Moresby, Papua
New Guinea. =

Compiled by

Jason Alonk y
Florence Jicki
Jacinta Mimigari

=== page 2 ===
Acknowledgement

We would like to convey our sincere gratitude to the following people for granting us the
opportunity to participate in this survey.

Mr, Ken Mondiai, Executive Director of Partners with Melanesians, Mr. Vincent Manukayasi,
Program Manager, Miss. Danga Mark, Research Assistant and the rest of the staff at PwM. We
are also indebted to Mr. Roy Garawa, the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF) West
Field Coordinator and Mr. Dickson Darebo, the Mapping Coordinator, for their assistance during
the trip. Much gratitude also to Mr. Walter (the Aiare village councilor) and the people of Aiare
village for their hospitability stay there. Also thanks to Mr. Samuel (the Umwate village Chief)
and the people of Umwate village for their hospitality. To Douglas Tumai (MDF Chairman) and
family for their selfless giving and hospitality, for their patience and kindness, we say thank you.

We owe our utmost thanks and gratitude to our three team leaders, Ms. Rose Singadan, Ms Janet
Gagul (UPNG) and Mr. Paulus Kulmoi (DEC). We also thank Jones Hiaso (UPNG) for teaching
us how to catch frogs. It was a wonderful experience. Thank you all for the knowledge imparted,
the Jaughs and for making our training a memorable experience.

Thank you!

J. Alonk, F. Jicki

=== page 3 ===
Introduction

The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) covers an area of over 360 000 hectares.
It is situated in the south eastern part of the Southern Papuan Ecoregion in the Ijivitari District,
Oro Province. It lies between the Owen Stanley Range to the southwest, the Sibium Range to
the southeast and Mt Lamington to the northeast. The area is comprised of 40 villages with
approximately 16 000 people scattered throughout the plateau. The approximate population size
within the study sites is around 100 individuals. The area is abundant in forest resources and vast
areas of the MPCA are covered in a variety of vegetation types from secondary regrowth,
montane forest to open grasslands. Higher altitude forests exist beyond 2000m.

Partners with Melanesia (PwM), is a national NGO which focuses its work on the Managalas
Plateau. PwM in its conservation programme aims at protecting the undisturbed environment by
carrying out awareness and in the process of establishing a conservation area.

From May 20" to June 4" 2006, PwM engaged UPNG scientists to carry out the third phase of
an on going biodiversity survey in the Managalas Plateau. The main objective of UPNG Post
Graduate student being part of this survey was to gain experience in field techniques and to
render assistance to the experienced field scientists. The information compiled on the flora and
fauna will be used toward the establishment of the Managalas Wildlife Conservation Area.

Methodology

Different sampling techniques are used for plants and animals in the field. A one hectare plot or
a line transect may be used for plant sampling. Mammals are usually trapped or spotted by spot-
lighting using visual encounters at night, while other vertebrates such as frogs, snakes and lizards
are captured during the animals’ active periods. Birds and bats are usually enumerated with the
aid of mist nets, and some times by visual encounters using binoculars. Local information is
some times useful and may be utilized. The sampling methods used in this survey are detailed

below.

Study Site Description.

Two sites were surveyed during this trip. The first site was at Nabumare, located at 09° 19°50"
S, 148° 13°50” E at an altitudinal range between 547-600m. It is in the lower Musa area towards
Aiare village. The second site was at Dakara, located at 09°16°27"’S, 148°14°50°°E at an
altitudinal range between 778-800m. It is about half an hour walk from Umwate village.

The vegetation of both sites are typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs are well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Flora Sampling

A 50m x 50m plot was established using compass bearing. At the 25m mark, a line transect was
placed across the plot for enumerating all plant species. Trees with a diameter at Breast Height
(DBH) equal to or greater than Scm were recorded within 1m on either side of the line transect.
Tentative identification and height of each tree were all recorded. Five quadrates measuring 5m x
5m were also marked out randomly within the 50 x 50m plot and plant species contained in each
quadrate were enumerated. Voucher specimens of all plants within the plot were collected for

=== page 4 ===
preservation at the UPNG Herbarium. This serves as a record of all plant species in the
Managalas Plateau, particularly within the surveyed sites.

Fauna Sampling

1. Mammals

Mammals were sampled using Tomahawk and Elliot traps, while mist nets were used for bats.
The Elliot and Tomahawk traps were alternatively placed every 10m interval in a 50m x 50m
plot previously marked out. At site 2 Tomahawk traps were placed along Kuman and Pingi creek
for water rats. Baits used included roasted coconut with peanut, ripe banana and tinned fish.
Species caught were later skinned and dried for preservation at the Natural Science Resource

Center, UPNG.

2. Birds

Birds were sampled using mist nets erected at about 30cm above ground level to 10/15 meters.
Visual identifications were done for birds too high for nets. Bird identifications follow Beehler et
al (1986) and Coates (1990). Local informants were also utilized for birds not encountered but
were known to exist in the survey areas. Calls were used to identify nocturnal birds.

3. Herpetofauna

Frogs were captured with naked hands as they are harmless. The frogs were found close to
streams, rivers and further inland - terrestrial frogs. Frogs collected were either hiding on/under
leaf litter, exposed on vegetation while others burrowed into the topsoil 10-15cm deep and they
had to be dug out. Frog capture was maximized after rainy periods. During the periods where no
rainfall occurred, few species were calling higher up in the canopy layers. Hence, the favorable
times or periods of collecting frogs are usually during wet weather conditions.

Although less time was spent on sampling snakes and lizards, some specimen were also
collected. The local people brought others in.

Results

Appendix 2 (Tables 1-4) provides a full list of plants and animals found within the two survey
sites. Figures 1-4 are pictures of some of the animals sampled at the two localities surveyed.

Mammals

Twenty species of mammals from seven families were sampled from the two sites (Table 2). The
families Muradie and Chiroptera had more species than the other families (Figure 1). Figure 1
depicts species distribution in each family and Figure 2 shows the species count from the two
sites, Nabumare and Dakara. All the mammal species found in Nabumare also occurred at
Dakara, including 30% more species that were not encountered at Nabumare. This could explain
species prevalence and endemism at higher altitudes.

=== page 5 ===

surveyed sites

Discussion

The preliminary results from the two sites were rich in the diversity of plant and animal species
sampled (Appendix 2). The Managalas Plateau encompasses a vast area and the number of
species documented so far may double with further surveys. There was a slight difference
observed in the general make up of the biota of the two sites sampled. Nabumare had more
species of animals than Dakara. The different species distribution is influence by factors such as
the altitudes, climatic conditions, vegetation types and the production time of the forest. Dakara
was at an altitudinal range of 778-800m, which is higher than Nabumare, at 547-600m. The
vegetation of both sites were typical of lower and mid montane forests, dominated by
Castanopsis acuminatisma on well drained ridges. Epiphytes, lianas, lichens, Zingiberaceae and
other fleshy herbs were well established with the mid-storey consisting of Pandanus spp, palms,
Calamus spp and the scrambler bamboo, Nastus sp.

Apart from our experience in participating in a biodiversity survey, we gained first hand
experience on various field methods that were used to sample the animals and plants. These
included trapping methods, transects for plant sampling and mist netting for assessing birds /
bats. Frogs sampling requires a lot of patience and effective hearing ability. We saw that it was
normally during the rainy period that the catch rate was maximized.

From this trip we were able to experience some unexpected problems that may arise in a
biological survey .We learnt that to collect good results one had to be patient at times, be open-
minded in any discussions and good public relations with the local people. These would avoid
problems such as loss of sampling time, loss of specimens due to domesticated dogs, and the
general lack of understanding from the local people.

=== page 7 ===
Recommendation
The following recommendations have been done after the survey.

1) Study sites should be confirmed and everyone in the area be informed of the survey
team’s arrival. No last minute decision for survey site location.

2) More awareness is required in the potential survey sites. There has to be prior ground
work done so there is ample discussion with the people and they are aware of all that is to
happen in there in advance.

3) Campsites should be restricted to survey team and field guides (or cooks) only.

4) Experienced personnel from PwM should always accompany trainees out in the field.

5) PwM should continue to engage students in such training because it helps in the capacity
building of our country’s up and coming young scientist.

Conclusion

We can say that this has been an exciting and very educational trip for us as we were able to see
what actually happens in the field and develop some skills that may be helpful to use in whatever
field we may be employed in. The training provided in the field was complementary to what we
learnt in school whilst also giving us much needed practical hands on experience in biological
field surveying. To PwM we say keep up the good work and we hope student engagement in
such surveys will continue.

General Overview of Statistics

- While every effort has been put in obtaining the correct statistic, there are some reservations for
human errors and missed data that may contribute to the correctness. Therefore can be subject to

changes when necessary.
But generally from the data, the following information, can be deduced and can make general

conclusions.

Number of Trees.

The Managalas Plateau consist of Eastern and Western Zone. The date from the Eastern zone is
obtained mainly from five village with assistance of some CBO’s and other persons who cared to
assist. The other rest are from assumption as we could not be allowed under certain restrictions. It is
deduced that the Eastern zone has around 230,000 coffee trees. This includes newly planted and old
over grown trees. Newly planted coffee trees constitutes about 5%, and this amounts to about 11,500
trees in the Eastern Zone alone.

The Western zone of the plateau, from the statistics obtained, there is almost about the same around
230 thousand trees. This also includes newly planted trees, however newly planted contributes about
7%, which amounts to about 16 thousands trees.

Including the whole Eastern & Western zone, the Managalas plateau has about 460 thousands trees.

Area covered by coffee trees.

From the data collected all areas are measured in square metres. Within a one square metre area it
contains about 2to3 trees, and with that, it assists in acquiring these figures.

The Eastern zone has about 57.41 hectares of coffee growing area. While the Western zone has
about 55.96 hectares. And the total Managalas Plateau has about 113.37 hectares of coffee growing
area, This area consists of old and newly planted area. As these is not much planting, these are about
6 percent of the area consist of new trees which is about 6.8 hectares.

Number of Bags (Parchment) per Season.

The total number of bags recorded is based on information (figures) gathered in 2006 season. The
figures may vary more or less, and is depended entirely on farmer commitmenv/activity and other
various factors in a season.

There are certain main factors affecting production which are;

i Unavailability of pulping Machine

This has become the most significant impediment in the numbers of production. Most farmers share
on the average ration of 7 farmers is to one pulping machine or either resort to manual hand pulping,
thus is a tiring and time consuming process. And so almost about 30% of cherry volume is lost un
catered.

=== page 23 ===
a Road Transport condition and Market (price) factor.

There has been some uncertainty in the marketing factors that discourage farmers from not been
busy on coffee production. 2006 has been a year where M.O.C.P (Managalas Organic Coffee
Project) and other agents offering door step marketing system. This initiative has certainly refocused
their attention into coffee activity which would lead to increase in volume in year to follow.

Previously pricing has been a real concern. Farmers often receive 70 toea to 80 toea per parchment
kilo. Some do not even sell their bags due to no proper access road networking. At the moment the
state of road is in a dire straights , needing urgent repair and maintenance. Consensus effort from all
sector of community must be gauged, whether it be local level government, community groups or
any non government organizations in alleviating this problem. The only accessibility is through four
wheeled vehicle, and in raining season access in none at all. These factors contributes a lot to the
volume of production.

Through MOCPs introduction of competive price ie.K2.50t per kilo, and other agents competing in
the area, would certainly encourage farmers in rehabilitating their neglected trees as viable cash

crop.
Data’s shown are 2006 volume, they are;

Eastern zone about 2300 bags and Western zone is about 2000 bags. Totaling up to about 4300 bags
in kilogram its around 4300x 50 = 215000 kg’s which is about 215 tones.

Numbers of farmers and family involved.

From the data obtained, there are about 1200 farmers on the Plateau. On the average there are about
3 family members in each garden. This gives total to about 3600 people involve in coffee production
in the Managalas Plateau. This figures is sure to increase given competition incentives offered by
MOCP and may be other buying agents on the site, thus may encourage more farmer involvement.

Problems Encountered.

As in most ventures, the enumeration exercise has its own share of problems. Most viewed this
exercise from negative perspective, thinking its for personal benefits, for whom I myself could not
work out. The level of co-operation from the Eastern zone is almost none, and often times faces
verbal abuse and at few occasion near physical confrontation. This problems were often instigated
by ill informed local leaders especially councilors who may have no knowledge or rather ignorant on
the aspect for initiative taken by Partners with Melanesia in putting MOCP on the ground, with its
business plan for the betterment of MDF (Managalas Development Foundation) for financial self
sustenance in enhancing its various programmes in the Plateau in the long run. Despite this hurdles,
the statistics has been somewhat collected and compiled with some handful of individuals who have
rendered their invaluable assistance and support.

=== page 24 ===
Basic Maintenance Of Organic Coffee Quality Process.
The following steps are been emphasized in the coffee production steps in maintaining best quality.

Harvesting.

Only ripe cherries (fully red) are being encourage to be picked. Mixture of green cherries, half ripe
cherries and over ripened (brown in colour) does not give uniform out look, and often a problem in
sorting. It is bound to have effect in the final product ie. Tasted and quality as cach has their variable

quality at the end.
Pulping and Fermenting.

It is encourage that within 24 hours of harvesting, the cherries must be pulped. Prolonging will
certainly have effect on the beans, ie been getting brown coating, as a result of heat gencral in the
bags or containers. Once when beans are affected, it eventually lead to detriment of quality.

Pulped beans must be kept in cool locations for fermentation. Metal containers are discouraged as it
may coat rusting on the beans. Once when rusting in coated it affects the quality greatly.
Fermenting for 2 days is encouraged this is ample time for removeral of mucilage (greasy coating).
Plenty of clean water must be used for washing until clean.

Drying

Most drying must be done on beds above ground level which is a recommended method. In rainy
days solar drying ie, building canvas roofing above drying beds. This method absorbs heat and helps
drying effectively. The method has been in use in some parts of Managalas area like Silibu, Dea and

Numba.
Drying of beans should take about 3 good sunny day; to show that it has been amply dried, tooth
mark should not appear on the bean when bitten, a method by which most farmers should use for

testing ample dryness.
Storage.

All dried parchment should be stored in a house that is free from smoke (fire) and open to moisture
absorption. They must be stored in a house shed and covered with canvas to avoid exposure.

All coffee parchment should not exceed more than three month in a storage, the longer it is kept the
danger of quality deterioration is high. After 3 months efforts must be made to sell off stock to any

agent who is offering better competitive prices.

Pricing.
To get better price it is best to organize group marketing ie. Farmer co-operation and the co-

operation should gauge competitive buying agents or company for better prices at the current
markets or markets recommend by coffee industries co-operation (CIC).

Executive Summary

From mere observation of its structure Managalas Development Foundation has
been unintentionally designed to function as a supra system consisting of various
sub-systems and systems of systems hence appropriating it to adapt oa training
strategy that will enhance the various sub-systems to function independently yet
collaborate with each other to meet the overall goals of the community based not-
for-profit organization's capacity building needs. [Very similar to the Melanesian
circular system of governance in which service delivery, community mobilizing and
etc. is often led by influential individuals however the emphasis is placed on overall
community welibeing. It involves active participation and interaction between
individual, groups of individual and communities. Collaboration and
interdependency has always been the norm].

The success of its various programs wili heavily Gepend on the efficiency of the
individuals involved thus the training strategy is to produce learning individuals who
will tasked themselves to undertake various activities of MDF as personal action
learning projects. It is anticipated that by the end of an individual action learning
project using “systems learning approach” the participant will have advanced
himself in his personal capacity whilst at the same time appreciating the overall
human resource capacity of MDF.

The ‘systems learning’ approach is based on Kolb.s experiential leaming cycle and
draws also Peter Checkland’s ‘soft systems methodology’. it emphasizes
participation and calls for open and active pctterns of communication based on
interdependent relationships’, and necessitates action to develop it. This requires an
appreciation of stages in group development and how to facilitate group
processes. The key is to see things differently, if we are to act differently - and we
need processes that enable this.

INTRODUCTION

Theatre is used to entertain as well as educate. Theatre has been a bridge between
entertainment and education and is used to share news, share history and or
educate communities. Jt is interactive where audiences discuss controversial and
sensitive issues in sexuality, H]V and or relaicd issues and other development
issues. Since HIV is linked to many sensitive and controversial issues, drama can
be seen as a powerful strategy to challenge certain attitudes and risky behaviours
and promote accurate information.

Theatre basically is to change the knowledge, attitudes, or behaviours of audience.
In this context, theatre will be used to educate people in the communities about
safer sex practices through drama performances, thus providing and enabling
environment for behaviour change.

Papua New Guinea, like many countries and cultures in the world, where more
than 75 per cent of the population are not too well educated, this media is very
familiar and popuiar and the skills are found in the community.

This manual will be used as a guide for facilitators of comnmunity based theatre
iainings. Representatives from district or community based Theatre Grouns will

be trained on the basics of theatre and the techniques which than could be used to
dramatise situations or issues affeciing ibe communities they come front.

Activity 1:
Facilitators’ Introduction

Who am I? Facilitator to begin by introducing himself or herself, i.e. their name,

Activity 2:
Participants getting to know each other

You are to choose only one exercise our of the following exercises below:

1,1 Ask participants tc get together in twos and introduce themselves to each for 5
minutes. and then ask each pair to introduce their partners to the whole group. (4
brief 2 — minute hiography of each participant should be obtained through this
technique). As each participant is presented, the trainer writes the participants
name on the flipchart which hangs on the wall behind the trainer.

1.2 Group stands in a circle. Plaver A (the facilitator) enters the circle and shake
hands with the plaver to their left. Player A says their own name first as they
shake hands. Player 5 says their own name. Player A repeats player B's name and
player B repeats plaver A’s name.

Plaver A: Maria
Player B: Jenny
Player A: Jenny
Player B: Maria

Player A iben moves on to the next player on their left. When plaver A has met
two or three players around the circle, plaver B follows, and so on. All players
meet and greet every other player twice, once as they move around the circle, and
once they are in their original circle position and standing still. The last person to
move is the player who was standing o the right of the player A at the
comunencement of the game. Afier the last player has:completed their circuit. the
whole group says ali the names together in order around the circle.

This is a most effective name game because each player makes hand to hand and
eve to eye contact while speaking to each other player. The status of all players is
kept even.

Keep strictly to exchange of names and handshakes only.

1.3 Name games are many and varied. This is the most common, and involves
sitting in a circle and involves rhythmic beats.

The group establishes a simple four beat rhythm. Beat one is slapping the
thighs, beat two is clapping, beat three is clicking the fingers of the right hand,
and beat four is clicking the fingers of the left hand. When the rhythm has been
established (not too fast) the first player says their name on the third beat (as
they click their fingers on the right hand) and then says the name of another
player on the fourth beat (as they click their fingers on their left hand). The
new player continues the sequence and so on.

For example: Slap clap Ezekiel Lames, slap clap Hohora Sari, slap clap
Julieanne Gore, etc.

Players keep the beat constant. This is good fund and excellent for rhythm
development, The game relies on all players having pre-knowledge of each
other’s names.

Activity 3:

Ice Breaker
3.1 Eye Contact

When people meet for the first time, they find it difficult to look directly into each
other’s eyes. This could be due to cultural reasons or because they are too shy to
look someone in the eye.

As actors one must directly look at the subject he/ she is talking to.

3.1.1 Walk around the room when the leader calls out, FREEZE with your eyes
focused on a person. Repeat again this time focusing on another person and
so forth,

3.1.2 Next ask participants to find a partner and stare directly into each other’s
eyes. Do this without distracting each other and do it seriously.

3.1.3 Still in pairs, this time one partner to shut their eyes while the other partner
studies his/ her facial feature. Give them about 3 minutes then ask the person
with the eyes open to talk about their partner's facial features. Then ask them
to reverse the roles so that they both have turns to describe each other's facial
features,

3.2 Trust Exercises
Members of a drama group need to trust other members of the group. The trust
exercise helps to build trust among the group members.

3.2.1 Ask the participants to find a partner about the same size and height. One
partner to shut their eyes while the other leads him/ her around the room,
guiding them to avoid bumping into things or other factors.

ORIGINS OF THEATRE

Theatre existed in the Civilization of the Western world for the lasi 3000 years.
Little information about the Origin of Theatre has survived. The information we do
have comes from wall paintings, decorations, artifacts, and picture writing system
that show the importance of successful hunts, seasonal changes, life cycles, and
stories of the gods. From these people have seen the necessity of passing along the
experience of the old to the young through art, storytelling and dramatising events.
Even today cultures that do not have written languages have developed some form of
drama to dramatise imagination and the spirituality of people.

Drama is part of most diverse societies’ cultural heritage and it mirrors daily
livelihoods. That is mainly because of its relationship to festivals and religious
practices. In most cultures, communities identify themselves in drama as
dramatization of specific issues reflect the cultures. Drama reflects reality and needs
an interpretation of it to which it has an effect on individuals. Drama provokes
reflection and in a way stimulates the analytic potential of individuals. And it creates
a mirror effect to which individuals look at themselves at a different perspective.

People are born with body languages which are the early steps of mankind, and
drama was very likely spontaneously embedded in those early steps. Theatre

emerged from myth, ritual, and ceremony. Early societies see connections between

certain actions performed by the group or the leaders in the group and the desired

agricultural cycle.

Rituals evolve along two main avenues. Rituals are accompanied by myths and the
myths enter the story telling tradition, gaining a life beyond original rites. This new
life allows the myths to move towards entertainment and admirable and pleasant
appearance. The two main avenues which rituals evolve along include;
* rituals, where myths are central, evolve into full blown religious worship, and

Although boundary between these trends sometimes seems narrow, the distinction is

Through these rituals. leaders, or actors of sorts, emerged. These acting or leadership

POPULAR THEATRE:

-In the Developing countries there are two types of Theatre: One is the Theatre which
takes place in a forma! context which is very much more European and is aimed at
smal] cultural elite in urban areas, and the other takes place in the open as an
instrument to communicate important messages for the community. There are many
encouraging experiences of popular theatre in some developing countries.

“Popular theatre is gaining increasing attention in the Third World as a tool for popular
education and community organizing. It finds expression in a number of forms including
drama, music dance, puppetry and poetry and is performed for — and aften by — ordinary
peasants and workers. Popular theatre is used as a means of bringing people together,
building confidence and solidarity, stimulating discussion, exploring alternative options for
action, and building a collective commitment to change: starting with people's urgent
concerns and issues, it encourages reflection on these issues and possible strategies for
change.

For three decades popular theatre has been used in processes of development
communication as part of adult education programmes. From these initiatives grew a
special type of popular theatre, called 'theatre for development.’ In workshops training
people in the use of popular theatre techniques an inventory of local problems is made for
later use in the plays. In each play one problem theme is explored by and for the local

community."
(By: Jaap R. Swart, Center for the Study of Education in Deveicping Countries/Radio Netherlands Training
Center, The Hague, The Netherlands)

The approach of popular or community theatre is that performances must be linked
to crucial analysis, organisation and struggle. The concept of community theatre
emphasizes the revolutionary value of art. Instead of being merely a pleasant and
gratifying spectacle, community theatre (and art) aims to distribute, to shake, to
move the society towards self and critical thinking and action.

Majority of the people in PNG are illiterate hence theatre has been identified as one
of the effective approaches in educating people especially in rural communities
about the HIV and AIDS and related issues , and about safe sex practices as wel! as
caring for people living with HIV. The objective of community theatre is to allow
values and behaviour to be discussed comfortably without directly challenging the
community or individual beliefs and values. And to generate further discussions in
communities on the issues of HIV and AIDS and the ways they can respond to
protect themselves and their children. The approach or the purpose of community
theatre is that communities use popular theatre as a medium to educate communities
on the basic HIV information. And since most of the Theatre Groups are district
based they are able to facilitate sustainability and local ownership.

Actor Space

in popular theatre the audience surrounds the performers while in classic theatre the
audience is facing the actors. However, it is important to divide the scenic space so
the actors can refer to their positions in a common language. There are various types
of acting stages. The most commonly used stages popular theatre are proscenium,
thrust, and in and around staging.

TYPES OF STAGING
1. Proscenium Staging

A Proscenium theater is a theatre space whose primary feature is a large archway
(the proscenium arch) at or near the front of the stage, through which the audience
views the play. The audience directly faces the stage, which is typically raised
several feet above front row audience level, The main stage is the space behind the
proscenium arch, often marked by a curtain which can be lowered or drawn closed.
The space in front of the curtain is called the "apron." The areas obscured or hidden
by the proscenium arch and any curtains serving the same purpose (often called /egs
or formentors) are called the wings. Any space not viewable to the audiences is
collectively referred to as offstage.

Above: an example of Proscenium staging - the interior of the Auditorium Building in
Chicago built in 1887. The arch around the stage is a proscenium.
