3. In The Round Staging

Theatre-in-the-round or arena theatre is any theatre space in which the audience
surrounds the stage area.

Theatre-in-the-round concept requires no stage curtain, little scenery and allows the
audience to sit on three sides of the stage.

The stage itself in this arrangement is typically round, square, or triangular, with
actors entering and exiting through the audience from different directions or from
below the stage. Such a space is usually configured with the stage on an even level
with or lowered below the audience in a "pit" or “arena” formation. This
configuration lends itself to high-energy productions, and is especially favored by
producers of classical theatre.

Theatre-in-the-round presents problems since actors at all times have their back
facing some members of the audience. However, it also allows for interesting and
realistic staging. Special consideration needs to be taken in regard to the set design,
so as not to hide any audience member's view of the performance.

Background

Environment and Conservation is a huge problem faced by our
community throughout the country in the global changes rapidly
happening; PWM is taking the lead in addressing the Conservation and
Land Use issues in the project site Managalas in the Afore District, with its
different partners. Each year, new concepts and strategies are spent on
community and institutional project to help people to understand the
basic function, roles and responsibilities of conservation and Land Use, to,
MAKE OUR ENVIRONMENT JUST, SAFE AND SECURE PLACE TO LIVE FOR
NOW AND FUTURE GENERATION.

There are several ways to devise different activities that could enhance
and create conservation issues to be easily understood by the community
members, by using Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication (
Theatre Arts Section). The most obvious one was in the area of Creative
Arts; however, to achieve solid results the workshop was conducted in
Poponedtta Town, Anglicare Training centre.

This workshop recognizes that one of the strategic way to create
awareness in the conservation Land Use issues is to involve the
community, particularly the youths and the senior members of the
community and expose their skills and abilities in different dimensions of
Art of Drama. This workshop illustrated the medium drama, exposed the
inner feeling of a person how they perceive Conservation and Land Use
issues in their community as evident in their drama session , the other

creative environment for community discussion.

I, INTRODUCTION

The District Wide Combine Forum is the last activity of a cycle of activities under the
Consensus Building and the Rainforest Literacy Program. The two programs complement
each other and therefore their activities form a cycle.

The Managalas Plateau has a total of 150 major clan groups and the clans are further
divided into 10 zones.

The Combine Forum serves as an avenue where all 150 clan members come together and
discuss their issues and problems. Representatives from partner NGOs, government
departments and other statutory bodies are also invited and where necessary response to
the people’s issues. In a way, we try to help the people find solutions to the issues in
which they themselves are and will be the cause of development.

For this year’s forum, a representative each from the Media for Development Initiative
and Department of Community Development were able to make it to the forum. Other
partner NGOs and government department, and others send their apologies as they were
caught up with their schedules.

Program starts at 2 pm with welcome speeches by Forum Chairman Douglas Tumai;
Community Representative Zone 5; PWM Executive Director; MDI Representative;
Department of Community Development Representative; & MDF Board Chairman.

The MDF chairman Malchus Kajia officially opened the forum and each participant then
did a brief introduction of themselves. (See attached for list of participants)

I. FORUM EXPECTIONS

the participants on what their expectations are after the Combine Forum. Each zone (10
zones) representatives were given the opportunity to say what they think. Unfortunately
there were no representatives for Zone 4 and 10.

CBO suspension to be uplifted and include them in project activities

® The 28 priority projects of 1997 reviewed in order to bring back peopie’s interest

* PWM, MDF & CBOs to understand their roles and responsibilities with regard to
the exit strategy
CBOs & MDF work together to reform the Consensus Building Process
MDF to be independent and take on responsibilities of the MCAP by putting into
practice skills and training already acquired

* PWM, MDF & CBO should really see where we are heading in terms of the
program activities since 1997

* To come up with collective ideas involving all communities and to see where we
went wrong/failed with regard to the exit strategy and to find the way forward

=== page 4 ===

PWM

* There should be coordination and cooperation between PWM, MDF & CBO for
the smooth running of the MCAP and that there should be transparency at all
levels

* All communities on the Plateau to come together and start all over again because
currently MDF are the ones running the project and as a result most clan members
did not attend the forum.

* Find out about the cause of lack of people’s interest in the project

* Bottom-up planning approach (Consensus Building process) is slowly dying out,
we have to find out why

management of PWM since 1997 when the organization was registered under IPA. [t was
during that same year when PWM signed the contract with RFN for funding. Since then
REN has been the main donor funding the major project components of PWM. Apart
from RFN there were also other donors that funded other supporting programs.

Mr Mondiai made it clear that he was employed in 2003 and was only aware of issues
from then on.

This list has not been reviewed since then and has become a major irritation for a number
of community members. The priorities have come to be seen as promises by PWM and
there is a resentment from the communities that no action as happened.

Dear Honorable Minister.

SUB: OBJECTION TO GOLDMINEX LTD MINING EXPLORATION LICENSE No. 1547
MANAGALAS PLATEAU, AFORE SUB DISTRICT, ORO PROVINCE

On behalf of the 18.000 people of Managalas plateau in Afore sub district of Oro province, | am
bringing the above matter to your urgent attention because your Department (Mines) and the
Mineral Resource Authority (MRA) have already given issued or renewed a mineral expioration
license to Goldminex Ltd to do exploration in Afore sub district of Oro Province.

The area identified as ELA 1547 falls directly within the boundary of proposed Managalas
Conservation Area which covers approximately 360.000 hectares of land covered with forests from
altitude as low as 40 m to 2880 m above sea level. This area is the home of the {8,000+ people from
150 clan groups who have been living there for generations.

The area that | have described above is on the eastern side of the Owen Stanley ranges, which is
home to some of this country’s unique flora and fauna including the CITES, [UCN Red List and
PNG Protected Species under the Fauna (Protection and Contra!) Act 1966 but not limited to the
following:

The Queen Alexandra Birdwing Butterfly ....te world’s largest butterfly

New Guinea Singing Dogs ...close relatives of the Australian Dingoes

7 species of the Birds of Paradise .... 2 believed to be new not vet described by science
3 new Species of Frogs ....not yet described or new to science

The Whistling Snake

Long-beaked Echidna

Numerous parrots and Cockatoos

The Doria’s Tree Kangaroo

BAIAwWi wise

Our organization, Partners with Melanesians (PwM). a national conservation and community
development NGO has been working with the locai communities since 1983 on a major
conservation and community development programme (see our profile). The Summer Institute of
Linguistic (SIL) has also been doing social and linguistic translation projects over the plateau since
1972. We have come so close to lodging our application to the Environment Council and here we
have this Mining Exploration License issued to Goldminex Limited. an Australian company.

=== page 2 ===
In the past the PNG Forest Authority demarcated the area as a logging concession called the Gora -
ltokama FMA. When it came to the notice of the Managalas community, the entire population
mobilized and lodged notices to refuse PNGFA because they oversighted the local landowners
rights over their forests and customary land. This was rejected outright thus the area was not
declared for forestry and logging and was excluded from the Provincial and National Forest Plans,
as the people opposed all forms of destructive developments, but opted for conservation and
sustainable development projects.

Currently. according to the community leaders on Managalas Plateau, only two or three people are
behind this mining activity and these three have signed the agreement by themselves without the
proper consultation and other due diligence processes with ail the indigenous landowners and
community members.

Our Organization has been involved with the Managalas people working on conservation and
community development activities for more than 20 years. we are fully aware of the negative
consequences of mining on the environment and the sociai status of the people who depend on the
environment for their livelihoods. We do not have te go far to see for ourselves the impact mining
have on the local people as there are evidence of environmental destruction and socio-economic
impacts such as situations confronted by the people of middie and lower Fly in the Western
Province, the Hungabungar River in Central and the Guava River in Bougainville. despite the
millions of kina coming from PNGSDP and Ok Tedi Mine Limited, Tolukuma Mine and
Bougainville Copper Limited. respectively. We definitely know that they will never fix the
probiems that were created upstream leaving huge ugly open cut landscapes that will continue to
have acid rock drainage and splits into the river system for thousands of years. There are scientific
evidences that the freshwater and riverine ecosystems such as those in the Fly River system will be
dead for almost 300 years after mine closure hence in the next 20-50 generations, the ecosystents
will never be restored quickly to its natural state.

From our predictions of the future of mining in Managalas. the most logical locations for any
mining waste dumping’tailings will be along the Musa or Barige River systems and obviously the
neyative consequences will be huge. Therefore. with the concerns of the Managalas people whom
we have been working with for many years. we strongly feel it is our responsibility to inform you of
our objection to the issuance of the mining exploration license of Goldminex Ltd over the western
sector of the Managalas plateau (ELA 1547). If mining is to occur we know for certain that the
entire ecosystem of Managaias Plateau including the Upper. Lower and Middle Musa valley will be
destroyed consequently affecting the people, the flora and fauna and the marine ard aquatic
ecosystems forever.

Managalas plateau is strategically linked to the proposed Kokoda World Heritage Site. which was
recently signed off by the Governments of Australia and PNG. with the Prime Minister Hon. Kevin
Rudd and Grand Chief Sir Michael Somare. The Managalas plateau lies directly east of the Kokoda
trail and so, the same consideration should be given to this areas as well as it has a historical and
biological significance. In World War Il. the Manayalas plateau was the path the American soldiers
followed to assist the Australian soldiers in the battles which were fought in the Kokoda area with
the Japanese. Therefore. it has a historical significance. plus cultural and biological importance for
the country.

Mining tor gold, nickel and other minerals for revenue and monetary benefits for PNG is a short
term development whereby the vast wealth generated fiom their industrial operations and
development will be transferred overseas by the mining companies and developer leaving behind
pittance for PNG. The entire area bold vast natural treasures worth far more then the gold and
minerals beneath the soil. and its best the minerals are left untouched and the natural treasures

=== page 3 ===
including the tropical rain forests on the surface are managed sustainably. In future when proper
management techniques are developed. the minerals can be allowed to be mined w hereby no andor
minimum environmental destruction and negative impacts from the mine occur that would affect
the natural environment including the local people.

Therefore. in view of all said above. we strongly object to the issuance of the Mineral Expleration
License Np. 1547 to Gokiminex Ltd over the land area known as ELA 1547 w Afore Sub-District

of Ore Province. Papua New Guinea.

The clan leaders of the 150 clans through their District Wide Combine Forum held at Ugunumo
village, from the 21-26 June 2008. have also experience dissatisfaction and anger at the manner this
ELA was awarded to Goldmine Ltd, and it will be interesting to see their letter that is on its way
trom the Managalas plateau down to Port Moresby.

Therefore, if you could kindly allow some of your busy time with us so that We can discuss this
issue with you. | would like to make an appointment for three of my staf¥ and | to meet vith you
and vour Departmental Secretary responsible for Mining anytime between the 22 - 26" of July

2008.

=== page 1 ===
Status Report (Desktop Study) on Queen Alexander Bird-wing
Butterfly (QABB) Survival In Response to Natural and Man-made
Threats to Habitat in Managalas Plateau, Popondetta, Papua New
Guinea.

T. MALA

CURATOR
ENTOMOLOGY
BIOLOGY DEPARTMENT,
UNIVERSITY OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA

For
Partners With Melanesia
25TH — 30TH MAY 2008

=== page 2 ===
Status Report (Desktop Study) on Queen Alexander Bird-wing Butterfly (QABB)
Survival In Response to Natural and Man-made Threats to Habitat in Managalas
Plateau, Popondetta, Papua New Guinea Undertaken from 25" - 30th May 2008.

INTRODUCTION

The Queen Alexandra's Birdwing Butterfly (QABB) (Ornithoptera alexandrae) is
the world's largest butterfly with female wingspans up to and over 250 mm
(Parsons 1999). QABB are confined to primary and advanced secondary
rainforest from sea level up to 800 m in the Popondetta Plain, Cape Hunt Ward,
and Afore regions of the Oro Province of Papua New Guinea (PNG) (Fig.1)
(Parsons 1999, Mercer 1999). QABB is monophagous on Pararistolochia dielsiana
in the Aristolochiacea family, a plant family famous for it's potent toxic
compound aristolochic acid (Mercer 1999, Mebs and Schneider 2002, Jicki
2002). However, several forms or types of P. dielsiana are known to occur with
the range of QABB. These types are largely distinguished by their flower shape
and color (Fig.2). Local conservation biologists have noticed a disparate usage
of these P. dielsiana types by QABB but to date no studies have addressed why
and reportedly one vine form is thought to be harmful to the larvae (pers.
comm. E. Malaisia).

The tremendous size of QABB, its natural scarcity, and limited range of the
species has made it a species of concem for conservation biologist (Parsons
1984, Gimenze 1996}. In addition, in the 40 years increases in the oil palm and
timber industries in the Popondetta region have fragmented and destroyed
large tracts of suifable habitat for the QABB (Parson 1984, 1990). QABB is
currently protected by domestic, the Fauna and Flora Act, and international
law, the Conservation on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES). At
present it is listed as a CITES | species (highly endangered) and import/export
and collection is prohibited.

A number of research projects on the QABB have been carried out over the
past 40 years. The first was a study by Ray Staatman that helped to illuminate
the life cycle of the QABB and some of its basic habitat needs (Staatman 1971).
Throughout the 1980's and early 1990's a number of surveys and studies of QABB
and its host plant were completed by Michael Parsons (Parsons 1984, 1990,
1991). These surveys helped defined the present range of the QABB on the
Popondetta Plain and verified the importance of the Managalas Plateau
population in the Afore area (Parsons 1991). However, Parsons work on the hast
vine led to erroneous classification of host vines by splitting P. dielsiana into

species P. meridonaliana and P. alexandrae (Parsons 1996, Jebb 1993).

1

4!

=== page 3 ===
However, legitimate recognition of Parson's new Pararistolochia species by the
scientific community has been lacking (Mercer 1999). Until further research
reveals otherwise P. dielsiana is considered by the most as the legitimate host
plant of QABB. in 1992, Larry Orsack carried out surveys on the Popondetta Plain
and with a collaborative group of international and local researchers,
politicians, and wildlife biologists produced a five-year management action
plan (Orsack 1992). The plan provided an action in order to preserve the
species.

Later extensive surveys and monitoring efforts took place as part of Oro
Conservation Project, largely funded by AusAID, in the Afore region (Mercer
1999). However, surveys were completed in outlying regions to determine the
final extent of the QABB populations, one in the Cape Ward Hunt region and
another in the Musa River region (Mercer 1999). However, the Muse River
population was later extirpated due to devastating drought fuelled fires in the
region in 1997 (Mercer 1999). The Oro Conservation Project was finally
terminated in 1997. However, low level monitoring continued to take place in
the Afore region and Popondetta Plain region through the 21s' century overseen
by a number of government agencies and NGOs. Recently, a small two-week
study on the host vine and the QABB by a University of Papua New Guinea
honour’s student in the Popondetta Plain and Afore regions (Jicki 2007).

In November 2007 Cyclone Guba struck the Oro Province dumping more than
72 cm of rain in less than 24 hours in some regions. The disaster greatly disrupted
the subsistence gardens of the local people and destroyed much of the
infrastructure in the region. Monitoring of QABB largely ceased and has only just
begun again in June/July of 2008.

While a number of research projects on the QABB have taken piace they have
not fulfilled the informational needs of local conservation agencies. Furthermore
the scientific rigor with which these studies were carried out is questionable and
what is currently known about QABB seems largely to be based on anecdotal
encounters and casual observation.

Evaluate Conservation and Survival Status of QABB.

Past efforts to conserve QABB have been hampered by a lack of understanding
of the fundamental life history traits of the butterfly and its host plant (Orsack
1992, Mercer 1999). In addition, incentives for landowners to maintain intact
forest are deficient. Proposed solutions to the dilemma have included eco-
tourism and butterfly ranging (Orsack 1992). The ability of PNG, Oro Province
and the butterfly to attract sufficient numbers of tourists to profitably sustain the
tourism industry is unlikely.

=== page 4 ===
Butterfly ranging is an attractive altemative and many within PNG have
experience in the insect trade. Indeed PNG is the only country in the world with
a government branch dedicated solely to trade and export of insects, the
Insect Farm and Trade Agency (iFTA) (Mercer and Clark 1989). However, there
are two hurdles that must be overcome for butterfly ranching of QABB to be
successful. First, the status of IFTA as a reliably operating agency must be
ascertained, as recently published literature suggests a breakdown of
functionality within IFTA (Small 2007). Second, the species must be down listing to
occur a formal recommendation must be made after or within the publication
of conservation management plan for the species. Due to the existence of a
number of data gaps the publication of a management plan at this point would
be irresponsible.

The objectives of this study is to fulfill these data gaps and provide those
involved in the conservation of QABB with quality information on the population
structure and life history of the QABB and its host plant, P. dielsiana. In order to
achieve this, the following specific priorities were observed:

e Evaluation of Conservation & Survival Status of QABB
Identification of threats of QABB

e Appraisal of Economical value of QABB, other bird-wing butterflies
and insects

e Provision of Appropriate Recommendations on QABB Habitat
Rehabilitation

=== page 5 ===
METHODOLOGY

Study Site:

There are essentially 3 WMAs around Popondetta town and within the study
area that support the QABB and other birdwing species. Numerous patches of
oil palm plots are interspersed between the WMAs, in addition to areas of high
human activity.

Sites visited in the target included Afore government station (S 09° 08.356’ and E
148° 23.369'}, Kawowoki (S 09 06.281' and E 148° 23.333), and Vanua (S 07
08.215’ and E 148° 23.783"). These areas are located at elevations of 751, 756
and 735 meters above sea level, respectively.

w= a». f ? ~ \ < a :
a nal SAAS ead 120 ' ‘
e uw © 20 owe tere te

Figure 1. Map of Study site {Managalas Wildlife Management Area}

Data collection:

Data was collected using a number of approaches including; site-seeing
observations, insect netting trials for demonstrations on life-stage taxonomic
identification of QABB and other butterfly species, interviews with locals, and the
use of interactive pictorial conservations to draw information on the corect
identification of species of the birdwings buiterflies from QABB.

Pictorial tips of the methods applied in this study to aid in the observations
follows.

=== page 6 ===
Site Visits

Figure 2 & 3. One of the forest patches that is home to QABB and destruction
from recent flood disaster.

Visits were made to Kowoki and Vanua areas. Sightings and collections of
specimen were done together with surveillance for QABB and other birdwing
species in their different life-stages was caried out by foot patrolling between
the three areas.

insect Netting & Demonstrations

Figure 4 & 5. Insect netting demonstrations to Kawowoki. Vanua forest
demonstration

These demonstrations were performed to mainly collect delicately species for

correct species identifications of QABB from other birdwing butterflies.
Illustrations were briefly given for the correct identification of adult male and

5

=== page 7 ===
female QABB and their juvenile stages, making comparisons with those of other
birdwing butterflies.

Interview & Meetings

Figure 6. Afore guest house. Figure 7. Kawoki guest house. Demonstrating the
differences in species of life-stages. Gauging views during a meeting with locals.

Interactive approach was considered here to obtain technical information and
in return providing appropriate technical advice and solution to queries brought
forward.

Observation

Information collection during interviews and meeiings were viilized io make
direct observation of presence or absence of QABB and other species. A useful
marker for the study to determine presence and survival of QABB was the
availability, abundance and the distribution of host plant species in the study
area. Local information was helpful for independent but often referenced
observations. Although local knowledge can be worth noting, offen the lack of
reliability in quantitative precision has always existed.

=== page 8 ===
RESULTS
Survival Status of QABB

Monitoring activities in the area were up to 1997 by the Oro Conservation
Project under funding from AusAID in the Afore region (Mercer 1999}. These
surveys were however completed in the outlying regions to determine the final
extent of the QABB populations, one in the Cape Ward Hunt region and another
in the Musa River region. Mercer 1999, reports that the Muse River population
was later extirpated due to devastating drought fuelled fires in the region in
1997, where this project was put to rest in that same year. Monitoring at very
small scale continued to take place in the Afore region and Popondetta Plain
region by a number of government agencies and NGOs. Only recently, a two-
week study on the host vine and the QABB relationship was carried out by a
University of Papua New Guinea honour's student under my supervision, in the
Popondetta Plain and Afore regions (Jicki 2007), looking especially at presence
of food vines {A. tagala, A. dielsiana and A. momanduil) and feeding
preferences.

The assessment of current survival status of QABB cannot quite clearly be stated
due largely to the limited timing of this study. Ample time is therefore required to
quantify the dynamics of their survival. Ongoing monitoring activities of the
QABB were disrupted by the disaster (Cyclone Guba) of November 2007, which
destroyed greatly much of the infrastructure and food gardens of the local
people.

There were a good number of sightings of GABB adults in the foot pairois taken.
However, comparably speaking, the frequency of these sightings was quite
lower than observations | made during my many years outings into the study
area (e.g. Parson 1991, Survey caried out for Conservation International) for
such and other entomological trips to Collinwood Bay, where O.meridionalis was
first ever found and collected by me. Locals interviewed and asked for sightings,
however indicated that the QABB population is sustaining but highlighted the
eminent threats from logging and human activities.

Threats (Natural & Man-made):

Obvious eminent threats were noted to exist that might have already affected
the QABB population. These among a host of other faciors included human
activities such as extension of oil palm fields, logging activities, and other
intensified human activities in response to population growth, and natural
disasters, all have a potential of destroying the QABB habitat.

=== page 9 ===
Extension of Oil Paim Fields

The recent extensions of oil palm field, both of private block-holder plots and the
Higaturu Oil palm have involved clearing of forest areas. A similar study such as
this was carried out in 1991 where | was part of, where we interviewed several
villagers from villages that are now gone. | have noticed that the expansions
have displaced several villages that were there in 1991. Such displacement
obviously increases social pressure to scavenge the surrounding forests thereby
increasing pressure on the forests habitat and QABB survival.

Population Growth

Pressure exerted on the local natural environment as a result of population
increase was apparent and observable and is deemed to be another important
factor that will influence the successful QABB population. Within the WMAs and
the study sites, increased human activities were noted that include extensive
subsistence gardening, regular combing of the woodlands for firewood, and the
general use of the forest products.

Logging

Logging activities are very common in the nearby regions of WMAs and has a
potential of expanding into the area. From the discussions and meetings held
with the locals, this was one other major potential QABB survival threats.

Reforestation

There are no plans curently in place to undertake rehabilitation of the
destroyed part of the habifat by reforestation. If this trend continues without
forward planning to reclaim wasted forest areas, then the ability to maintain
QABB population and other important species in the area over the next few
decades is dubious.

Natural Disaster/Floods

Disasters such as those of 1997 drought fuelled fires in parts of the area
especially Musa river (Mercer, 1999) that was affected, could occur at sites
where savannah or manmade grassland patches adjoin forest vegetation with
important food host species. Imesponsible clearing of forests (that is occurring)
and promotion of grassy and herbaceous vegetation will certainly encourage
bushfires in times of drought and dry season.

Experiences also from the 2007 Cyclone Guba disaster that devastated many
local communities in terms of infrastructure and food gardens can be seen as a

8

=== page 10 ===
potential risk for the survival of QABB. This can come about when feeding and
host plan species in the local area becomes destroyed by the disaster.

Butterflies & their host plants:

The essential component of the critical survival of QABB and other birdwing
species is and feeding ecology associated with their life-cycle, which include
how each individual species interact with host plant species at particularly
caterpillar and adult stages. This bulk of information is very important for the
local people, as they are the direct custodians and caretakers of the butterflies.
in order to ensure a sustained monitoring of the survival of the QABB population
in the WMA, locals need to correctly identify QABB at each life-stage and
equally identify the corresponding life-stage, from other birdwing butterflies.

This sort of information and the practical field training works may be required to
impart this very important piece of information. This is important because
interviews and communication with locals regarding taxonomical identifications,
often did misidentify, which indicated a need for practical training and
awareness in future.

Economical Value of QABB:

QABB is a protected species and cannot be harvested for any commercial
exploitation, whilst the other birdwing butterflies can be farmed, harvested and
sold commercially. Although QABB is not exploitable, the non-market value for a
pair (male and female) is at $US 10, 000 approxmately and is listed as a CITES |
species.

Other birdwings butterfly species are on CITES 2 which can be harvested for
export at market-value. It is noteworthy that direct harvesting from the wild is not
allowed and is not encouraged. It however can be farmed in order to maintain
a sustainable supply population from which harvesting can be made. The price
list of birdwing butterfly species is appended as Economical Group of Insect —
Lepidoptera (Butterflies & Moths) & Coleoptera (Beetles & Weevils) Please ref. to
Attached lists.

Outcomes of Meetings:

Meetings were held at different sites with locals in a bid to obtain information
related to the objectives of this study. Information related to the importance of
species to plant host relationships of QABB and other birdwing butterflies was
imparted as the need for it was apparent since the locals are the rightful
custodians of this rare creatures and their survival is in many ways connected to
their livelinood.

=== page 11 ===
During these meetings general impression was made by the locals for the need
to foster the concept of conservation from a rejuvenated paradigm. In this case
conservation which transpired mutual benefits was largely expressed. One
apparent examples of such mutuality in benefits was the need to venture into a
tangible insect farming project. It was also expressed that for over 20 years of
involvement with the Wild Life Management Area (WLMA}, there was a general
lack of tangible benefits. Venturing into Insect Farming would bring sustainable
monetary benefits to the locals, at the same time the maintaining of QABB and
other species diversity within the area.

An Insect Ranch and a guest house in the area have been constructed at their
own initiative. The establishment now requires Department of Environment &
Conservation (DEC) to give approval and also grant export license for their
insect specimens to be exported to overseas markets. This group of people from
what is known as DataCol WMA would like the establishment to serve equally as
WEI and IFTA. The reason being that, harvested and fixed marketable insect and
butterfly specimen often lose market value due to damages sustained while
transported to Wau for inspection. They also suggested that DEC would approve
of this proposal to help aspiring insect farmers in Oro and the Southern region as
a whole.

Figure 8 & 9. Ranch establishment and Guesthouse

10

=== page 12 ===
Figure 10. Greenhouse nursery for host plant species

DISCUSSION

Potential threats to the survival of QABB and related species were identified and
highlighted providing specific details. Among these factors of influence
presented, logging activity in the area and oil palm has been seen as potential
risk factors. The monetary benefits associated with logging and oil palm were
seen to be more attractive to the local people who are the custodians of the
WMaAs who claim previously have not had adequately and tangibly benefited
since the establishment of the conservation areas. Influence of logging activities
and also the lucrative oil palm indusiry can however be suppressed by
encouraging incentive-based conservation practice in these areas.

Whilst observations made during this rather short visit has provided some basic
insights into the questions posed an extended time period in future can allow for
a full-scale species inventory. Anecdotal entry of such data is misleading
especially when information is required for management purposes.

Due to the general inadequacies in the monitoring and QABB management
skills of the local people, further workshops and practical field demonstrations
are encouraged. This is a way forward for responsible management of QABB
and other species by locals. This brings us to the idea brought forward by the
locals for an incentive-based conservation as has previously being discussed
extensively by Orsak (1999). This in fact is ‘gap’ identified. DECs approval for
Insect Ranching and issuance of a license would be a step in the right direction

VW

=== page 13 ===
when QABB conservation is priority of the government. in this concept of
incentive-based conservation rigorous training workshops on insect farming
techniques and related themes would urgently be taken as a prerequisite step.

RECOMMENDATIONS

From this desktop study there are essentially three (3) recommendations made
for an urgent consideration to pursue.

e Establishment & Approval of Managalas Insect Ranch

Since the people of DataCol & Nakoda, totaling approximately 3,000 plus
people, have initiated the establishment of an Insect Ranch, the DEC must
come in for the instrumentation of its approval.

e Import & Export License (Managalas Insect Ranch)

In line with the approval, the license for specimen inspection and mobility
(domestically and internationally) just as done at WEI and IFTA would be
required.

e Ongoing Workshops on Insect farming
Of the more urgent is the need for the local people to be able to attain the right
skills level in the management of insect farming, harvesting, postharvest storage,
and handling of valuabie but delicate insect specimen.

Please note that a proposal and itinerary of Insect Farming Workshops fo be
undertaken on an on-going basis is aftached.

12

=== page 14 ===

My heartfelt thanks to Mr. Winter Moi (Former DEC staff) for the preliminary
briefing of QABB sightings in Popondetta area from January to 25" May 2008. |
am very grateful also for the generous assistance provided by Millie and Tony of
Afore guesthouse and Bradley Dabadaba (Literacy Coordinator — East MDF).

| would also like to extend my word of thank you to the LLG Councilors, Pastors
and Spokesman Mr. Solomon of Kawowoki area for the support and assistance

Lastly but not the least, the Sponsors, Partners With Melanesia for the financial
input and to Jacinta Mimigari (Conservation Planning Officer) for logistics and

2. Executive Summary

The following Report provides a Summary of the four phase preliminary Biodiversity Survey done
on the Managalas Plateau, in November 2004, November 2005, May 2006 and April 2008 basically
to identify the Biodiversity Significance of the Proposed Managalas Conservation Area.

Very high diversity of species inhabits the mountains of the Proposed Conservation Area that may
play a major role in diverse species distributions that can be so attractive to the tourist, scientists,
researchers and the public at large. The Managalas Conservation Area is in its proposal stage,
required biological information’s to be recognized diverse and unique in its natural resources,
especially the important species, endemic, protected, rare and threatened. The information’s were
much required by Partners with Melanesians (PWM), that it funded the four Biodiversity surveys.
After all the biodiversity surveys, the managalas community through PwM is now furnished with the
needed biological information’s of the area. Should that be sufficient biological information’s,
Department of Environment and Conservation be convinced that the area be declare a Conservation
Area.

Habitat loss, degradation and fragmentation are the most critical challenges to maintaining
biodiversity globally. Like most areas of New Guinea, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse
array of fauna and flora, but at the moment is poorly documented. Biodiversity surveys have been
carried out but the true biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete. Ones the area has gained its
Conservation Area status then further survey and research will be done to investigate the
biodiversity of the area.

3. Objectives of the Biodiversity Survey

The conservation Area remains un-exploited by major developments, except for mini sustainabie
projects enhancing human well-being. The 360 000 hectare area were categorized into ten zones for
proper and equa! dissemination of conservation related programs for all to be aware and understand.
Small projects encouraged by Partners with Melanesians were introduced in different zones to help
to generate small cash income for the local landowners. The projects are so small that they have little
biological effects, which can change the ecosystems of the living organisms and plants, but it may
not be that threatened to many fauna and flora species of the area. The area is virtually high profiles
that make this conservation area a place encouragable for future generations and education,

Both the plants and bird species remain widely distributed and were common for any traditional
purposes to people. Species depletion occurs only when major destruction’s takes place, reducing
population density. After the third biodiversity surveys, bird species were more widely distributed
than the mammals, reptiles, amphibians, except for the insect population that inhabit all vegetation
types at all levels of different elevations.

Main objectives Partners with Melanesians would like to have in place for the conservation area,
were the biological information’s. The unique and the important species have to be identified for a
better recognition of the area that can attract tourist, researchers, scientist and the public at large. For
that, such requirements were important to identify with the yearly biodiversity surveys to provide:

The main purpose of this investigation was to carry out a preliminary assessment of mammals, birds
and herpetofauna that are present in the Managalas proposed conservation area. This investigation
was done to:

(A) Assess the Conservation status of protected species

(B) Identify immediate threats to those animals and other potential threats.

(C) Provide a checklist of both fauna and flora that to our knowledge protected by
CITES, protected by our acts of Parliament.

4, Introduction

Managalas Plateau, for it's conservation area, stretches from the Foothill Mountains of Sibium in the
south-east, Owen Stanley Ranges in the south-west, Owalama Ranges at west, and Guava Ranges in
the north-west with it's high diversity, stretching to the lower altitude plains towards Oro Bay. Much
of the lower plains of the conservation area is disturbed vegetation's, due to high number of villages
that much of the area have been cultivated for subsistence cash cropping, which includes small
plantations of coffee, vanilla, and coconut. The upper mountain and hills remains very high in it's
natural resources, may deplete through careless management's and other major developments. The
area has been divided into 10 zones for equal dissemination of conservation related activities and
viable projects that can generate cash income to the local people of the area.

The proposed Managalas Conservation Area encompasses about 360 000 hectares of the pristine
rainforest compromising of the lowland hill and Montane forests in the Managalas Plateau, Ijivitari
District, Oro province. The forests are intersected by many creeks and rivers that form the main
catchments for the Bariji and Musa River. The area is bordered by the Owen Stanley range, to the
Southwest and the Sibium range to the Southwest. Popondetta town and the famous Kokoda Trail
are situated north of the Proposed Conservation Area.

Like most areas of NG, the Managalas Plateau harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora, which is
poorly documented. Hence having the area declared a Conservation Area, this can allow further
research into the rich diverse forest. Biologist from the University of Papua New Guinea and officers
the Department of Environment and Conservation have so far carried out three Biodiversity Surveys
but the true biodiversity of the plateau is far from complete. This is evident from the diverse frog
fauna sampled during this survey, because frogs habitats were good indicators of a rich and vibrant
environment.

To have a very good biological data of Managalas Proposed Conservation Area, various biological

Birds

Bird species have larger ranges than other animal groups. They also are inhabitants to different
stories of the forest. Species lists involve applying different methods. Managalas area is very large
and has different altitudes, that different species can be observed. Bird surveys of this proposed
conservation area involves few different methods for species identifications.

e A transect-line was established for approximately Ikm and plots were set, in which mists
nets, and mammal traps were layed out to capture birds, mammals’ insects and reptiles.
Specimens were capture and identified. Only unique pecimens were collected to represent
the area. Many species were common indicator, and release after catch.

e A visual observation was done during the day and night of species that were hard to catch in
mist nets. These observation can be done using the established transect-lines, or generally
within the site of surveys.

e Hire of local hunters using traditional methods, (spears, bows and arrows, traditional traps,
and village dogs.

e Conducting biological resource utilization surveys. This method is done to have local
knowledge’s of fauna species being experienced in the area.

Mammals

different methods similar to that of the bird surveys. As stated in the bird surveys, except that

distributed along rivers and streams for aquatic frogs, and away from water bodies for non-aquatic

frogs.

7. Results of the Surveys

The Managalas Proposed Conservation Area covers a land area of approximately 360,000 hectares.
It is a plateau situated within and around the Owen Stanley Range to the South and West, the Sibium
range to the South East and Mt. Lamington to the North and East. The Managalas Plateau
encompasses a wide variety of vegetation types from alpine forest at an altitude of 3800 metres to
tropical rainforest to the mountains and hills as well as savannah grassland and anthropogenic
garden areas. The Plateau is isolated from most of the urban centres within the Oro Province as a
result of poor road conditions.

The plateau has very high biodiversity, with different fauna and flora species, common to rare and
protected. Being a large area, ranges of each fauna species depends entirely on how far each species
can travel. Some are only confined to their required habitats and the food sources in each vegetation

types.

4. Endemic species
Out of the four-biodiversity surveys conducted in the area, only Queen
Alexandria Bird- wing Butterfly was recorded endemic within the Proposed
Conservation area. The findings from these biodiversity surveys are not final.
Therefore, it is hoped that future surveys might discover species of endemism or
new discoveries to both fauna and flora.

12. Sacred Traditional Areas
The four biodiversity surveys have not encountered any traditionally sacred areas, except for the

cemeteries to all the villages within the proposed Managalas Conservation Area. The biodiversity
surveys have not fully covered the entire land mass of the plateau to finalize sites that were regarded
as sacred traditional areas. It is believed there are certain areas at few sites that were sacred to the
local people at their own village boundaries.

13. Recommendations
Given the uniqueness of the forest within the conservation area, we highly recommend that the forest

be conserved. The following are offered for guidance.

- Proper trapping tracks into the forest or important sites such as camping or resting sites are
identified to allow minimal disturbance.

- The pine is a tree of scientific an historical significance. Scattered stand of these species can
be identified and mapped out, both within and outside of the proposed conservation areas and
these areas must be protected.

- The mixed castanopsis forest is very sensitive to Human disturbance. Conversion of these
forest types to grassland is already a common feature in the highlands of Papua New Guinea.
It is strongly recommended that these stands be conserved.

- Proper record of plant animal uses is established. This requires someone with good
knowledge of traditional beliefs and rituals to be able te readily access traditional knowledge.

- Proper methodology or experiment must be designed to optimally access the ecology of the
area. This should also encompass a full botanical reconnaissance survey. Permanent study
plots are established and consistently monitored.

14. Conclusions

The biodiversity surveys of Managalas Proposed Conservation Area have covered zone |, zone 2,
parts of zone 4, and parts of zone 7. There are ten zones within the proposed conservation area, of
which, 6 were initially not covered in the biodiversity surveys. Reasons for not covering the whole
area, is because of the fact that, the four surveys have in general covered the lower, mid and the
higher altitudes of the plateau. However, after the area is declared, detail biosurveys and reaearch of
the entire proposed conservation will be carried out.

The out-come of the biological findings from the four surveys are quite encouraging to have the area
recognized to be declared a conservation area. Many fauna species of importance were recorded
with the avi-fauna and the mammalian communities. No new findings were encountered with the
birds and mammal species of the area, but it is believed that new discoveries were done to the
herpetho-fauna community, especially the frog species of the areas, Murayane mossy mid montane,
inland of Anatua village and Dakara, Humate village.

Background

Environment and Conservation is a huge problem faced by our
community throughout the country in the global changes rapidly
happening; PWM is taking the lead in addressing the Conservation and
Land Use issues in the project site Managalas in the Afore District, with its
different partners. Each year, new concepts and strategies are spent on
community and institutional project to help people to understand the
basic function, roles and responsibilities of conservation and Land Use, to,
MAKE OUR ENVIRONMENT JUST, SAFE AND SECURE PLACE TO LIVE FOR
NOW AND FUTURE GENERATION.

There are several ways to devise different activities that could enhance
and create conservation issues to be easily understood by the community
members, by using Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication (
Theatre Arts Section). The most obvious one was in the area of Creative
Arts; however, to achieve solid results the workshop was conducted in
Poponedtta Town, Anglicare Training centre.

This workshop recognizes that one of the strategic way to create
awareness in the conservation Land Use issues is to involve the
community, particularly the youths and the senior members of the
community and expose their skills and abilities in different dimensions of
Art of Drama. This workshop illustrated the medium drama, exposed the
inner feeling of a person how they perceive Conservation and Land Use
issues in their community as evident in their drama session , the other
aspects of the arts will be addressed in due course time if similar
opportunity is given and please see the interview by the participants
after the closing ceremony DVD attached.

When we know why our community is not conserving and proper planning
for the usage of the land, then we can mitigate or hopefully stop
completely or strategize for a better community. The solution lies within
the community, the participants told us how they want to solve their own
problems by using the medium of Drama to create constructive and
creative environment for community discussion.

Artistic Product

The primary target for Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication
through the application of Community Sustainable Arts Education, in
using Drama helped different members of the communities in the target
locations within Managalas Development Foundation broaden the scope of
understanding. Towards the end of the workshop we achieved the
following results,

1, Basic Drama Skills
2. Different Techniques of Drama

=== page 6 ===
Written three scripts related to conservation and Land Use anid
finally performed for public at the Angiicare Training Centre

3. Produce the Photographs of the workshop from Day i- day 5

4. Video shoots of the workshop end its various sessions and
activities

5. Finally, the participants admitted that they are now very confident
to conduct awareness by using Drama

This project was coordinated and executed by the MIAC in partnership
with PWM under artistic cocrdination and direction of Mr. Motsy David,
Theater Arts Staff at the University of PNG as part of PWM Effective
Communication and Awareness Training. The Community Sustainable
Arts Education Strategy acted as the mirror of the society, decause it is
one of the most effective medium of communication and also empowering
the Members of the Managalas Development Foundation. The project
certainly make aware the peopie in the project area and other target
areas the consequences tc realize their abilities and creative skills so they
can meaningfully contribute to their own community and the country. The
Conservation and Land Use issues are of great concern for everyone,
drastic effects it nas on our country both economically and sociatiy. The
Melanesian Institute of Arts & Communication through the workshoo
contributed artistically to minimize the environmental calamities and most
importantly through this treiring we will change the attitudes and the
behaviors of the people.

My concentration in this carticular workshop was to build a solid
foundation for sustainable and continuous promotion and preservation of
Conservation and Land Use by suing Drama. There are huge amount of
people in the target areas which are illiterate and ignorant of the
importance of PWM and MDF roles end it primary responsibilities must
consistentiy informed the community to various mediums of information
dissemination such as Dram.

1. Advocacy, Communication sna Social Mobilization activities for the
people in the target areas through the Community Sustainable Arts
Education program under Drama. It stimulated and created avenue for
community discussion on how best they can solve the issue of
Conservation and Land Use. This medium is very powerful tool to identify
some possible solution to the community problems. It is our firm believe
that through this exercise we have idenzfied and advice MDF and PWM
how best they can devise some possible strategies to overcome this
pressing issue of Conservation and Land Use issues.

The Community Theatre members are willing to work with Host
Institution MZAC ( Theatre Arts Section)and other stakeholders such as
Police Department, Community Policing, Establish Youth Association in
verious areas, Churches, Informal Sector Association and National
Cultural Commission for advice and possibie assistance for manpower

=== page 7 ===
and other relevant organization that we will be closely working with them
to improve their artistic skills.

2. To increase the awareness on the importance of Roles, Responsibilities
and its functions so the people must appreciate and respect the
significance of conservation and Land Use.

3. Development of a better understanding of the school children for the
future generation. Making use of all organization’s experiences in control,
share experiences, best practices and lessons learned for the benefit of

drama to dramatise imagination and the spirituality of people.

Drama is part of most diverse societies’ cultural heritage and it mirrors daily
livelihoods. That is mainly because of its relationship to festivals and religious
practices, In most cultures, communities identify themselves in drama as
dramatization of specific issues reflect the cultures. Drama reflects reality and needs
an interpretation of it to which it has an effect on individuals. Drama provokes

POPULAR THEATRE:
In the Developing countries there are two types of Theatre: One is the Theatre which

takes place in a formal context which is very much more European and is aimed at
smal) cultural elite in urban areas, and the other takes place in the open as an
instrument to Communicate important messages for the community. There are many
encouraging experiences of popular theatre in some developing countries.

“Popular theatre is gaining increasing attention in the Third World as a tool for popular
education and community organizing. It finds expression in a number of forms including
drama, music dance, puppetry and poetry and is performed for — and often by — ordinary
peasants and workers, Popular theatre is used as a means of bringing people together,
building confidence and solidarity, stimulating discussion, exploring alternative options for
action, and building a collective commitment to change: starting with people's urgent
concerns and issues, it encourages reflection on these issues and possible strategies for
change.

For three decades popular theatre has been used in processes of development
communication as part of adult education programmes. From these initiatives grew a
special type of popular theatre, called ‘theatre for development.’ In workshops training
people in the use of popular theatre techniques an inventory of local problems is made for
later use in the plays. In each play one problem theme is explored by and for the local

community.”
(By: Jaap R. Swart, Center for the Study of Education in Deveioping Countries/Radio Netherlands Training
Center, The Hague, The Netherlands)

The approach of popular or community theatre is that performances must be linked
to crucial analysis, organisation and struggle. The concept of community theatre
emphasizes the revolutionary value of art. Instead of being merely a pleasant and
gratifying spectacle, community theatre (and art) aims to distribute, to shake. to
move the society towards self and critical thinking and action.

Majority of the people in PNG are illiterate hence theatre has been identified as one
of the effective approaches in educating people especially in rural communities
about the HIV and AIDS and related issues , and about safe sex practices as well as
caring for people living with HIV. The objective of community theatre is to allow
values and behaviour to be discussed comfortably without directly challenging the
community or individual beliefs and values. And to generate further discussions in
communities on the issues of HIV and AIDS and the ways they can respond to
protect themselves and their children. The approach or the purpose of community
theatre is that communities use popular theatre as a medium to educate communities
on the basic HIV information. And since most of the Theatre Groups are district
based they are able to facilitate sustainability and local ownership.

Introduction:

Explain the main element of a script. Every play has to have a theme or a topic for
example ‘It Takes Two to Tango’. and a plot or story line (the incidence and events),
and the intention or message. Five or six scenes of 5 minutes each should be enough
for a 30 minute play.

A script should have different parts: First, an introduction to the topic which presents
the main characters and the story. The introduction in a play has to be such that it
captures the attention of the audience right away. Second, it has to present a conflict
that relates to the topic. Thirdly it has to build suspense so the audience will be
questioning the main issues. Fourthly, the tensions have to reach a climax which has
to be surprising and appealing to the audience. Finallv, the script has to provide a
solution with which the audience will indentify. The concept of climax is very
important. There has to be a progress to reach the climax.

Before writing the script, it is important to create a simple story line or synopsis,
with a short description of each character and scene. Complete dialogues can be
written later.

only three or four characters, with a conflict and a solution to the conflict. The

initial plot should also have some allowance for comic situations, jokes, music, etc.

Actor Space

in popular theatre the audience surrounds the performers while in classic theatre the
audience is facing the actors. However, it is important to divide the scenic space so
the actors can refer to their positions in 2 common Janguage. There are various types
of acting stages. The most commonly used stages popular theatre are proscenium.

TYPES OF STAGING
1. Proscenium Staging

A Proscenium theater is a theatre space whose primary feature is a large archway
(the proscenium arch) at or near the front of the stage, through which the audience
views the play. The audience directly faces the stage, which is typically raised
several feet above front row audience level. The main stage is the space behind the
proscenium arch, often marked by a curtain which can be lowered or drawn closed.
The space in front of the curtain is called the “apron.” The areas obscured or hidden
by the proscenium arch and any curtains serving the same purpose (often called legs
or, tormentors) are called the wings. Any space not viewable to the audiences is
collectively referred to as offstage.

3. In The Round Staging
Theatre-in-the-round or arena theatre is any theatre space in which the audience

surrounds the stage area.

Theatre-in-the-round concept requires no stage curtain, little scenery and allows the
audience to sit on three sides of the stage.

The stage itself in this arrangement is typicaliy round, square, or triangular, with
actors entering and exiting through the audience from different directions or from
below the stage. Such a space is usually configured with the stage on an even ievel
with or lowered below the audience in a “pit” or "arena" formation. This
configuration lends itself to high-energy productions, and is especially favored by
producers of classical] theatre.

Theatre-in-the-round presents problems since actors at all times have their back
facing some members of the audience. However. it also allows for interesting and
realistic staging. Special consideration needs to be taken in regard to the set design,
so as not to hide any audience member's view of the performance.

1 Background

In May 2011, Paul and | were invited by Partners with Melanesians inc (PWM) to talk to farmers and
inhabitants on the Managalas Piateau in Oro Province on the impact and coping strategies of extreme
weather patterns such as Drought. As project staff on the National Agricultural Research institute's PIP
project titled: ‘drought preparedness’. providing such information was a major project objective.
Confirmation of our participation eventuated in a visit being proposed and confirmed for August 2011. This
report outlines the activities and outcomes of our two day visit to the Managalas Plateau in the Afore
District of the Oro Province in Papua New Guinea in August 2011. L Kurika

My previous visit to Afore was to assess the after-effects of the 1997-98 drought with colleagues from the
Department of Agriculture and Livestock. | was eager to return to the Managalas Plateau fo educate people
in how they can prepare themselves and their communities if there is a drought. P Osilis

Google
4

1.1 Partners With Melanesians Inc.

Partners with Melanesians Inc (PWM) is a national, “not for profit’, non-government organization (NGO)
currently focused on conserving natural eco-systems and promoting community development in certain
locations in Papua New Guinea (PNG). The organization has worked with the Managalas Plateau
inhabitants for over 23 years and continually support and provide helpful information to assist the people in
conservation initiatives such as the recently started Managalas Conservation Area Project (MCAP).

1.2 The Managalas Plateau

The Managalas plateau is situated between 600-1,000m in the midst of the Owen Stanley Range (to the
south and west), with the Sibium Ranges to the south-east. Mount Lamington to the north and the
Hydrographers to the east. The plateau covers about 300,000 hectares of area and has an extremely
diverse environment, mooriands, mountains, hills, savannah, anthropogenic grassland and gardens.

=== page 7 ===
Awareness Trip Report L Kurika & P Osilis

The plateau is inhabited by about 15,000 people from about 150 clan groups who live in 70 village
communities. The people are mostly subsistence farmers who depend almost entirely on the environment
for their livelihood. Basic government services is restricted to a number of community schools, a top up
school, two aid posts, and a station and health centre at Afore. The Summer Institute of Linguistics
introduced an adult titeracy programme to the plateau in the 1960's which since then has helped paved the
way for more recent development initiatives on the Plateau. This relatively isolated and remote area Is
linked to the provincial capital, Popondetta, by a poor quality four-wheel drive road and foot tracks. There is
an airstrip at Afore station but it was overgrown with weeds and was not in use at the time of this visit.

The remoteness of the area, poor state of infrastructure like roads and airstrips and lack of markets pose
great challenges to cash income generating initiatives such as the production and sale of coffee. The
abundance of natural resources in the area and the high quality agricultural land has attracted in the past
decade a lot of interest from potential investors in timber extraction, oil palm plantations and mineral
mining. However the communities have actively opposed these interests due to the lack of consultations
with resource owners and the failure by interested developers to guarantee benefits and/or environmental
protection.

1.3. The Managalas Conservation Area Project

The Managaias Conservation Area Project (MCAP) is managed by PWM with support from various Donor
agencies; the main one being Rainforest Foundation Norway. The ultimate plan is for the Managalas area
to be declared a conservation area under the relevant conservation laws of PNG to enable the people of
Managalas to retain and transfer their inherited natural resources to future generations. The core
programmes under MCAP are: (i) consensus building, (ii) conservation and (iii) training and capacity
building. The overall objectives of the programmes are to promote conservation of natural eco-systems,
prevent unsustainable ways of resource exploitation and encourage smali-scale eco-enterprises to
generate revenue for the communities to meet their modest needs. The programmes are implemented
through a network of players that include: the Managalas Development Foundation (MDF), also an NGO,
and eleven smail community based organizations (CBO). For eco-enterprises and income generation,
PWM has been working closely with the local CBOs and community groups to promote the production and
marketing of organic coffee, village artifacts and handicrafts, okari nuts, peanuts, forest products,
vegetables and garden produce.

2 Workshop on Drought at Afore Station

The Managalas area like many rural locations in PNG received the full brunt of the negative impacts
caused by the 1997-98 drought. Both NARI staff, Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis visited Afore station on two
separate occasions in 1998. Kurika visited on an RAF flight that delivered relief food to the station while
Osilis was a member of the team that visited the area by road and conducted an appraisal of the food
security and water situation in Oro Bay and the Managalas area.

In the 1997-98 drought, the forest and grassland areas within the vicinity of Afore station were totally
ravaged by bush fires. There was a bad shortage of water and as a result people either left their villages to
resettle in places where they could access water or had to walk long distances to fetch water. Many food
gardens were destroyed and hence relief food was air-lifted to Afore station.

With the experiences of the 1997-98 drought still vividly fresh in people’s memories one can imagine the
sense of apprehension that can arise as a result of the recent news flashes in the media about a severe
drought looming to occur next year, 2012. To dispel any sense of apprehension amongst communities and
create awareness on drought, an awareness workshop on drought was conducted at Afore station.

=== page 8 ===
2.1 Workshop Purpose

The purpose of the workshop was to equip the CBO Managers and trainers with information on drought
and recommended drought coping strategies for them to disseminate to their respective communities to
prepare the communities to cope with the negative impacts of a severe and/or prolonged dry weather
period.

2.2 Sponsorship, Facilitators and Participants

The workshop was organized and sponsored by PWM and facilitated by Patrick Vuet, Conservation Officer
with PWM. The awareness on drought was conducted by Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis, staff from the
Drought Project with the National Agricultural Research Institute (NARI), based at NARI’s Southern
Regional Center at Laloki in the Central Province. There were a total of 38 participants who attended the
one day workshop. They included MOF Board Members, CBO Managers, Activity Coordinators, Gender
Officers and various community representatives from Afore District Zones 1-9 (Appendix 1. List of
Workshop Participants).

2.3 Workshop Terms of Reference

A Terms of Reference (ToR} was prepared for the workshop. The NARI Drought Project staff were
assigned the following workshop duties and responsibilities:

¢ Impart the basic ideas on the causes of drought and its impact on the lively hood of the
communities/people
Use case studies of other areas around the world that have been affected by droughts

e Basic ideas on the type of food that can withstand drought conditions

e Deliver posters or pamphlets containing information on drought. There are ten CBOs within the
Managalas Project areas.

e Deliver basic information on the concept of food security.

2.4 Workshop Programme

The workshop on drought awareness was conducted on Thursday 11” August 2011 at the MDF guest
house at Afore station. The workshop commenced with opening statements from Patrick Vuet and Luke
Mambe, Project Director for MDF on the purpose and the expected outcomes from the workshop. This was
followed by the core activity of the workshop which was the awareness on drought. The information
presented was put together in accordance with the five duties and responsibilities outlined in the agreed
ToR of the workshop between PWM and the two NARI staff, Louis Kurika and Paul Osilis. The awareness
campaign included the following:

e Poster Display
¢ Power Point presentation on climate change, 1997-78 Drought and its impacts on PNG and NARI
recommended drought coping strategies
e Session on preparing a Cropping Calendar
e Distribution of A4 portfolio posters and information leaflets on climate change and drought to
representatives of the ten Community based organizations
e Distribution of seeds: open-pollinated corn variety - Suwan and High Protein White corn varieties
to workshop participants
e An interactive session during which some important community perceived issues on climate
change, drought and food security were noted and discussed.
The workshop ended on the afternoon of Thursday 11” August 2011. On Friday 12” August 2011, all
facilitators returned to Popondetta and then returned via air travel to Port Moresby the next day; Saturday
13” August 2011.

=== page 9 ===
Awareness Trip Report L Kunka & P Osilis

3 Workshop Outcomes

The workshop was a success. It attracted a large number of participants despite its location; many of
whom had walked long distances to attend. Workshop facilitators were able to cover all workshop
requirements (as outlined in the workshop ToR). An overwheiming amount of information was provided and
open-pollinated com seeds were distributed so that farmers can use the seeds to replant, unlike hybrid
cor seeds. Participants were not only able to learn about drought impact and coping strategies but
understood the presentations and exercises well enough to raise questions and issues on related topics
such as insect pest management and the recording of traditional knowledge on famine and bush foods.

During the workshop we felt, first and foremost, that it was essential to clarify and dispel any sense of panic
or apprehension over the prediction that a drought with a severity equal to the 1997-98 PNG drought would
occur in 2012. We explained that the forecasting of an El Nino event that would cause a drought(s) was
quite complex and dependent on calculations from experts who are monitoring climatic developments at a
regional and global scale. We stressed that the primary importance at present is for communities to be
made aware of droughts and how to cope with their negative impacts.

3.1 Some Community Perceived Issues on Drought and Food Security from
the Workshop

3.1.1 Taro beetle, a problem in taro gardens
Taro beetle damage on taro cultivars was reported to be a problem in all nine Afore Sub-district zones.

Resolution(s): Taro beetle damage is a problem that NARI can immediately address through the
use of the two chemicals Bifenthrin and Mustang. The technology is available and NARI staff do
conduct training on taro beetle control upon request from various clients. A demonstration plot for
taro beetle control work can be established in collaboration with farmers at Afore station to
demonstrate how and when to apply the treatments and the effectiveness of the control method. It
may also be worth the effort to conduct some studies on taro beetle population in the gardens and
their breeding sites to see if the pest can be controlled using some form of cultural method. Other
reported insect pests e.g. cut worms and caterpillars can be controlled using Plant Derived
Pesticides (PDP) like chilli, derris plant and extract from the neem tree. This technology is
available with NARI whose Crop Protection Staff do conduct training on how to prepare and use
PDP to control insect pests.

3.1.2 Training on food processing and preservation e.g. how to make cassava flour
The need for practical demonstrations on the methods involved in making flour and jam was raised.

Resolution(s): The A4 portfolio posters supplied to each CBO Manager at Afore station contains a
number of recipes on how to process and preserve certain staple crops like cassava and bananas
in storable products like flour and chips. Food processing involving the processing of the
perishable staple crops to storable products is one of the important coping strategies for drought.
NARI does have experts in post harvest, processing and storage who can conduct training on food
processing and storage technologies; based at NARI's Momase Regional Research Center at
Bubia, in the Morobe Province.

=== page 10 ===
3.1.3 Documentation of traditional knowledge on the utilization of bush and famine foods

The recording of traditional knowledge on bush and famine foods for future utilization was realized and
understood to be a very important issue.

Resolution(s): Reports on experiences from the 1997-98 drought reveal that many rural
communities survived by eating bush and famine foods. There are quite a number of bush and
famine food plants that people have resorted to during times of food shortage. These include
banana corms (Musa sp.), Pueraria lobata, wild yam (Dioscorea sp.) and tulip (Gnetum gnemon).
The use of some is widespread while others are utilized only in certain places. However, the
knowledge on traditional recipes on how to prepare and utilize many of these bush and famine
foods often remains with the older generation and is in danger of being lost. NARI has documented
a number of these used by coastal and highland area communities in PNG. Each of the 30 A4 size
portfolio posters that were distributed to the CBO Managers at the workshop contains details on
foods and practices suitable for extreme weather patterns such as drought. There are however,
many more still out there that need to be documented and the knowledge passed on to the
younger generation. This has to be done on the Managalas Plateau as part of a strategy to
strengthen the community's ability to cope with droughts.

3.1.4 NARI Drought Project to utilize MDF base at Afore station as a Resource Centre

A query was raised for further NARI collaboration and participation by the PIP Drought Project at Afore;
continue drought awareness.

Resolution(s): The NARI Drought Project does not have the resources to separately undertake any
long-term programme activity at Managaias but it could collaborate with PWM and MDF to be
involved in certain specific activities that require NARI expertise and involving NARI released
technologies, especially in the area of food security. Some of the possible activities that NARI
could be involved in at Managalas are:

* Introduce drought tolerant and other useful crops and to encourage farmers to
maintain diversity of their food crops in gardens.

Introduce the rope and washer pump technology for accessing underground water
sources.

Conduct training on food processing and storage.

Conduct training on taro beetle control and use of plant derived pesticides.
Conduct training on seed and vegetable production.

Introduce small livestock like goats, ducks and chicken.

Establish fruit and nut orchards of both exotic and native species.

Conduct training on vegetative propagation method on certain fruit and nut species.
Rapid propagation of African yam and taro using mini-setts.

Rapid propagation of bananas using banana bits.

7.2 Appendix 2. Information delivered in relation to the Workshop ToR

7.2.1 Cause of droughts and its impacts

Droughts in Papua New Guinea are caused by the El Nino phenomena which is associated with the
unusually cold currents and high pressure systems that cause the air above the ocean to fall instead of
rising resulting in no condensation and little or no rain occurring. In addition, the high pressure areas push
clouds and air currents i.e. easterly winds downwards and away resulting in sunny cloudless weather.
Droughts occur when the cold currents stall the high pressure systems for long periods.

Predicting El Nino events is however a complex process because it involves analyzing and understanding
the relationships between multiple weather attributes and their patterns over time. There currently is no
certain indication from El Nino predicting models that a drought with the severity of the one experienced in
1997-98 is imminent and will occur next year in 2012. As illustrated in the PowerPoint presentation, the
prediction was based on historical data on the trend in occurrence of droughts in PNG since the 1950s. At
best, it only offers a clue on the possible time period of when to expect another severe drought in PNG.
What is important is that instead of delving on the debate on whether or not the drought will occur in 2012;
we should focus our attention on pro-actively creating greater awareness amongst communities on
drought, its impacts and relevant coping strategies to strengthen their ability to cope with the impacts ofa
severe drought.
