Reports on the impacts of the 1997-98 drought in PNG indicate that an estimated 1.5 million villagers (40%
of the total rural population) suffered severe and life-threatening food shortages (Allen & Bourke 2000,
Bourke 2000, Haley 2000, Lemonnier 2000). There was an 80% reduction in production of garden food due
to depleted soil moisture. Over 400,000 people had grossly inadequate supply of drinking water, were
drinking water of questionable quality or were carrying water for long distances i.e. more than 30 minutes
walk. Certain institutions and community schools had to be closed due to lack of water while a number of

13

=== page 18 ===
small urban locations like Kerema, Kundiawa, Balimo, Rabaraba and Tambul experienced water supply
problems. There were anecdotal reports of an increased incidence of diarrhea, maiaria, typhoid, skin
diseases, respiratory ailments and dysentery. Extensive fires occurred in forests and grassland with
reports of large number of village houses burnt by bushfires with several accounts of people burnt in these
fires. Many airstrips were closed due to smoke and haze for as long as three weeks. The water volume in
the reservoirs of two major hydroelectric stations at Sirinumu (Central Province) and Yonki (Eastern
Highlands Province) dropped. At Sirinumu the water level fell to 20% water holding capacity disrupting
power supply in Port Moresby. The OK Tedi Mine did not operate from August 1997 to March 1998 and the
Government reported the drought as a contributing factor to the massive slide in the value of the PNG Kina
from PGK1 = US$0.72 in September 1997 to about PGK1 = US$0.40 by April 1998.

In rural areas, many crop varieties perished which resulted in a loss to the genetic diversity of staple crops
such as taro and sweet potato and there was a severe shortage in planting material to replant gardens. As
garden foods became scarce people were forced to rely heavily on eating bush and famine foods like pangi
(Pangium edule), marita (Pandanus conoideus), sago (Metroxyion sagu), tulip (Gnetum gnemon) and figs.
In some locations, even these were destroyed by bush fires. Fires also destroyed hunting grounds and
bush resources needed to build houses. As the food situation became desperate there was an increase in
stealing, more frequent disputes over land, crops and animals and a break-down in law and order. People
were forced to use their savings or cash from the sale of cash crops, livestock or from relatives to buy store
foods whose demand and price increased as other sources of food disappeared. The ‘wantok’ system
helped a lot of people and there was increased pressure on those formally employed to support their
relatives at home.

7.2.2 Case studies of other areas around the world

The catastrophic impacts of drought in other parts of the world are clearly evident in news flashes in the
internet nowadays indicating about some 12.4 million people in the horn of Africa including Somalia,
Kenya, Ethiopia and Djibouti being affected by the worst drought in 60 years. Scientists have attributed the
drought to the La Nina conditions that prevailed from June 2010 to May 2011 in the Pacific. There nas
been no rain in 2011 during the norma! wet period from late February to the end of March and if the
situation continues there will be no crop harvests in September. Indications are that the impacts of the
drought are made worse by the artificially high price for food and the civil conflict. There have also been
reports of food aid stolen and sold at markets in Somatlia. The worse affected communities are those in the
ethnically diverse and over-populated regions. The drought is affecting food security and putting millions of
people in urgent need of assistance. Tens of thousands of people have already died. In Southern Ethiopia,
malnourished children have been flocking into feeding centers and the country is teetering on the brink of a
food crisis. Suspected measles outbreak combined with acute malnutrition is thought to be the cause of
deaths. The United Nation’s Food Programme has been bringing 5,000 tons of food a month into
Mogadishu to help the famine hit Somalia where tens of thousands of people have been fleeing the country
to neighboring Ethiopia and Kenya.

7.2.3 Basic ideas on type of food that can withstand impacts of droughts

While the drought with the severity of the 1997-98 drought is capable of causing total devastation to food
gardens there are certain types of food crops that have a higher tolerance to dry conditions and minor
droughts i.e. with a less than six months duration. NARI after the 1997-98 drought through a World Bank
funded project on drought, evaluated and identified a number of drought tolerant varieties of sweet potato,
cassava and banana for the lowland and highland environments. Of these, both cassava and certain types
of triploid bananas like the kalapua, yawa and Cavendish bananas can tolerate minor drought conditions.
These types of bananas are big, robust and have huge and thick pseudostems that preserve moisture to
support plant growth during dry periods. Cassava has the ability to withstand moisture stress by closing its
stomata to reduce moisture loss and thrives well under direct sunlight. It however contains cyanogenic
glucoside (HCN) which is a toxic chemical that is harmful to humans. Most edible varieties are sweet (<100

The African yam (Dioscorea rotundata) is another crop that may prove useful because it can grow in
extreme climatic conditions. It is important therefore that we encourage farmers to increase planting of
these around their homes using best farming practices like mulching and composting.

have an advantage over the traditional staple crops because after harvest and drying they can be stored
for later use. These along with NARI released early maturing sweet potato varieties and other short-term
vegetable crops like pumpkins (Cucurbita moschata), aibika (Abelmoschus manihot), beans (Vigna
unguiculata), amaranthus (Amaranthus spp.) and karakap (Solanum americanum) are useful crops to plant
after droughts to quickly re-establish household food supply in the affected communities while they wait for
the more long duration staple crops to mature.

Food plants gathered from the wild like choko leaves (Sechium edule), sago, marita, tulip, swamp taro
(Cyrtosperma chamissonis) and many more that are extremely useful during droughts. Sago can be stored
but lack of water during a drought often affects processing. Some may survive under the protection of the
forest but can also be destroyed by bush fires. The coconut remains the most extremely useful nut during
dry periods, as a source of healthy and nutritious drinking water and a source of food.

Wild animals, fish and other marine foods from the sea and mangrove habitats are also an alternate food
source. Lastly, processed food from supermarkets and canteens such as rice, tinned meat, tinned fish,
dripping and flour contain protein and energy providing valuable supplements to diets of those who can
afford them during droughts.

A4 sized, portfolio posters on the various drought coping strategies, information bulletins on Climate
Change and Drought and open-pollinated corn seeds were provided to representatives of the ten
Community Based Organizations after the awareness workshop at Afore station.

7.2.5 Basic information on the concept of food security

According to Bourke (2000), food security is high if people have access to land and can grow most of their
food requirements and who also have access to cash income to buy food during periods of food shortage.
The most resilient production systems are the diversified systems where a wide range of food crops are
grown either on their own or integrated with cash crops, fruit and nut species, multi-purpose tree species
and even with livestock. A good example of a resilient production system is the one practiced by the Tolais
in East New Britain Province. There you find the hardier food crops like triploid bananas (ABB groups) and
singapo taro grown interspersed with various types of fruit and nut species and perennial greens under
coconut plantations. In addition to this, each family may have a block of cocoa and other food gardens
located in the foothills of the Baining Mountains in secondary and virgin rainforest. Here the tripioid
bananas, singapo taro and leafy greens like kalava (Ormocarpum orientale) and Valangur (Polyscias
verticillata) which are perennial, hardier and require less maintenance can withstand minor droughts and
act as a permanent source of reserve food. The other staple crops like sweet potato, cassava, taro are
planted in the main food gardens with vegetables. Some of these crops especially vegetables and peanuts
are grown for sale at markets. In this production system the peopie are not only able to produce food for
themselves but also produce and sell copra and cocoa to generate cash income which they can use to
purchase store food to supplement their dietary needs. Food and nutritional security can also be enhanced
if people are looking after livestock or able to extract food for consumption and sale from the environment
like choko leaves from the forest or mud crabs from the mangrove habitats. However, the harvesting of
such resources need to be properly monitored to prevent over harvesting. Lastly any food that can be
stored like sago, and rice and flour from the store would definitely boost the food security situation in
places where they are consumed.

Under the Rainforest Literacy (RFL) Program, there is the Script Writing Workshop. It is the

that encompass issues/difficulties/problems fromand for the communities of the Managalas

theatre scripts to perform from, thus relaying the discussion points both from flip charts and
theatre performance.

The 2011 Script Writing Workshop was held on the Plateau, Zone 5, Ugunumo Village. This
2011 Script Writing Workshop is that from which came the second involvement of the
Theatre Group ~ Kuaefienami Theatre Group.

Participants were the Theatre Group, Zone Facilitators, Activity Coordinators, some CBO
Managers, the translation groups (BNEA/EBI), the MDF Staff and two PWM Staff.

started with /dentifying the topics. Four topics were identified (some from the 2010
Combine Forum) and then arranged the participants into four groups to produce a story for
each topic. From the stories, we were than tasked to identify the /earning objectives while
the theatre got the stories to compile the script for the drama. From the learning
objectives. we identified the trigger questions from which communities would use to
answer the issues from Clan Group Discussions, Zone Forum and the culmination at the
Plateau Wide Combine Forum,

PURPOSE

The Script Writing Workshop, as mentioned above, is to identify the issues/topics, in
addition to the ones from the Plateau Wide Combined forum, and that from which scripts
are compiled. From the scripts we extract: 1) Learning objectives and 2) Trigger Questions

for each topic identified.
From the stories we compiled learning materials in the form of flip charts/shell books and

the same materials are used by the theatre groups to write scripts and perform plateau wide

dramas.
The learning objectives and trigger questions are catalyst that raise community
understanding and discussions in trying to find strategies to address the shared issues on the

plateau.

PROGRAM: Conservation
ACTIVITY:. CA Border Patrol & Zone Boundary Mapping

INTRODUCTION

Zone Boundary Mapping & Conservation Area (CA) Border Patrol were combined activities
undertaken within the given timeframe of two weeks for this 2™ field trip. This follows after
informing beforehand the zones concerned (2, 3, 5 & 6) regarding their Boundary Mapping and
informing Kingsford Nichoi on the continuations of the CA Border patrol.

This particular report will encompass these two activities as implemented by the Conservation
Planning Coordinator (CPC) & the Conservaticn Support Cfficer (CSO) with the assistance from
Zone CBOs concerned, Kingsford and the 3 most cheerful strong young men as carriers. These
activities mostly invelved hiking ridges and steep mountains especially the interior and the exterior
of the Managalas Proposed Conservation Area (MPCA) and also to meet with the concerned
communities which wouldn’t be accomplished if it wasn’t for the assistance. Apart from these
activities, we were also able to moniter the progress of the Pogani reforestation programme and
continue to carry out awareness while there for talks with the Pogani Community
leaders/Chiefs/eiders on CA border patrol.

PURPOSE

|. Zone Boundary Mapping
The primary purpose of this activity is to map out the internal Boundaries of the Managalas

Proposed CA (MPCA) that is divided into their +: Cultura! zones. Because of the vastness and the
physical geography of the area, there were only 4 zones selected for a start this year i.e. zone 2, 3
(East) 5 & 6 (West)

ll. CABorder Patrol

The Purpose of this activity is to patrol the villages inhabiting the fringes as well as the villages that
directly border with the Proposed CA. This is basically to find out the status of the Proposed
Boundary line of the Conservation Area in terms cf having meetings with the Paramount
Landowners/leaders/elders/spoxesperson and coming to a consensus. It is entirely their decision to
either extend the boundary to inciude them within the CA or vice versa.

METHODS/PROCEDURES

These 2 activities were planned to be implemented within the timeframe of 2 week. Given the
timeframe to implement the different activities over the vast physical Geography cf the Managalas
Plateau, the strategy undertaken was assigning the Zone CBOs to carry out Zone Boundary
Mapping while the PwM officers with the assistance from Kingsford and his local youths to

=== page 3 ===
implement the CA Border Patrol. A table in the attachment will show the schedule undertaken to
implement the activities.

CA Border Patrol
The CA Border patrol was more a continuation from where Kingsford Nichoi has started last year

when he was the Conservation Officer on the ground for Managalas Development Foundation
(MDF). He and his team have done the first leg of the Border Patrol from Tetebedi to parts of Musa
and down to Bareji where he finally stopped. Hence, this time, it was from Sigara to Siana and all
the way down to Pogani. This was basically to conduct meetings in those areas as stated above
respectively to find out the status of the CA boundary mark.

RESULTS
Unfortunately, PwM officers only met up with the Zone CBOs of 5 & 6 while zone 3 & 4 never
showed up due to reasons unknown. With concerns of the time limitation, the team decided to go
ahead with the Zones in the East to implement their Zone Boundary Mapping.

In addition, the 3D Model of the Managalas Plateau display was used to visually point out the zones
concerned whereby the Zone Managers were able to point out their Zone Boundaries. In doing so,
it helped out to identify the areas to collect the coordinate points when using the GPS.

The PwM officers were able to teach the basics on how to collect the Coordinates and note it on
their exercise books for the record. Then we left them to take on the task of getting the GPS
points.

For the CA Border Patrol, it was a team made up of 2 Pw officers (Patrick & 1), Kingsford and 3
local youths that implemented this particular activity. We patrolled over steep snountain ridges,
crossed rivers, waterfalls to get to Sigara & Siana. Even our last leg to Pogani was quite exhausting
because we had to walk on pebbles & unsteady, rough surface rocks just by following the river
channels downstream until we reached Pogani Wara Buum.

There were only 2 meetings held at Siana village and Pogani village. Yhe elders/chiefs from Siana &
Sigara attended the meeting while the same was done in Pogani as well.

In the attachment is the 2 separate meeting minutes fer Siana & Pogani respectively. However,
here are the outcomes of the meetings respectively;

1) The Siana Chief has expressed their concern now that they have reaiised the threats they are
facing in terms of ongoing illegal logging and the proposed Oro Bay township extension to include
their land into the proposed CA. In consensus were the Chief and spokesman for the other 2 clans
of Avaora and Marareja from these 2 villages that border with the Siana chief's Land Boundary as
they are all for Conservation.

2) As for the Pogani Peopie, it is a different story were they are mostly confusing PwM werk with
other NGC who have came before such as Conservation Meianesia that left with a bad record,
Aixer all, it was ali a misunderstanding so it was all discussed and made clear during the meeting.
Hence, ai! their chiefs, elders, community leaders decided to make aware PwM’s work and most
importantly with the information that they have obtained from the discussion would help settle
their land issues. it will be discussed further below.

=== page 5 ===
RECOMMENDATIONS & DISCUSSIONS

For the Zone Boundary mapping, it was implemented as tasked by the zone CBO managers of 5 & 6
of East and the coordinate points were provided to Patrick to produce the internal Boundary
mapping. Gradually overtime, all the zones within the MPCA will be covered.

The meetings that were conducted during the CA border patrol had the common concern for
LAND.

In the case of the Sigara and Siana villages, they share land Boundaries and the fact that all of
Mitataora Clan of Sigara‘s land are within the MPCA while three Clans (Uera, Marareja and Apaora)
of Siana have only part of the land within the MPCA. We did not have to go that far because they
have seen for themselves the damages that are already been done by the ongoing illegal logging
and they face yet another development threat of Oro bay Township and potential prospecting of
mineral resources on their land. With all these that is happening around, the only way is to
safeguard their resources and their environment as a whole.

Action Points

1. It is only considerate that Siana people’ s part of their land on the outer CA boundary be
included as it is a gain to protect as much as possible a bigger landmass of forest area.

2. The Siana and the Sigara people still need Environmental awareness to strengthen &
extend the work of CA. Also to empower the community to mobilise in terms of making
well informed decisions to combat development threats.

3. The Zone CBO responsible (that would be zone 6) must be able to reach out to these
isolated people in terms of information sharing, update on CA work and awareness etc...

For the Pogani people, the misconception of NGO’s work was labelled the same all across whereby
PwM’s work was confused with Conservation Melanesia’s work (CM). CM’s reputation left behind
was not all that good when it ceased work on a particular area on the Plateau. It created an
opportunity for someone smart enough to show invalid documents to the ill informed community
to extend logging into parts of Pogani area. The worst part from information gathered so far is that
PwM proposed CA map was used to falsely claim land rights with support from an expired CM
WMA certificate. Hence, it has created a situation where they see our presence as a threat to them.
Through the meeting, everything was being clarified including our Organisation’s profile and our
work, the initial CA Map and the CA process. The response we got was mixed when we touched the
topic of CA boundary. Hence, now that the pogani chiefs, elders and community leaders are better
informed, they are able to disseminate the correct information to the pogani community. Apart
from this activity, reforestation was monitored as well and it seems that it all comes down to the
issue of land.

INTRODUCTION

The emphasis on Management Plan is very vital for the sustainability of the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area. On that note, Workshops were conducted to train & educate the Managatas
community to prepare to take on the responsibility of the core Management team where it is required
of them as stated in the Conservation Areas Act 1978. As principa! stakehoiders in the whole
conservation process, it is compulsory that the targeted groups within the community need to
undergo these workshops to understand what is required of them and in doing so, they are able to
consensually develop the Management Plan & appoint the people that will fully represent the
community based on sound & fair judgment guided by the terms & conditions required under the Act
to implement the Management Pian at the community level. In saying this, apart from other
Workshops, Management Plan Workshop itself was conducted firstly in 2004, followed by 2008 then
in 2011 and now is the 4 time, this workshop has been run.

Now looking at all the 3 past workshops, it has beer noticed that, there were no evaluation done after
each workshop so as to keep track of the information transfer to the participants in terms of
enhancing their knowledge as the workshops progressed on. The fact that the Proposed Managalas
Conservation Area is yet to be declared and hence, it gave time to run the Management Pian
workshops ahead. However, the issue identified was not knowing exact'y if they (participants) have
really captured the contents of the workshoos. Thus, monitoring & evaluation on a smalier scale is a
vital component that has been missed out and so it was included in this fourth workshop. It has been
also emphasized strongiy at the Partners With Meianesians (PWM) Midterm planning that in order to
measure the success of your implementation of activities ‘s to moniter & evaluate not only at the end
of the year but at intervals after every individual activity. This is to try & fill in the gaps as much as
possibie to ensure the issues are kept et 4 minimum

PURPOSE

With this evaluation, it is more of a summary assessment for all 4 management Pian workshop held.
Simple Questionnaire was designed to evaluate & assess the expected cutcome of the 4 Workshops
and to make improvements where possible.

METHODS

The methods undertaken for this Evaluation was using Questionnaires to get the participants views,
also from observation and side talk as well. Previous Management Plan reports were also used to
assess the expected outcome if fulfilled and to identify the iccpholes.

=== page 13 ===
RESULTS

From the findings, this is a summary of results gathered so far
A) Management Plan Reports assessment

With the four reports, it looks as though most of the expected outcome were being fulfilled beginning
with the introduction of the management plan concepts & guidelines in 2004 with conservationist
Philip Holden then in 2008, Jacinta Mimigari facilitated and the participants came up with the draft
Management Plan after identifying the environmental issues on the plateau. The third workshop was
a team effort of PWM team that went in to continue from where the (2° Workshop) stopped at and
the participants came up with the proposed Rules and penalties & CA Committee proposed
management implementation structure. They have also identified the stakeholders who will be in the
CA Committee as well. So with the forth MP workshop, it was also a follow up workshop in which the
rules and their penalties had to be looked at properly in order to finalize it into the documentation,
The roles & responsibilities of a CA committee had to be understood as well and the CAMC members
need to be confirmed too.

B) Questionnaires

Now the Questionnaires try to capture the participants especially when the facilitators know already
who their participants are and the fact that it is a follow up workshop.

Questions 1 & 2

=== page 16 ===
Discussion

Based on the reports, Questionnaires and also observation, this results show very interesting facts
that can be pointed here. With this evaluation, there were challenges encountered during these
analysis, however, there is enough facts to guide this evaluation process.

Management Plan Workshop Reports

From the top, from al! the Workshop reports, the expected outcomes were gradually produced in
terms of drafting the Conservation Management Plan with contents of identifying their environmental
issues and countering it with Land use Plan that captures all activities regulated by the rules/laws
consisting of modern & traditional concepts combined together that is applicable up in the Managatas
Piateau. The participants were able to propose the CA implementation structure with the identified
key stakeholders who will make up the CA committee members. Even from the beginning, the
required participants to attend this workshops is particularily tne zone CBO managers (community
representation) and the Ward Councilors ( Government representative at the community local level)
as they will be acting as inter-phase of the impiementation process of actual the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Plan between all stakehoiders. Only in the 4 workshop, were most
of the agenda were on reviewing ali of the above especially the rules and its penaities, the prooosed
CA implementation structure and the committee members. The twc most important agendas within
this session was the CA Committees roles & responsibilities and Bottom up planning with emphasis
on the importance of involving the Ward & district clan that captures the conservation needs
especialiy to fund the Managaias Corservation Area Management when declared. A government
representative was there to stress on this point with regards to the protocols in place that enforces
the Management Pian to function.

Questionnaires

Now building on this, the questionnaires come into play in order to find out the practicality at each
zone level beginning with the participants’ consistency in attendance to the workshop as they were
follow up workshops. Some ciscoveries were made which looked at both facilitators and participants
as well so it will be interesting to discuss oa these.

Limitations

One of the challenges as the evaluator for this Vianagement Pian Workshops was te cesign a
simplified Questicnnaire that captures the realistic views of the participants that is in deptn to really
give an insight of their knowledge capacity and in terms of information dissemination to their
respective zone & ward levels. Because of the time factor, the questions were much in general,
however, as pointed above, those were the 2 most important objectives to assess from the feedback
given which wasn’t clarified at the top of the Questionnaire form. Other than that, observations
during the workshop did back up the evaluation process. There were only 40 copies made which in
fact were intended for the expected participants. So priority was given to the councilors and CBO
managers to answer the questions.

=== page 17 ===
Feedback assessment

When looking at the objectives of the Questionnaire, it was worked out that since the first question
was directed to the participants who attended the past workshops, they were the only ones required
to answer the first questions in terms of what they understood of the CA Management Plan after
attending all 4 workshops. From this also, the consistency of the participants were worked out to see
who were the regular attendees and as shown from table 1, only 10 were regulars while the rest were
all first time participants. Hence, from this result, it was later decided to cluster the participants into
two groups of one which is the regulars “PARTICIPANTS A” and first timers as “PARTICIPANTS B”

After assessing the feedback from PARTICIPANTS A, it can seen that the number of regular
participants seem to drop due to few reasons picked up along the way as they want results in terms of
declaration has taken awhile. The participants’ notion was that they wanted action to take place after
the concept was introduced and at the same time, to take them through the documentation of the
management plan. However, when the political hold up prolonged, it created loopholes for people to
lose interests and so they want some of the tangible benefits to eventuate. The longer it takes; people
tend to lose interests in the project all together so there needs to be applicable options to tighten the
loopholes

For the Participants B, although most of them are observers and the selected Rangers in each zone
which made up part of the increase of participants; it does give an overview of what people at each
zone level see this project. So from the results from table 3, it can be seen that majority had a fair idea
on the (i) roles & responsibilities, (ii) rules & penalties & (iii) CA implementation structure. The reason
being more time was spent on these three agendas with group discussions & activities that got
involved much of their participation. As for (iv) finalized CA Committees, they have their doubts on
who will truly represent their community in the Committee, hence, they were unsure and wanted
more time to be given for them to consensually decide in their respective zones who will represent
them. (v) Bottom up planning was stressed as a need for way forward to link the very marginalized to
the key service providers and so call for a separate workshop to go through it in detail.

Hence, looking at both groups, there are similarities however, for first timers, it's a new learning
experience for them and they are eager to learn more while the regular participants want visible
benefits that will motivate and practically apply their knowledge in their respective wards & zones.

=== page 18 ===
Action Plan

i.

The participants need to register and confirm their participation to PwM after a letter of invitation
is given out to attend a workshop. This will heip keep a record of the participants in terms of
follow up workshops.

In relation to the first point, to really monitor the participants in terms of information
dissemination to their respective zones, try to pay a visit to a zone after a workshop has been
carried out two weeks or three.

To tighten the loopholes; SLA’s must be strengthened to motivate them to take on conservation.
The SLA’s must be realistic that is applicable in that particular zone so that is sustainable.

Facilitation skills — it can be seen that one reason to keep the interest of the participants is looking
at it at the participants angie where facilitators need to assess their approach in facilitation and re-
adjust if one style does not work out. Some tips to consider;

i. Try paraphrase information in the handouts/sheets to be given with simplicity accompanied
with more visuals such as diagrams, charts, pictures etc... this is to jitustrate a point with
convincement

ii, It cam be very convincing if examples with visuals of similar situations to be used curing
worksnaps/trainings

iit. Try re-adjusting styie of aporoach of facilitation that does iess talking and more action in terms
of getting them involved from the heginning to the end such as doing 2 lot of activities.
This must be done by making them feel at ease to open up

iv. In between try to use energizer to keep them awake

v, Do a bit of practical by going outdoors & use their surrounding environment to illustrate a
point.

vi. Give opportunity to participants to share their experiences and learn from one & other and in
the event, point out the challenges they ‘ace and how they heve resoived them

vil. in terms of presentation, try to be brief, attractive and it covers the most important parts
resembling a ‘MIN! SKIRT’ as learnt from a facilitator in the Sub Regional Training.

vill. Always recap & stress a very important point as the workshop goes along such an example
was from observation was their fear of the rules & penalties with the land use plan seen as
permanent. However, it wes stressed during sessions that it is subject to review and can be
amended according to the outcome (5-3years}

This is long term recommendation; however, it’s brought forward as it is vita! in this regard. As we
know the challenge of breaking down science terminologies to the locals, it is best a simple
dictionary should be developed with descriptive definitions & illustrations.

=== page 19 ===
ry

It was a lesson learnt as the evaluator in terms of designing the Questionnaires.
i. The questionnaire must have a title, purpose and objectives in order to keep focus as guidelines

ii. The questionnaire must break down scientific terms into simple descriptive words in order for
the participants to give the answer you want.

It is very vital to include Evaluation at the end of every activity implemented.

Conclusion

This is an evaluation done by using a combination of techniques such as Previous Management
Workshop reports, Questionnaires and Observation during the 4'" Workshops. it has been seen
that it most effective to monitor and measure the success of an activity when an evaluation is
carried out at the end of an activity. It ensures to keep up with the pace and also to make
improvements if need be so it is a win win situation for both facilitators & the participants. Hence,
in future, it will best to include Evaluations in all work plan programs.

1 INTRODUCTION

The submission for declaration of the Managalas Plateau as a Conservation Area (The Act) under the
Conservation Areas Act was submitted by community representatives from the plateau with the support by
Partners with Melanesians (PwM) to the Minister for Environment & Conservation Hon. John Pundari in the
presence of Oro Governor, Hon. Gary Juffa and Member for Sohe. Thereafter as required under the Act
advertised in the newspaper in early 2013. The 90 day period for objection lapsed lapsed on 18 May 2013.
An objection letter dated 18 March, 2013 was sent to the Minister for Environment & Conservation by the
President of Afore Local Level Government, Hon. Douglas Garawa MPA on behalf of the landowners in the 18
wards of the Afore LLG. The Department has not responded to the objection letter by the President of Afore
Loca! Level Government to the Minister for Environment & Conservation although a draft response letter was
prepared during the year. No satisfactory reasons have been provided by the Department for the long de __in
responding to the objection ietter. One year has lapsed after the submission for declaration of the
Conservation Area was given to the Minister for Environment & Conservation on 8 November, 2012. As a
result the President of Afore LLG has stopped al project activities on the plateau until he receives the
response from the Department. This has affected properiy planning and funding arrangement for project
activities especially activities leading up to the official declaration of the Conservation Area after its approval

2. BACKGROUND

“ A PEACEFUL AND SELF RELIANT COMMUNUAL SOCIETY LIVING IN HARMONY WITH NATURE”

This is the vision of Managalas people through their duly constitution entity , the Managalas Development
Foundation (MDF). Can we work together to achieve this vision was at the center of discussions at the
Ugunomo Forum.

The Managalas plateau in Oro Province of Papua New Guinea harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora. And
more significantly the plateau is home to the Queen Alexendra Birdwing Butterfly, the world’s largest
birdwing butterfly which is listed on Appendix | of the CITES Convention and which is only endemic to Oro
Province of Papua New Guinea. The proposed Managalas Conservation Area covers 360,000 hectares of
pristine rainforest comprising lowland mountane forests and is also the water catchment area of the Popondetta
plains, The total population of the area is 18,000 under the Afore Local Level Government of the Ijivitari
District. The people live in 75 villages made up of 152 sub-clans with ten (10) tribal groupings and speak four
(4) dialects.

The people on the Managalas Plateau are well aware of the impacts of large scale environmentally destructive
projects like logging, mining and oil palm plantations. Having being working with international and national
NGO partners since the early 1990’s the area is now in the process of being designated as a conservation area
under the Conservation Areas Act of 1978. The Managalas people submitted the Managalas Proposed
Conservation Area Appiication to the Minister for Environment and Conservation on 8" of November, 2012.
As required under the Act, the public advertisement was placed in the newspapers (Post Courier) for
stakeholders to view and file any objections if any. The advertisement appeared in the Post Courier on 18
February, March 4, March 18, April 1, April 29 and finally May 13 2013. The 90 day period expired on 18
May 2013. The President of Afore Local Level Government, Douglas Garawa filed an objection in a letter
dated 18 March 2013 wherein he raised a lot of issues why the Minister should not make the NEC submission
for it to approve the CA declaration and for the proposal to be shelved until such time the Managalas people are
able to manage the project themselves. The Department to date has not officially responded to the objection
letter by the President of Afore LLG and no reasons have been given for this long delay in responding to the
objection letter and no reasons have been given by the Department for this long delay in responding to the
President’s objection letter..

PROJECT TITLE: LEGAL INTERVENTION FOR DECLARATION OF MANAGALAS
CONSERVATION AREA UNDER THE PNG CONSERVATION AREAS ACT

TASK/OBJECTIVE: To institute legal proceedings to force the Department of
Environment and Conservation to invoke provision of the Conservations Areas Act to
have the Managalas Plateau declared as a Conservation Area under the Act.

DURATION: Six (6) Months
PERSONNEL: Maximum two (2) Lawyers (one Senior and one assisting Counsel)

LOCATION: Port Moresby and Managalas Plateau, Afore Local Level Government area,
Oro Province.

INTRODUCTION

The Managalas Plateau is a raised valley lying between 600 — 2000 meters altitude
above the coastal plain of the Oro Province, Paupa New Guinea. It sits between the
Owen Stanley Ranges to the South and West, the Sibium Ranges to the south-east and
Mount Lamington and the Hydrographers to the north and east. The 360,000 hectares of
the Plateau encompass an extraordinary diversity of environment including alpine heath
at 3,800 meters, mountain and hill forest, savanna, anthropogenic grassland and gardens.

Like many of the mountainous mid-altitudes valleys of PNG, the Plateau is an area of
high quality agricultural land and relatively dense populations. The surrounding
mountains, by contrast, are generally infertile and little populated. Over 20,000 people
from around !50 clan groups live in over 70 village communities on the Managlas
Plateau. These are largely subsistence farmers and depend almost exclusively on the
environment for their livelihood. Five dialects are found on the plateau that together
makes up five broad languages (Barai, Namiai, Samoi, Omie and Ese).

The Managalas Plateau is relatively isolated and remote from urban PNG. It is linked to
the Oro Provincial Capital, Popondetta, by a poor quality for-wheel drive road and by
two airstrips as well as by foot-tracks. This allows limited sale of coffee and other
produce during dry conditions but high freight costs and poor maintenance prevent
regular trade. Government services are restricted to a number of community schools, a
top up school, two aid posts and a station and Health Centre at Afore. The Summer
Institute of Linguistics (SIL) introduced an adult literacy programme to the Plateau in
the 1960's and this has provided an important foundation for many of the development
processes now taking place on the plateau.

Over the past decade, a number of proposals for timber extraction, oil palm and mining
development have been presented to the Managalas Plateau. While welcoming the
opportunity for development, Managalas communities are actively opposing many of
these projects due to poor consultation with resource owners and the failure to guarantee
benefits or environmental! protection.

=== page 46 ===
The Managalas piateau in Oro Province harbours a diverse array of fauna and flora and
isand more significant is that the plateau is home to the Queen Alexendra Birdwing
Butterily, the world’s largest birdwing butterfly which is listed cn Appendix } of the
CITES Convention and which is only endemic to Oro Province. The proposed
Managalas Conservation Area encompasses the foothills of the Sibium Ranges to the
South-East, the Owen Stanley Ranages to the South-West. Owalama Ranages to the
West and Guava Ranges to the North-east and stretches to the lower plains of Orobay.
The area is 360,000 hectares of pristine rainforest comprising lowland mountane forests
and is also the water catchment area of the Popondetta plains. The total population of the
area is 18,000 under the Afore Local Level Government of the Ijivitari District. The
people live in 75 villages made up of 152 sub-clans with ten (10) tribal groupings and
speak four (4) dialects. The people are mainly subsistence farmers with main income
from organic Arabica coffee.

The people on the Managalas Plateau are well aware of the impacts of large scale
environmentally destructive projects like logging. mining and oilpalm plantations so
have been working with international and national NGO pariners since the early 1990's
to have the area designated a conscrvation arca under the Conservation Arcas Act of
1978. Their efforts have paid off when finaily on November 8 20!2. they presented a
submission together with the Governor for Ore, Mon. Gary Juffa to the Minister for
Environment & Conservation to have the area declared a conservation area (refer to
attached newspaper article). While there are few steps before the National Executive
Council approves the submission to get the Governor General to declare the area a
Conservation Area as required under the law, this is a significant break-through for the
people of Managalas Plateau.

FIRST QUARTER SUMMARY REPORT

Date: 20.06.14

Climate Change and Community Reforestation

INTRODUCTION

Climate Change and Community Reforestation as the 4" Key Component strategy of PwM
programs is well into its 2° year of existence since included in 2013. With the ideal of
linking the gap of Conservation efforts holistically in its entire project sites, all its activities
have taken on a one step at a time approach. The very first activity under this component
started last year in 2013 was prioritized on information dissemination alone mainly on
Awareness raising in all its 3 sites and only an exception of Managalas project site local
CBOs underwent a Community Basic Climate Change Awareness Workshop to assist in
conveying the correct information to their respective communities. However, there is
more to be done in terms of Awareness raising and so it continues to be implemented this
year. Much of the activities has been revised in terms of its implementation timeframe.
There are number of factors that limit this program component which will be highlighted
further in summary and what has been done so far and what is yet to be done.

ACTIVITIES IMPLEMENTED SO FAR

As seen from the work plan, in terms of paper work and attending to meetings,
conferences and trainings were followed by two project field trips beginning with Inaina
to continue with the Community Awareness as an activity done in April from the 15" to
the 17” and the Karimui trip was taken in conjunction as a team with other Key
component programs in April also from the 22” tothe 28". With Karimui’s Case, it was
a planning trip hence, all PWM Key component programs were introduced with their work
plans for this year and hence, particularly for Climate Change and Community
Reforestation, Materials produced as Posters with Videos were left behind for PwM
project officer based in Karimui to work closely with Local CBO “KCRMP” to implement
the Awareness in August as planned.

Reports compiled followed after in May with the focus centered on World Environment
Day Event preparations lead up to June 5™ in liaison with other NGO partners and DEC

=== page 4 ===
bE

with OCCD. GEF concept paper was approved and Planning Grant was released by UNDP
to conduct Planning Workshop for inaina and Managalas/ Pogani respectively for
Community Reforestation project and SLA programs to develop a full proposal in which it
is in its final stage of polishing before submitting to UNDP. This is in support of its program
of Community Reforestation closely linked to Climate Change.

Notice that Managalas activities is currently on halt however, in July, the renewable

energy appropriate technology has been identified and will be delivered to the project site
Local CBOs for communities to utilize.

Overall, for project field implementation is only three (3) activities with one (1) for each
project site fer this year

1. Managalas —“ Research Energy Alternatives”
2. Inaina—“ Climate Change Community Awareness”

3. Karimui— “Climate Change Community Awareness”

FACTORS OF LIMITATION

1. Funding is only one donor (RFN) and its focus is on Conservation and it’s
supporting Key components of RFL, CB and SLA. However, this is justified with the
fact that more workload in terms of facilitating the 8 CA steps in the 3 project
needs more resources, effort and time. Based on past experience of many years of
PwM operation in rural communities, it needs stringent strategic approach hence
activities identified must be rationally chronologic which explains the approach of
one step at a time.

2. Compilation of Climate Change Database. ( recording and documentation) This is
one of the main challenge that is faced by many organization so as this is the first
for this component, Officer responsible is still in the process of researching and
collecting data within PwM library, internet and other resource books outside.

3. Establishing and strengthening Partnerships and Broaden Networks. This is very
important in this regard as in terms of collaborative effort through exchange of

information, co-financing and Technical expertise to address climate Change in all
project sites.

Conclusion

Nevertheless, all activities with its objectives in the 5 year master work plan still remains
however its timeframe is being revised accordingly. Hence, it needs support from other

relevant stakeholders to realistically specify the issues and link it with the compatible
Action plans in respective community's situation.

Project name: PWM Conservation and Sustainab!e Livet!heod Alternative Projects in Papua New Guinea

Organization: Partners With Melanesians Inc.
Project period: 2013 - 2017
Project purpose: PWM have three project areas therefore the following are the three main project purposes as per their project area

situations:

A. Managalas Conservation Area Project
Traditional landowners are empowered to be involved in any decision making related to planned development projects as well as playing an active role
in efforts to protect and utilize their local environment and its natural resources.

B. Karimui Proposed Conservation Area Project
Communities are empowered to conserve and develop their natural resources sustainably so that present generations will not compromise the

livelihood of future generations as well as realizing and maintaining their traditional cultural practices.

C. Inaina Proposed Wildlife Management Area Project
The local communities are empowered to participate in the protection and utilization of their natural resources as well as in any decision making in

relation to the development of their natural resources.

Has any of the 5-year expected results (outputs) been changed? If yes, please explain.

There are no major changes to the 5-year expected results (outputs). However with the late inclusion of Managalas Conservation Area Project work
plan activities and budget, there will be changes to work plan activities within the expected 5-year activities. These new activities in Managalas
Conservation Area Project were developed from the clan group discussion and the District Wide Combine Forum in August and December respectively

last year 2013.

However these new activities have being slotted into each programme areas for year 2014 where the expected 5-year results (outputs) remain the
same as per all programme areas.

=== page 10 ===
What upcoming events both on national and local level may affect the project during the coming year?

As per the national Papua New Guinea Calendar, there are no national and local level events that will have impacts or affect the projects during the
coming year 2014. However, in Managalas and Karimui, the open members of Parliament are facing election petition matters which might end up in

| courts of disputed returns where there is high hopes of by-elections in these two area. As for Inaina, the disputed open member seat was nullified by
the court of disputed returns last year and the electorate in Kairuku-Hiri are having their by-election which ended on the last week of January 2014. A
winner of this seat will be declared in the month of February, 2014.

Other comments relevant to the annual planning?

The only comments that PWM can provide will be the Managalas Conservation Area Project (MCAP) issues and problems that needs to be dealt with |
before the area can be declared as a Conservation in Papua New Guinea. PWM had no problem in submitting the Managalas Conservation Area
Project Application to the Minister for Environment and Conservation Hon. John Pundari in November, 2012. There was only one objection to the
application by the Afore Local Level Government (ALLG) President Mr. Douglas Garawa during the 90 days public advertisement for the public to
object. However it has taken more than a year for the Department of Environment and Conservation to respond to the objection by the ALLG
President,

Due to the prolong respond to the ALLG president by the Department of Environment and Conservation, the remaining 2013 half year activities were
suspended but only two activities were conducted by the Managalas Development Foundation and two of Managalas leaders. The first was in August
2013 as The Clan Group Discussion on the East and West of Managalas Plateau. The second was in December 2013 The District Wide Combine Forum.
Out from these only two activities, the ALLG President decline to attend as he wanted to know his objection respond from the Department of
Environment and Conservation.

However from the above two activities, the Managa!as Clan and Community ieaders developed their own annual activities and wanted PWM to take
the activities seriously so that Managalas Conservation Area Project can be declared as a Conservation Area as per CA Act 1976 in Papua New Guinea,
Therefore all activities below are the relevant annua! planning activities derived from their Clan Group Discussions and the District Wide Combine
Forum. PWM have agreed to consider these activites and allocate funds after prioritizing them in our first annua! pianning.

Allin all, with the inclusion of Managalas Conservation Area Project work plan activities for the year 2014, the other two project areas Karimui and
Inaina remain same with their work plan activities with slight changes of activities.

14) The International Trade of Endangered Species (Fauna and Flora Act (1978)
gives effect to the CITES and PNG is bound by its own Laws relating to
CITES and we are bound to take positive action to protect the QABB.

14)Despite four (4) biological surveys undertaken in the past by friends of the
Managalas plateau including the Department of Environment and
Conservation, the Science Faculty of the University of Papua New Guinea,
and Partners with Melanesia, there is a diverse array of fauna and flora of the
Managalas plateau that remain to be discovered and documented. Hence
having the area declared as a Conservation Area can allow further research
into the rich diverse ecosystems of the area.

Threats to Conservation & Sustainable Natural Resources use

15) The major threat on the environment and the forest ecosystems is from
agriculture; conversion of primary forests for both subsistence food production
and commercial cash cropping activities like growing coffee- undertaken by
the local communities to enhance human wellbeing.

16) There are potential threats from the private sector; especially companies who
are interested in industrial logging and mining in and around the proposed
conservation areas. Initially there was an intrusion and overlap with mining
Exploration Lease (EL 1547) but the boundary map has been adjusted
amicably between landowners, the Minerals Resources Authority, and the
Conservation Environment Protection Authority (CEPA) to allow mining
exploration activities to be undertaken outside the boundary of the proposed
conservation area.

17) Several industrial logging propositions have been made but landowners in
the conservation area have and are still objecting in preference over
conservation and small scale ecoforestry to meet local requirements including
housing, construction of schools and health centers.

Community Su apacity and Future Sustainabil

18) The Managalas communities were educated through a literacy program
through the University of Papua New Guinea since 1984 on the issues related
to the destruction of the natural forests and the biodiversity. As a result, all the
Managalas clan elders and chiefs agreed in at a public forum at zone 6
(Numba) in 1997 to have the entire Managalas plateau officially declared as a
conservation area to protect the habitat for the QABB and the forest for the
future generations.

19) The respective government agencies at the Provincial and Local level have
also given their support and endorsement on the declaration of Managalas
Conservation area; Oro Provincial Executive endorsement on 2” December
2008 followed by Afore Local Level Government endorsement on 8" June
2011.

20) At the invitation of the Managalas communities, the Partners with
Melanesians (PwM) a national Non- Governmental Organization (NGO) has
been working in the area since 1997 mainly in raising awareness and building
capacity with funding assistance from the Rainforest Foundation of Norway up

nF

=== page 3 ===
to present with a total expenditure of some PGK10 million. PWM Focal
Programs in the past had been;

Education, training and awareness

Scientific research, data collection and analysis
Support for alternative income earning options
Facilitate conservation area declaration

21) Notable achievements include education and awareness of local
communities, conservation commitment of 360,000 hectares; establishment of
base line socioeconomic and biological data; and establishment of a
community based organization for the area; the Managalas Conservation
Foundation (MCF) with its Board, management and 5 -year organizational
strategic plan.

22)There are some level of alternative income earning opportunities that have
been supported over the years for sustainable livelihood purposes especially
Arabica coffee at small holder level: and as it is one of the few areas in the
Southern region, it has huge potential for increased production and marketing
at premium prices with eco labelling.

23) There is also opportunity for eco-tourism, there is an initial plan to develop an
eco-tourism industry on the plateau under the Conservation Area and besides
that tracking along the famous Black Cat/Ghost Trail from Abau up into the
Owen Stanley Ranges to upper Musa round Dorobosoro and into Aiari, Suari
and into the Managalas plateau (the path used by the American soldiers in aid
of the Australians) at Kokoda is now in the pipe line and it is predicted that it
will be receiving visitors so employment opportunity and other spin-off benefits
will be tremendous for the area along the lines of Kokoda Trail.

24) A geographical, socioeconomic and biological profile of the proposed
Managalas Conservation Area is annexed to this NEC submission as “Annex
A’ that includes information on the people, biodiversity, people's commitment
and support for conservation area declaration.

25) PwM and the MCF are working together under an existing collaborative
partnership Memorandum of Understanding on the mobilization and joint use
of both financial and technical resources for the conservation area program.

26) Through an exit strategy PwM developed between PwM and MCF, all
management responsibilities will be handed over to MCF to maintain and
manage the proposed Conservation Area once declared.

27) In line with the National Protected Area Policy which the NEC approved in
2014 (NEC Decision No. 5/2014) that provides for sustainable financing for
protected areas, the NEC consider and approve the amount of K8 Million to
cover initial costs for the management of the Managalas Conservation Area.
These includes costs for developing the Management Plan for the
conservation area including land use plans, establishment of the Managalas
Conservation Area Management Committee, training of local rangers and
funding of sustainable income generating projects for the local communities in
each zones in the project area.

29) An Endowment Fund is investment fund set up by an institution or
organisation in which regular withdrawals from the invested capital are used
for on-going operations or other specified purposes. Sustainable financing is
required to pay staff, purchase equipment, engage with local communities,
conduct natural resource monitoring and enforce rules for the protected area.
The interest generated by the resulting investments provides financial security
for protected areas. Local communities in the area will benefit in the form of
jobs, training, sustainable income generation and development projects. This
is important due to the fact that the land where the protected area is
established are owned and controlled by customary clan groups which is
recognised by the PNG Constitution and relevant laws in the country.

30) In line with the Governments Public Private Partnership and outsourcing
policy consistent with Pillar 6 objectives of PNG Vision 2050, field
conservation area management and sustainability issues including education,
awareness and capacity building functions will be outsourced to Partners With
Melanesians and Managalas Conservation Foundation by the Government

3.0 LITERATURE REVIEW

3.1 General Background of Coffee Production
Coffee production in Papua New Guinea accounts for approximately 1% of the world production

according to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). After oil palm,
coffee is Papua New Guinea’s second largest agricultural export, employing approximately 2.5
million people.

Coffee is the highest foreign exchange earner for Papua New Guinea, the majority of which is
grown in the Eastern Highlands Province, the Western Highlands Province and Chimbu. With the
industry not derived on a colonial plantation based system, production is largely by small farmers
with land holdings that grow as little as 20 trees per plot in coffee gardens alongside subsistence
crops. Predominantly in isolated places, the product is mostly certified as “organic coffee”.

Coffee production in the country dates back to 1926 and 1927 when the first Jamaican Blue
Mountain Coffee seeds were planted. However, the Coffee Research Institute claims that coffee
was introduced to British Papua in 1890, although it is widely accepted that commercial production

3.4 Origin, Distribution and Uses

Coffee may have originated from Africa (Ethiopia esp. Arabica coffee) or South America. All species
are small trees (shrubs) and when left to grow, will reach a height of about 10m. Coffee is widely
cultivated and distributed throughout the humid tropics as a cash crop. Arabica coffee is important
in East Africa and is also cultivated in the highlands of Brazil as it prefers a cooler climate. Robusta
coffee is suited to production on lowland sites in the humid tropics and is extensively grown in
Brazil while Liberica coffee is grown in West Africa and Southeast Asia.

In PNG, only arabica coffee and robusta coffee are grown. Arabica is mostly grown in the highlands
and robusta is grown on the.coastal lowlands. P-oduction figures show that 95% of arabica and
only 5% of robusta are produced in PNG.

Like cocoa, coffee is used as a beverage. The relatively modern process is the preparation of
roasted coffee from the coffee seed. Other uses are masticatory (chewed as a stimulant) in Ethiopia
and can be fermented as an alcoholic drink.

3.5 The Coffee Industry in Papua New Guinea

3.3.1 A Brief History of Coffee in. Papua New Guinea
It is generally accepted that coffee was first introduced into the Pacific area in the late 18" century

by Dutch sailors. The first official record of its introduction to PNG is a note in the Annual Reports
of British New Guinea of coffee being planted in “a small botanical garden”. This same source
advised that by 1892 the crop was thriving in the Rigo district and that extensive plantings had
been established in the Sogeri area by 1898. Cartlege makes mention of the first research being
carried out by these pioneers. They were experimenting with direct planting of seed in the field.

Up to 70 hectares of coffee growing in the Papua area in 1908 with an export value of $915 in 1905
and 1908. Cartlege notes that the reports refer to at least three plantations in the Sogeri area and
that implementing of rubber with coffee was practiced. It is also reported that coffee was being
cultivated in Oro Province in the vicinity of Sangara with as much as 73 tons being produced in
1940.

The first plantings on New Guinea side were made by the New Guinea Department of Agriculture
close to Wau in 1928 and 1929. Coffee seed was first introduced into the highlands region by
Lutheran Missionaries in the pre-war years, this seed being taken from planting at the Dregerhafen
and established on their mission station at Asaroka in Eastern Highlands and Ogelbeng in Western

8.0 DISCUSSION

The outcome of the activity was a success in marketing of the Managalas Organic Coffee from the East
zones (Kawowoki, Afore and Yoivi) all the way to Lae, Morobe Mountain Coffee Mill. It took almost 4
months to actually get results from the activity implemented. From the initial baseline information given by
Mr. Damien Ase, to the primary data collection at the plateau, to the actual implementation of the activity,
it was a very challenging task especially for a new employee of the organization.

The main idea was to help the farmers access a better market price other than the price they got from the
road buyers. The road buyers normally paid K1-K2 per kilo for the parchments and provide their own
container for shipment to the mills in Lae or as far as Goroka and Mt. Hagen, however, from the local
community's perspective, this wasn’t a fair price given to them. Hence Partners With Melanesians Inc. had
to take the initiative to help its local NGO on the plateau, The Managalas Conservation Foundation in
facilitating the process of the coffee marketing from the plateau all the way to the Morobe Mountain
Coffee mill in Lae.

A total of 286 organic coffee bags (brown bean) were collected from the three (3) zones weighing about
10854 kg. Zone 7A gave 86 bags, 78 gave 39 bags and Zone & gave 161 coffee bags, a total of 286 organic
coffee bags. The transport in the plateau was met by PWM in the hire costs as well as materials. After all
286 coffee bags were collected; the logistics in Oro Bay was arranged as mentioned in the methodology.

In Lae, the CBC representative and the SL¢ Officer both did arrangements fiom transport, logistics to the
dischargirg of the 20 foot coffee container at the Morobe Mountain Mill. The negotiations of the payments
were done by the CBO representative (Mr. Peter Sokane) and the Mill Manager vehich was agreed that
within 10 days the payments would be deposited into Partners account, however, it took 2months for the
payments to be done. This was;

INTRODUCTION

The trip started as scheduled during planning on the aforementioned date. The Project Manager and
the reputable vanilla trainer from the Highlands Vanilla Project Ltd- Mr. Mark Gozapao, was
flown from Goroka to Port Moresby on the 18" October, 2018 to conduct the training. He was
advised to come to the office to sign the standard Short Term Engagement contractual agreement,
as well as introducing himself to PWM PM and MCF PD upon the arrival and he did as was told.
We were scheduled to travel to Popondetta the next day. which is the 19" October, 2018 but it was
a troublesome flight and was thus cancelled. Consequently, all passengers booked for this flight
were advised to check in early the next morning — Saturday, 20" October, 2018.

We arrived at 7:00 am in Girua airport (Popondetta) and were met by Managalas Conservation
Foundation SLA Coordinator- Mr. Ezekiel Garui with the vehicle intended for hire and we all went
straight io SHU Guest House. All funds allocated for food and other prioritized activities to conduct
the training were given to Ezekiel while Mark and I refreshed ourselves as we woke up very early
in the morning to board the plane.

PURPOSE

The purpose of this trip was to conduct Quality Vanilla Training for the vanilla farmers at the
plateau. Apparently, vanilla is a new commodity recently introduced to the farmers in Managalas
Plateau and hence, through the collaboration of Partners with Melanesians (PWM) and Managalas
Conservation Foundation (MCF). we've decided to engage aforesaid trainer with extensive
experience in this commodity to conduct Quality Assurance Training. The significant purpose of
conducting this training is to enhance our vanilla farmers” production shrewdness; so that they can
be able to produce quality vanilla beans that can be marketable at international markets for prudent
income generation henceforth.

The training was scheduled from Monday-26" to Friday- 30" October, 2018 at Basabe Village,
Afore Station.

DISCUSSION

¢ Discuss the program activities scheduled in the reporting period been carried out as
per the work plan

All planned activities were executed as projected prior to the travel. We arrived at the venue a day
carlier and went over to assess things to ensure everything was prepared as anticipated. During the
venue visitation on Sunday afternoon- 21“ October, 2018- we had a chat with the local village
councilor — Cr. Mathew and he was overwhelmed with exhilaration as it would be the first time his
village ( Basabe village) to host such trainings. He was appreciative indeed for given such an
opportunity to host the training and gave us assurance to involve his community to assist us to
ensure the training progress successfully in the next 5 days.

Monday-22"" October 2016

All participants assembled in the training venue at 8:00 am to commence training. The expected
number of participants were 30, however, stupendous increment of 20 additional participants
increased the number 50 participants. Consequently, the training venue was overcrowded, causing
difficulties for the participants to move around during group discussions. Therefore, group
discussions were called-off to avoid this quandary. The unregistered participants who cannot not be
able to find the space inside the hut were seen standing at the verandah and some were standing
outside while listening and taking notes of what’s been said.

#1)

Pic 7 & ¥- Showing the number of participants and how crowded the training room was. Some even sit on the stairways and
verandah while determined ones site on the window frames taking notes and listening to the facilitator.

During the morning part of the session after the introduction, Mr. Gozapao he went straight to the
first part of the session; VANILLA, IT’S ORIGIN & the CURRENT GLOBAL ECONOMIC

13

=== page 4 ===
POWER. Mr. Gozapao’s intention of highlighting these points was to motivate farmers to cultivate
and produce healthy beans required and recommended by international vanilla marketing board.
Moreover, he reiterated on the importance of the training and underiying reasons requiring all
farmers to produce healthy pods.

Tuesday 23"° October, 2018

On the above mentioned date, he emphasized profoundly on:

a) Site Selections (Ideal soil structures and desirable topographies)
b) Planting Methodologies ( Direct Planting & Nursery Planting)

c) Mulching ( how to make quick and effective way of providing nutrients
d) Field Management:-
i. Looping and Tipping Methods
ii. Pollination ( fastest way- newly introduced)
iii. | Flower Tipping to prompt vanilla plant to produce flower as quick as convenient
iv. Convenient way of bean pruning
e) Harvesting Pod- how to identify the matured pods awaiting harvesting.

Wednesday 24" October, 2018

On Wednesday, the farmers were all taken to the nearby vanilla garden for practical. All
techniques learnt during the theory sessions in the past 2 days were precisely demonstrated out
on the field and all participants were certainly enthralled. Many showed satisfaction when the
trainer overtly put into practice what were said and the participants erudite the information very
well.

During the practical session, Mr. Gozapao also exhibited the proper and required procedures
widely used in mulching, pruning, fastest and effective way of pollinating and budding to exhort
the plant to sprout flowers at early stage. This process was recently introduced to enable cach
vanilla plant to produce more beans within a shorter period of time to increase productivity.
Undoubtedly, the participants were fascinated with the techniques they learned from Mr.
Gozapao during the practical and thus showed contentment.

After the field visit, all participants were urged to walk back to the training venue to complete
the afternoon session. The afternoon session was all about questioning and answering of
questions to eliminate vague issues that transpired during practical and theories in regard to
topics covered thus far.

| Thursday- 25" October, 2018 |

The morning session was basically a recapitulation of all topics covered thus far to ensure the
participants amply understands that were covered. Many questions were raised and were all
answered satisfactory before the lunch.

After the lunch, the participants prepared firewood, water and other compulsory items to commence
practical on KILLING & DRYING PROCESS. The practical was done right in the village and
even none participants came to observe and certainly learned some skills on how to prepare the
harvested pods and convert them to A grade beans. He further displayed the storage techniques after
the killing process to preserve its charming aroma as it plays significant role in grading during the
sales as well.

After ending the demonstration re the killing and storage process, the participants went back to the
training room for last session. Thirty questionnaire sheets containing 15 simple questions all written
in pidgin were delivered to all participants to fill regarding the training as part of the assessment.

When collecting the questionnaires, it clearly reveals that participants understood all lessons taught
in the last 3 days. However, the only concern raised was for such training to be conducted twice in

S6

=== page 7 ===
the plateau as many farmers are concurrently into vanilla cultivation. When each participant was
asked to disclose the number of vanilla tress in their gardens, I was amazed to discover that almost
80% of the participants exceeded 100 plus trees. Hence, vanilla would inevitably be another major
cash crops apart from coffee. Subsequently, it is foreseen that if the local farmers produce quality
beans by following all standardized procedures disseminated by the trainer, vanilla will
undoubtedly supersede coffee by becoming the major cash crop for substantial income generation
due to its exceptional global price per kg.

No major hindrances or problems encountered during the training. The only notable problem was
the capacity of the training venue unable to sustain the number of participants. Nevertheless, this
didn’t hinder interested and unregistered participants from listening and taking notes during the
training from the outside of the hut.

RESULTS/FINDINGS

I cannot summarize on the result and the finding at this time. Therefore, | need to take another trip
March 2019 to Managalas purposely to visit vanilla gardens in the plateau and to see if there were
new gardens made after the training and to see the final produce ready for market. As per Mark
Gozapao, a requirement for a bean to be graded as A grade are:

U 1Scm( +) in length

(ii) Black in colour

(iii) Produces strong vanilla odour

(iv) All beans straight and not curvature

Having the above rudiments as prerequisite for assessment, it'll be more convenient for me to visit
the gardens and the beans harvested and are ready for sell. After undertaking the filed visit, I will
compile a comprehensive summary for all to glance through and comment should deemed
necessary as part of the conclusion of this reporting.

CONCLUSION

Vanilla is an expensive commodity and hence its price per kilogram has already enthused a lot of
farmers to venture into vanilla cultivation. Affirmatively, in the next few months, | am anticipating
a lot of new vanilla gardens to emerge in the plateau inevitably.

During the training, the local farmers realised that coffee requires a lot of odd jobs but the
remuneration package after selling doesn’t value the amount of job entailed during the processing.
Likewise, the cost involves in transporting this commodity to the nearby market is also excruciating
for low and average income earners. Despite vanilla warrants skills, placidity, commitment and
concentration to produce prudent outcomes, when evaluating its transportation cost with the coffee,
vanilla isn’t troublesome. Hence, is another advantageous attribute that will induce the farmers to
venture into it,

The training was well conducted and all participants were satisfied. However, most of them
proposed for MCF/PWM to arrange for another training for those farmers who missed out on this

one.
Highlands Vanilla Project also assures farmers of buying their product using the current price

henceforth.

=== page 8 ===
RECOMMENDATION

Highlands Vanilla Project to conduct another training somewhere in Koruwo Ugunomo, or Koeno
in 2019 as per the farmers’ demand. During this proposed training, those farmers who ventured into
vanilla farming will also bring their beans to the trainer for grading and buying during the training.
Since Highlands Vanilla Project also involves in buying the beans, it is undoubtedly advantageous
for the vanilla farmers in Managalas Plateau because the trainer will also became their buyer

simultaneously.

committee members. The trip was planned for in collaboration with CEPA to jointly
fund the implementation of the activity. Letters were prepared by MCF Project

with the four representatives from Managalas whom will represent the LOs in the CA
comnnittee.
